p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: Before you can research well, you have to know where answers are likely to live. That means understanding how the U.S. legal system is structured and what primary sources of law govern. Think of this chapter as the map you study before the trip. Every research question you ask in this course eventually lands on one or more of the primary sources described here, and knowing how those sources relate to one another is what lets you make smart decisions about where to look. A researcher who does not understand the hierarchy of authority cannot tell a source that settles a question from one that merely informs it, and will burn time reading material that could never control the outcome. This chapter is also the ground the Question Method stands on. When Chapter 3 asks you to write a research question and choose the source most likely to answer it, the choice will come from the US legal structure you are about to study. Learning Objectives Identify the sources of primary legal authority in the United States Describe how the law on a single topic can come from an overlapping set of constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, and case law Use the structure of the U.S. legal system to plan your research Distinguish mandatory (controlling) from persuasive authority in a given jurisdiction Apply the hierarchy of legal authority to determine which source governs a particular issue

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: The United States has a federal system, which means governing power is shared between the federal government and the states. Each level has its own constitution, its own legislature, its own agencies, and its own courts. The law itself comes from a handful of primary sources: constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, and treaties. Knowing what each one is, and what each one can and cannot do, is the first step toward knowing where to look for an answer. Constitutions set up the structure of government, define the limits of government power, and guarantee individual rights. A constitution is the supreme law of its jurisdiction, so any other law that conflicts with it is invalid. The U.S. Constitution structures the federal government and, through the Fourteenth Amendment and the doctrine of incorporation, also limits much of what state governments may do. Each state also has its own constitution, supreme within that state so long as it does not conflict with federal law. Statutes are laws passed by a legislature, such as the U.S. Congress or a state legislature. Once enacted, they are first published as a standalone document called a slip law . They are later gathered chronologically and published in bound volumes called session laws . Then they are organized by subject into collections called codes, like the United States Code for federal law. A statute is the considered, generally applicable judgment of the elected legislature, and it can create rights, impose duties, prohibit conduct, and set up entire regulatory schemes. Regulations are rules created by government agencies, like the Environmental Protection Agency or the Department of Labor, under authority a statute delegated to them. Regulations fill in the technical detail that statutes leave to the agencies. A statute might direct an agency to set “safe” exposure limits for a workplace chemical; the regulation supplies the actual number. Properly adopted regulations carry the force of law. Case law is the body of published judicial opinions.When an appellate-level judge writes and publishes an opinion, that opinion generally becomes part of the law, binding future lower courts in the same jurisdiction under the doctrine of stare decisis . (There is some nuance here that you’ll find covered in Chapter 5 .) Some case law is common law , rules courts created where no statute governs. For example, much of tort law comes from judicial decisions alone. The rest of case law interprets and applies constitutions, statutes, or regulations. Treaties are formal agreements between the United States and foreign or tribal nations. Once ratified, a treaty has the force of federal law and can preempt conflicting state law or older federal law.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
s: The Interplay of U.S. Legal Authorities
t: The U.S. legal system grew out of the English common law tradition, where law developed case by case through judicial decision. Over time, legislatures began codifying areas of law, which produced the modern dual structure of judge-made and legislatively enacted law. A few domains, like negligence, defamation, contract formation, and much of property law, remain governed mostly by common law because their principles are flexible and have been refined over centuries of judicial decision-making. Courts have proven better suited than legislatures to the incremental, fact-sensitive elaboration these doctrines need. Other areas, like environmental protection, securities regulation, tax, or immigration, demand comprehensive statutory frameworks and agency oversight, because they require uniformity, technical precision, and the ability to update rules as circumstances change. In practice, most modern legal issues pull in all three at once: statutes set the framework, regulations supply the detail, and case law interprets and applies both. Because power is split between federal and state governments, a single issue might be governed by federal law, state law, or both, depending on the subject. It might also involve statutes, case law, and regulations at one or both levels at the same time. An employment dispute, for example, might implicate a federal statute (Title VII), federal regulations (EEOC rules), federal case law interpreting both, a parallel state anti-discrimination statute, and a state common law claim like wrongful discharge, all together. So, as you research, you have to keep all of the authorities that might apply in view. This is one reason secondary sources (Chapter 4 ) are so useful early on. They can describe the whole landscape of an area and point you to the relevant authorities, which saves you from tracking them all down yourself and protects you from the dangerous assumption that the first source you find is the only one that matters. These sources also act on each other. Statutes create agencies, which then write regulations. Courts interpret both statutes and regulations, and they fill gaps with common law where no statute applies. Courts can strike down regulations they find invalid, and legislatures can pass new statutes that override a court’s reading of a statute. Courts can also strike down statutes that conflict with the Constitution. The result is a moving system in which authority is constantly being created, interpreted, revised, and occasionally invalidated. Examples of complex areas of U.S. law: Environmental regulation. Congress passes the Clean Air Act (a statute). The EPA writes emissions standards under that Act (regulations). Courts interpret the statute and the regulations when disputes arise (case law). No single source tells the whole story; the rule that governs a particular smokestack emerges only from reading all three together. Tax law. In Rowan Companies, Inc. v. United States , 452 U.S. 247 (1981), the Supreme Court struck down Treasury regulations that interpreted “wages” inconsistently for different tax purposes. Congress responded by amending the Internal Revenue Code through the Social Security Amendments of 1983 to allow exactly the differentiation the Court had rejected, effectively reversing the decision through new legislation. It is a textbook illustration of the legislature having the last word over a court’s reading of a statute. Constitutional law. In Texas v. Johnson , 491 U.S. 397 (1989), the Supreme Court struck down a law criminalizing flag burning, holding that it was symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment. Here the court had the last word, because the conflict was between a statute and the Constitution rather than between a court and a legislature over a statute’s meaning. This constant interplay is why you always have to check that your authority is still valid. A statute you plan to cite might have been struck down by a court. A case you want to rely on mi

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: Not all primary authority carries the same weight, and two distinctions decide most of it. Primary versus secondary. Primary authority is the law itself: constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, and treaties. Secondary sources explain, interpret, or analyze the law, but they hold no authority to bind government or citizen action. For research, secondary sources are usually where you start and primary authorities are usually where you end. Sort it The law itself, or writing about the law? A section of the Arizona Revised Statutes on a landlord’s duties Primary Enacted text from a legislature is the law itself. A regulation in the Code of Federal Regulations Primary A properly adopted regulation carries the force of law. Ranking below its statute does not make it secondary. A law review article analyzing a recent line of cases Secondary One scholar’s analysis, however persuasive, is commentary on the law. A United States Supreme Court opinion Primary The court is deciding the law, not describing someone else’s account of it. A section of the Restatement (Second) of Torts Secondary Influential, and courts often adopt Restatement sections, but until a court does, it is the American Law Institute’s summary. An editor’s headnote printed above a judicial opinion Secondary The opinion is primary. The headnote is a publisher’s summary of it and is never the law. Binding versus persuasive. Binding (also called mandatory or controlling) authority is authority a court must follow; persuasive authority is authority a court may be influenced by but need not follow. An authority binds your court only when it comes from home: your jurisdiction’s own constitution, statutes, and regulations, the decisions of courts above yours in the same system, and the federal law that applies there. Everything else, including other jurisdictions’ primary authority, decisions of courts at the same level or below, and all secondary sources, is persuasive. Sort it Before the Arizona Court of Appeals, on Arizona contract law An Arizona Supreme Court decision on the issue Binding A higher court in the same system. An Arizona statute governing the contract term Binding Home-jurisdiction enacted law. A Ninth Circuit opinion predicting how Arizona courts would rule Persuasive A federal court’s reading of state law does not bind that state’s courts, however carefully reasoned. A New Mexico Supreme Court decision on identical facts Persuasive Another jurisdiction’s primary authority. It is law in New Mexico and an argument in Arizona. An Arizona Superior Court ruling on the same clause Persuasive A lower court in the same system cannot bind the court above it. A section of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts Persuasive Secondary sources never bind, unless and until an Arizona court adopts the section as Arizona law. Preemption. Under the Supremacy Clause (Article VI), federal law overrides conflicting state law in areas where Congress has constitutional power to act. Preemption can be express or implied; where federal law sets only a floor, states may be stricter. Whenever you research a state-law question in a federally regulated area, ask whether federal law preempts the state rule first. Put it in order A direct conflict, in a field Congress may regulate: which controls? Arrange these from the authority that prevails over all the others down to the one that yields to all of them. The U.S. Constitution Supreme over every other source, federal or state. A federal statute Valid under the Constitution, and supreme over state law under Article VI. A federal regulation Carries the force of federal law, but only within the statute that authorized it. A state constitution Supreme within the state, yet it yields to valid federal law, including a valid federal regulation. A state statute Must conform to the state constitution and to federal law. A state regulation Exists only by delegation from a state statute.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: Persuasion can also travel further than a single case. The shift from contributory to comparative negligence in tort law shows how persuasive authority can gradually reshape binding law. The change started slowly, was advocated in secondary sources like the Restatement of Torts, was adopted by a few courts, and eventually became the majority rule across the country. What began as merely persuasive became, jurisdiction by jurisdiction, binding. In practice: Watching Persuasive Become Binding. California’s switch is a clean specimen. For decades the state followed contributory negligence, under which a plaintiff even slightly at fault recovered nothing. Nothing binding required a change. What existed was persuasive material: scholarly criticism, other states’ decisions, and comparative rules already in force elsewhere. In Li v. Yellow Cab Co., 13 Cal. 3d 804 (1975), the California Supreme Court drew on exactly that body of non-binding authority and replaced the rule with comparative fault. The moment the opinion issued, the persuasive material had done its work and the new rule was binding on every court in the state. If you had researched this question in 1974, the best answer would have been “contributory negligence controls, but the persuasive weight is running the other way,” and that second clause is the one a client needed. Reflection Point. When would a persuasive decision be worth more to your client than a binding one? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: A solid grasp of this structure lets you do three things: Decide where to begin. Which level of law governs this issue? If the area is comprehensively codified, start with the statute. If it is common-law territory, start with cases. If you are not sure, start with a secondary source that will tell you. Sort binding from persuasive sources. Which authorities must you follow, and which can you cite for support? That judgment sets how much weight to give each source and how hard to keep searching for something better. Track how sources interact. How do statutes, regulations, and cases shape one another? A complete answer often means assembling several sources rather than finding a single one. Working this way keeps your arguments grounded in the right authorities, which is most of what people mean when they call a memo well researched. It also feeds directly into the Question Method introduced in Chapter 3 : every cycle there begins by asking which authority can answer the question at hand, and this structure is where that answer comes from.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: The mistake that does the most damage early on is treating the first source you find as the whole answer. A single statute or case rarely tells the full story when regulations and judicial interpretation are also in play, and stopping too soon leaves a gap exactly where the governing rule lives. A related error is confusing persuasive authority for binding authority, then building an argument on a case your court has no obligation to follow. Watch the jurisdiction line carefully, because a perfectly good California decision does nothing for you in an Arizona court. And do not skip the validation step. Authority that was good law last year may have been amended, overruled, or struck down since, and citing it as though it still controls is the kind of error that follows you into practice.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: U.S. law comes from five primary sources (constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, and treaties), layered across one federal system and fifty state systems. Within any jurisdiction, the hierarchy runs constitution over statute, statute over regulation, with case law interpreting all three or, where no statute governs, supplying the rule itself as common law. And for any given court, an authority is either binding, meaning the court must follow it, or persuasive, meaning the court can listen and still say no. This structure is what will inform where you look to answer your research questions. Key Takeaways U.S. law comes from five interconnected primary sources: constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, and treaties. Most modern issues involve multiple types of authority at once. The hierarchy of authority determines which source controls: constitutions over statutes, statutes over regulations, and so on. Mandatory authority is law a court must follow; persuasive authority is law a court may consider but is not required to follow. Read the law as interlocking parts of a system that is always evolving, which is why validating every authority is a required step, not an optional one.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: The following exercises test your understanding of which sources of authority are involved in different scenarios and why. No searching is required; that begins in Chapter 2 .

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: A client comes to you with this: she was fired from her job at a private company in your state after a routine drug test detected marijuana. She holds a medical authorization to use it under your state’s law, though marijuana remains prohibited by federal statute regardless of state authorization. She used it only at home, never worked impaired, and had no written employment contract. She wants to know whether the firing was legal. Do not answer her question; you cannot yet, and that is the point. Instead, using the chapter’s map of the sources of law and its employment-dispute example as your template, identify every layer of authority that might bear on her situation, and for each layer write one sentence predicting what it might contribute to the eventual answer. Deliverable: a table with one row per authority, three columns: the level of government, the type of source (constitution, statute, regulation, case law), and your one-sentence prediction. Self-check: a complete map reaches both levels of government and at least three source types, and every entry should be traceable to something the chapter or the scenario told you, a prediction, not a guess about doctrines you have not met. If every row landed at one level or in one type, reread The Interplay of U.S. Legal Authorities; this fact pattern was built to resist a one-box answer.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
t: A trial court in Arizona is hearing a negligence claim, an area the chapter told you is governed mostly by common law. The parties have put seven authorities in front of the court. Classify each as binding or persuasive for that court, with one sentence of justification tied to the chapter’s rules: (a) a decision of the Arizona Supreme Court on the duty at issue; (b) a decision of the Arizona Court of Appeals on the same duty; (c) a decision of the California Supreme Court on nearly identical facts; (d) a decision of a different Arizona trial court; (e) a decision of a federal district court sitting in Arizona discussing Arizona negligence law; (f) a section of a well-regarded treatise on negligence; (g) a decision of the U.S. Supreme Court interpreting the U.S. Constitution on a point raised in the case. Then one final sentence: for the authorities you classified as persuasive, when does the chapter say a court is most likely to follow them anyway? Deliverable: the seven classifications with justifications, plus the final sentence. Self-check: every justification should invoke a rule the chapter stated, higher court in the same system, home jurisdiction, primary versus secondary, and nothing else. If you found yourself wanting to research Arizona law to answer, stop; everything you need is on the page, and needing more means a classification is leaning on something other than the chapter’s rules.

p: Chapter 1: Foundations of Legal Authority
s: Exercise 1.3 — Who Gets the Last Word?
t: The chapter told two stories about authorities acting on each other: Rowan Companies , where Congress overrode the Supreme Court’s reading of a statute by amending the statute, and Texas v. Johnson , where the Court struck a statute against the Constitution and the legislature had no reply. In two or three sentences each, explain who held the last word in each story and why. Then answer the question the two stories together set up, in two sentences, using only the interplay rules the chapter stated: what determines which actor gets the last word, the identity of the actors involved, or the kind of conflict between the authorities? Deliverable: two short explanations and the two-sentence answer. Self-check: your final answer should turn on the kind of conflict, a statute’s meaning versus a constitutional limit, not on which institutions happened to be involved. If it turned on the actors, reread the two stories side by side. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
s: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: Legal research platforms are commercial interfaces that index and make searchable the primary and secondary authorities that courts, legislatures, and agencies produce. The three major commercial platforms are Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law, and each provides its own research tools and editorial enhancements. Free alternatives, including Google Scholar, CourtListener, eCFR.gov, GovInfo.gov, and Congress.gov, provide access to many primary sources, though with fewer research tools than the commercial platforms and, often, less complete coverage of older or unreported material. Each platform organizes its content into searchable collections such as by source type (cases, statutes, regulations, secondary sources) and by jurisdiction. Before you run any search, set the appropriate jurisdiction and source-type filters. This one step saves an enormous amount of time by keeping irrelevant results out of your way. A search for “reasonable accommodation” run across all jurisdictions and all source types returns an unusable wall of results; the same search confined to Ninth Circuit cases returns a set you can actually read. This chapter is about how the platforms work and the mechanics of searching them (how to navigate and get filtered results). It is deliberately kept apart from the strategy of searching (what to search for and how to recognize the best source), which is the subject of Chapter 3 ’s Question Method and the source-specific chapters that follow. Learning the mechanics first means that when strategy questions come up, you already know how to execute the search the strategy calls for. Learning Objectives Identify the major legal research platforms and their core features Distinguish between natural language searching and terms-and-connectors (Boolean) searching Build basic searches using the core Boolean connectors AND, OR, and NOT Use expansion operators (! and *) to capture different forms of the same word Apply jurisdiction and source-type filters to focus your results Select when to use a broad search and when to use a narrow one

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: Databases change, and they change often. Interfaces get redesigned, features get renamed, and new tools appear every year. A few features, though, are common across platforms and stable over time: a central search box, the ability to filter by jurisdiction and source type, a citator for validating authority, and some system of topical classification. If you learn the underlying concepts rather than the location of a particular button, your skills will carry from one platform to the next and survive the next interface redesign. Explore The parts every legal database has A schematic search screen. No platform looks exactly like this, and every platform has all of it. Select a region to see what it is for and what it is called elsewhere. Search bar. Accepts a citation, a plain-language description, or a terms-and-connectors search. Most platforms guess which one you typed, so a stray connector word can change how your search is read. Jurisdiction. Limits results to a court system or state. Set it before you search. An unfiltered search returns authority that could never bind your court, and it buries the authority that can. Content type. Cases, statutes, regulations, secondary sources, briefs. The type of question you are asking tells you which to choose, which is the subject of Chapter 3 . Browse and topics. Tables of contents, indexes, and the publisher’s topical classification (Key Numbers on Westlaw, topic headings on Lexis). Browsing shows you where a provision sits in its surroundings, which a search result never does. Results and filters. The result list, with filters for date, court, reported status, and search-within-results. Narrowing after the search is usually faster than rebuilding the search. Citator flag. The signal beside a document (KeyCite on Westlaw, Shepard’s on Lexis, BCite on Bloomberg Law) that later authority has treated it negatively. A flag is a prompt to read the later authority, never a verdict.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: A legal citation tells you three things: what type of source it is, where it was published, and when it was published. A case citation typically appears as Party v. Party , Volume Reporter Page (Court Year). The reporter and volume tell you where the opinion is published; the court and year, in the parenthetical, tell you immediately how much authority the case might carry in your jurisdiction. Read closely A case citation, part by part Robles v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC , 913 F.3d 898 (9th Cir. 2019) A statute citation identifies the title and section of the code where the law lives: the title number, the code abbreviation, and the section symbol followed by the section number. Read closely A statute citation, part by part 42 U.S.C. § 12182 (a) (2018) A regulation citation follows the same logic as a statute but points to the Code of Federal Regulations rather than a statutory code. Read closely A regulation citation, part by part 28 C.F.R. § 36.303 (a) (2023)

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: When you already have a citation, you are able to retrieve the authority in a legal database by entering relevant portions into the search bar. Enter only the location portions of the citation (volume, reporter, page, or title and section), not the party names or the year. The location portions are what the database indexes; the names and year are descriptive and can actually interfere with a clean retrieval. Check yourself Retrieve, don't search A memo cites Robles v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC , 913 F.3d 898 (9th Cir. 2019). What do you type to pull the opinion? Robles v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC, 913 F.3d 898 (9th Cir. 2019) It will often work, but the names and the parenthetical give the database more to misread. On some platforms a long string is run as a search and returns a list. 913 F.3d 898 Volume, reporter, page. That is the address the database indexes, and it returns exactly one document. Robles Domino’s 2019 That is a search, not a retrieval. It returns every document mentioning those words, including later cases that merely cite Robles .

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: When you do not already have a citation, when you do not yet know what you want to find, you have to search the database to discover sources that might be relevant. What to search for and how to spot the best results are covered in later chapters. This section is about the mechanics of searching a legal research system. There are two basic ways to search a legal database, and choosing between them is one of the first decisions you make when you sit down to research. Many systems have added semantic searching through generative AI chat interfaces. These are covered in Chapter 15 , but are best used after you understand and are able to make the critical judgments required when using the basic ways to search described below. Natural language searching lets you type a description of your issue in plain terms, almost like asking a question. The database uses algorithms to rank results by how closely they match what you typed. It is a good way to start when you are still exploring and do not yet know the precise legal terminology, because it does not require you to know the magic words. It tolerates ordinary language and returns the documents it judges most relevant. Terms-and-connectors searching (also called Boolean searching) is more precise. Instead of letting the database guess what you want, you tell it exactly what to look for: which words must appear, which words must be near each other, which words to exclude. This is the right tool when you know what you are looking for and need to be sure you find everything relevant, because a well-built Boolean search returns every document that satisfies its logic and nothing that does not. Most research starts with natural language and moves to Boolean precision as your questions get more specific. You do not have to choose one over the other; they work well together. Chapter 9 covers the full precision toolkit once your research has narrowed. This chapter introduces the foundation you will build on there.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: AND: both terms must appear somewhere in the document. Use it to require your concepts to co-occur. Example: landlord AND habitability. A document mentioning only one of the two will not be retrieved. OR: either term may appear. Use it for synonyms and alternate ways of describing the same concept. A good search for “landlord” might include landlord OR lessor OR owner. This widens your results to catch sources that use different words for the same idea, and missing a synonym is one of the most common ways researchers miss relevant authority. NOT (or BUT NOT): the first term must appear; the second must not. Use it to drop an irrelevant context. Example: marijuana NOT prescription. Use NOT carefully, because it removes every document containing the excluded term, and it can quietly discard relevant results whenever the excluded term happens to co-occur with your issue. Quotation marks: the exact phrase must appear in exactly that order. Example: “reasonable accommodation”. This is your most powerful precision tool when you know the exact legal standard you are after, because it cuts out the noise of the two words appearing separately and unrelated.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: ! (root expander) retrieves all words sharing the same root. Example: employ! retrieves employ, employee, employer, employment, and employed all at once. This keeps you from missing results because a source used a slightly different form of your term. Be careful, though, because the expander grabs words you did not intend. bit! retrieves bite, biter, bitten, and biting, but also bitter, bitcoin, and bittersweet. The longer and more distinctive the root, the safer the expansion. * (single-character wildcard) fills exactly one character position. Example: wom*n retrieves woman and women . Use it when a word has common variant spellings or inflections that a root expander would not catch. Sort it Does it widen the net or tighten it? Adding OR lessor OR owner to landlord Widens OR accepts any of the alternatives, so more documents qualify. Adding AND habitability to landlord Tightens AND requires both concepts, so fewer documents qualify. Putting quotation marks around reasonable accommodation Tightens The words must now appear together, in that order. Changing employee to employ! Widens The root expander accepts every word beginning with those letters. Adding NOT prescription Tightens Every document containing the excluded word is dropped, including relevant ones. Changing woman to wom*n Widens The wildcard accepts either spelling.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: A search string is your current research question translated into the database’s language, which is why a vague question produces a vague search. Two habits make the difference between a search that works and one that buries you. First, before you run anything, brainstorm both the lay term and the legal term for each concept: fired and terminated and discharged; or landlord and lessor; or lease and rental agreement. Lawyers, judges, and ordinary people describe the same thing in different words, and the source you need may use a word you did not think of. Use OR to gather all the variants for a single concept in one search. Second, connect your distinct concepts with AND so the results discuss all of them at once. A search like (fired OR terminated OR discharged) AND (disab! OR “medical condition”) requires both a separation concept and a disability concept to appear, which is far more useful than searching either one alone. Start broad. Connecting two or three core concepts with AND gives you a manageable set while you are still orienting yourself, and it forgives the fact that you do not yet know the precise terminology. As your questions get more specific, moving from exploratory to focusing to application, your searches should narrow to match, adding the precision tools from Chapter 9 : proximity connectors (/n, /s, /p), frequency operators (ATLEAST), and the strategies for closing out a project. The progression of your searches should track the progression of your questions. The practice database below holds eight invented case summaries. Five are on point for a client who believes she lost her job because of a medical condition; three are not. Run the same problem both ways and watch two numbers: how many documents come back, and how many of the on-point five are among them. Search lab One question, two ways to search Alvarez v. Copper Basin Mining | on point. The employer terminated a shift supervisor two days after she disclosed a seizure disorder. The court held that the timing supported an inference of disability discrimination. Brandt v. Sonoran Freight | on point. A driver was fired after requesting leave for a medical condition. Summary judgment for the employer was reversed. Chen v. Desert Valley Hospital | on point. The nurse was discharged for absences caused by her disability. Whether the hospital offered a reasonable accommodation was a question for the jury. Delgado v. Pima Staffing | on point. The agency fired a disabled warehouse worker whose prescription medication was flagged under the employer’s drug policy. Ellis v. Mesa Unified School District | on point. A teacher alleged she was dismissed because of multiple sclerosis, a chronic illness. The court applied the burden-shifting framework. Farrow v. Canyon Kilns | off point. A kiln operator was injured when a co-worker fired the furnace before the safety check. The disability benefits claim was resolved under workers’ compensation. Greer v. Tucson Transit | off point. The city terminated a bus route contract. Riders with disabilities challenged the change under the public services provisions. Hale v. Ironwood Apartments | off point. A landlord’s duty to repair does not depend on a tenant’s medical condition. The lease was terminated for nonpayment. The natural-language mode here is a simple stand-in that ranks documents by how many of your words they contain. Commercial engines are more sophisticated, but they behave the same way in kind: anything loosely matching comes back, in an order the engine guessed. The terms-and-connectors mode does exactly what you tell it. Try the first preset, then ask why a search with two sensible words found none of the five. Try the last one and see what NOT cost you. Then type your own. Reflection Point. Why does the method have you draft the research question before you choose a database or a search syntax? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: The most frequent platform mistake is searching before setting the jurisdiction and source-type filters, which floods you with results from courts and source types that could never answer your question. After that comes leaning too hard on a single set of search terms; if you only ever search for “fired,” you will miss every case that says “terminated” or “discharged,” so brainstorm synonyms and join them with OR. NOT deserves its own caution, because it is easy to exclude a word that sometimes travels with the authority you actually want and quietly delete good results in the process. And the root expander rewards a little restraint: a short root like bit! drags in bitcoin and bittersweet, along with the biting and bitten, so reach for the longest, most distinctive root that still captures the variants you need.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: Legal research platforms are the infrastructure you use to reach primary and secondary authority. Understanding the difference between natural language and Boolean searching, and knowing when to use each, is the foundation of efficient research. Natural language gets you moving when you are unsure of the vocabulary; Boolean gives you control once you know what you are after. The expansion operators and connectors here form the basis of the precision toolkit you will develop in Chapter 9 . Key Takeaways Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law are the major commercial platforms; free alternatives provide access to many primary sources but with fewer tools and less complete coverage. Natural language searching suits exploration; Boolean searching suits precision retrieval. Brainstorm lay and legal synonyms and join them with OR; connect distinct concepts with AND. Always set jurisdiction and source-type filters before searching.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: The following exercises test your ability to translate a question into a search, compare search modes, and retrieve known sources from their citations. Before every search, record the jurisdiction and source-type filters you set and why.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: A mail carrier was bitten by a customer’s dog while delivering a package, and she wants to know whether the dog’s owner is liable for her injuries. Identify the distinct concepts inside that question. There are at least three. For each concept, build a synonym set of at least three terms joined by OR, then connect the concept sets with AND into a single terms-and-connectors search. Watch for the root-expander trap the chapter warned about: a short root drags in everything that shares its letters, so test every truncated term against what it would actually sweep up. Deliverable: your concept list, the synonym set for each, and the final search string. Self-check: every concept has three or more synonyms, no synonym set relies on a single word, and any root expander you used survives the drag-in test. If a synonym set built honestly from plain, everyday language is a passing set at this stage; the legal terms of art for this area arrive with Chapter 4 ’s toolkit, and no set fails here for lacking them.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: Run the dog-bite question twice on the same platform: once as a natural language search, in a plain sentence, and once as a terms-and-connectors search, built as this chapter taught, synonym sets joined by OR for each concept, concepts connected with AND. Set your jurisdiction filter to your state and your source-type filter to cases before either search, and record both. Compare the first ten results of each run. Deliverable: your search notes, both queries as entered, both filter sets, and three sentences on how the result lists differ: what each mode surfaced that the other missed, and which you would trust to start this project. Self-check: if your three sentences could have been written without running the searches, run them again and look harder. The differences are specific, and the chapter told you what kinds of differences to expect.

p: Chapter 2: Introduction to Legal Research Platforms
t: If you already have a citation, you do not search. You retrieve. Here are three citations, one case, one statute, one regulation: Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier , 484 U.S. 260 (1988); 42 U.S.C. § 12101; and 29 C.F.R. § 1605.1. For each, first label the citation’s anatomy, every location part and what it tells you, and then pull the document using only those location parts. No words in any search bar. Deliverable: the three labeled anatomies and, for each document, the retrieval path you used. Self-check: if at any point you typed subject-matter words into a search box, you searched. Close the tab and retrieve properly. The skill being drilled is recognizing that a citation is an address, and addresses are for going to, not for asking about. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Legal research is a moving series of questions that continues until you find the answer you need or must stop for practical reasons. Collecting sources is easy; a pile of printouts is not research. The skill is knowing what you need at every stage. Good researchers pause and ask themselves things like: What type of question am I asking now? Is this the right level of inquiry for where I am? What source can best answer it? To a beginner, those pauses feel like interruptions. That is because it is not yet instinctive as it is for experts, and so it feels like an extra step. The Question Method builds the those pauses into the process: craft a question, research the answer, synthesize the answer into your writing notes, and craft the next question. With a well-crafted question in hand, you will find where to look faster, understand what you find more clearly, spot gaps and ambiguities sooner, and know with some confidence when your research is actually done. Learning Objectives Articulate the Question Method and distinguish it from passive, collection-based research Draft precise, well-scoped research questions at each stage of inquiry Identify the type of question being asked and select the source best suited to answer it Distinguish a research map, a research log, and an annotated research outline, and explain where each belongs in the research process Use a research log to document each cycle of research, recording the research question, method, and findings Synthesize research findings into an annotated outline Recognize analytical closure and practical closure, and use the research Explain how the Question Method integrates research and writing

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: The Role of Questions in Legal Research, Analysis, and Writing
t: Three terms carry this chapter and everything after it, and if you arrived here without the Introduction, here they are in brief. The legal issue is the problem the law must resolve, the reason the file landed on your desk. The macro question is that issue framed as the single big question your finished document exists to answer: the question presented in a memo, the issue on appeal in a brief. A research question is the micro question you ask and answer along the way, one of the many subquestions whose answers, assembled, resolve the macro question, and it is what this book always means by the term. You never research the macro question directly; held alone, it makes every passage look relevant and buries you. You write it down where you can see it, hold exactly one research question at a time, and let each answer hand you the next. The macro question is the destination; the research questions are the steps. (The Introduction develops this vocabulary in full.) Research and writing are one iterative process, but early-career researchers tend to split them in two. Research becomes a prewriting phase where you gather everything that might conceivably be useful. Writing becomes a later phase where you sift through the pile. That split reliably produces three problems: you feel overwhelmed about where to begin analyzing the material; you struggle to organize the research and structure the argument; and you discover major gaps too close to the deadline to fix them comfortably. The Question Method closes that split. Each answer you synthesize becomes a heading in your annotated outline, and findings become the bullets under it. You have started writing and organized your research in the same motion, and you can move to the next question knowing that nothing you found has slipped through the cracks. Questions are working tools in legal analysis. As you move through a project, asking questions lets you take stock of what you have learned, see where the gaps are, and fold new information into the argument you are building.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: The Five Steps and Intermittent Checkpoints
t: Step 1: Write your research question . State the one thing you need to know right now as a question, in terms that reflect what you currently understand. This is a research question in the Introduction’s vocabulary: a micro question, not the macro question your document will answer. Be specific. A vague question gives you vague results. Your research map, or the answer you just found, will usually supply the question. Step 2: Research to answer it. Choose the source most likely to answer the type of question you are asking. Search. Read. Track. Step 3: Write down what you found. In your research log, record your research question, the method you used to attempt to answer it, the source you consulted, what it told you, and your next research question. Add the synthesized answer to your annotated outline. Step 4: Identify your next question. Based on what you found, what do you still need to know? Write it down. Step 5: Repeat. Cycle through Steps 1 through 4 until no substantive questions remain, and add any new questions the source raised to your research map. Checkpoint, Reflect and Evaluate: Before you close out your research, review your work. Are your sources current? Authoritative? From the right jurisdiction? Did your sequence of questions capture the full scope of the issue? Build it as a habit into every cycle, then perform it formally at the end, rather than saving it for a separate phase.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: Done Usually Means Done for Now
t: Step 5 tells you to keep cycling until no substantive question remains, and that is right. It is worth being honest, though, about what “no more questions” usually means in practice. It means no more questions for now. When you take your notes and start turning them into a full draft, you will very often find gaps you could not have seen until you tried to write the argument out. A connection that felt solid turns out to need a case you do not have. An element you were sure you understood raises a sub-question the moment you have to explain it on the page. None of that means your research failed. Research and writing are cyclical, and they feed each other. So the goal is not to track down every authority you might conceivably need before you write a single word. Chasing that kind of completeness is slower rather than faster, and it runs up a bill your client should not have to pay. The efficient move is to stop once you believe you have most of what you need, start writing, and let the act of drafting show you which gaps are actually worth closing. Stopping for now is a real research decision, not a loss of nerve, even when it leaves you with the nagging sense that there might be a little more out there.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: Why This Method Works: Making Your Thinking Visible
t: The blank page is paralyzing because it asks you to produce something out of nothing. The Question Method replaces it with a prompt. At every stage, you are answering a specific question, and each cycle leaves behind a small, discrete piece of writing. Those pieces pile up in your research log and annotated outline, so by the time you sit down to “write,” your outline is a first draft hiding under bullet points. You will then just be organizing and refining what you have already sketched out. There is a name for the habit the method trains: metacognition, which means thinking about your own thinking. It is the ability to monitor what you know, recognize what you do not know, evaluate whether your current approach is working, and adjust when it is not. Expert legal researchers are metacognitive all the way down. They keep asking themselves: Do I understand this well enough to move on? Is this source actually answering my question? Have I missed something? Each step of the Question Method cycle corresponds to a metacognitive act. Explore The cycle, and the question each step asks of you 1. Write the question | self-monitoring. What do I currently need to know? You cannot write the question without noticing the edge of your own knowledge. That noticing is the skill. 2. Research to answer it | strategic selection. What is the best way to find this out? Naming the type of question is what turns a guess about where to look into a choice. 3. Write down what you found | self-assessment. Did I find what I needed? If you cannot state the answer in your own words, you have not found it yet. 4. Identify the next question | self-regulation. Where should I go next? The answer you just wrote down tells you, and then the cycle begins again. Checkpoint | self-evaluation. Is my overall approach working? Not every cycle, but at intervals: are the sources current, authoritative, and pointed at the question the project is really asking? Each step asks you to make a judgment, not just perform a task. You are training yourself to think like a researcher.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Writing forces you to be honest about whether you actually understand something. It is easy to read a case and feel like you grasp the rule. It is much harder to state that rule in your own words, in a single sentence, and connect it to the question you asked. If you cannot, you have found a gap, and finding it now beats finding it in the final hours before a major filing deadline. Writing as you go also protects you from collecting a stack of sources and then realizing you no longer remember why each one mattered.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: The method uses three tools that work together. The Research Map is your plan. It lists the questions your writing must answer, each with leads to the sources that might answer it, organized by the logic of your analysis. The research log is your record of the research process . It captures every question you asked, each method you used, all the sources you consulted, and every answer you found, in the order you found them. The Annotated Outline is your record of the research product . It organizes your verified findings by legal issue, so each section lines up with an element, a factor, or a sub-question in your analysis. As you finish research log entries, you move the synthesized findings into the right section of the outline and mark the question answered on your map. One way to keep them straight: the research map tells you where you are going, the research log tells you where you have been, and the annotated outline tells you what you know. Follow a single question through all three. It is born on the map, often handed to you by a secondary source or by the answer to an earlier question. You work it in the log, sometimes over several entries if the first source only partially answers it. Once you have a verified answer from primary authority, that answer, not the question, goes into the outline, and the question is marked answered on the map. The map holds questions; the outline holds answers.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: A research map is a list of the questions you need to answer in your writing to reach a conclusion about how the law applies to your client. You build it over time from the sources you encounter. Questions land on the map from the assignment and the file, from the answers to earlier questions, from sources that answer more than you asked (an encyclopedia entry or a case will often point to several later questions and cite the authority for each), and from your own curiosity about the facts. Next to each question, note any leads: citations you think might answer it, recorded before you have read them. Add questions as you discover them, but file each one where it belongs in the analysis, so a sub-question sits under the question it narrows. Mark each question open, answered (with a pointer to its place in the outline), or parked, meaning done for now on purpose. Two kinds of questions stay off the map. Questions about your client’s facts go on a separate fact-gathering list, because no database can answer them. And the orientation question you ask just to learn an area’s vocabulary stays in the log, because the map holds only the questions your writing must answer. When you finish one line of reasoning, the map tells you which question to take up next.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: A research log captures your process and your results in one place, so you can put the work down and reenter it later without starting over. In law school, research arrives in stable chunks: you get the assignment, you do it, you turn it in. Practice is not like that. You will be pulled off a project midstream for weeks or months, and when you come back, the log is what tells you what you asked, what you found, and what you were about to ask next. Be kind to your future self, and build the habit of logging your efforts. One more thing before you build the habit: the entry template below is deliberately overly explicit. It is a scaffold for learning, and seven fields is more than most working researchers keep forever. There is no single right format for a research log. The right format is whatever gets your future self back into the research fastest, and that is personal. Start with the full scaffold, notice which fields are doing real work for you, and adjust until the log fits your process. What cannot be cut is the function: process and results, captured well enough that you can leave the work and return to it cold. The research log opens with your macro question, written once at the top of your document so you can always check that you have not drifted onto a tangent, and then entries that capture each step in your research with seven fields: Research Question. Write your current question here. Question Type. Definitional, Exploratory, Focusing, or Application (each defined in Types of Questions, below). Method. The research method you used to locate the source you used to answer the question. E.g., secondary source, annotated code, citator, key numbers, search, lead from the map, etc. Findings. The key information, holding, rule, or definition, in your own words. Source Consulted. Citation. Next Question. What do you still need to know? Notes. Anything else: related sources to check, flags, connections to other questions. Filling in the Question Type field is not busywork. As you will see, naming the type forces the diagnostic step that tells you which source to consult and roughly where you are in the arc of the research process. The Findings field does similar work if you let it. Begin each entry by saying whether the source fully answers your question, partially answers it, or only redirects you, and then record what it said. That one clause makes you say out loud whether you have an actual answer or only a lead, which is the difference between real progress and the comfortable illusion of it. The Method field matters most when you return to the project after an extended period. Research in practice often has gaps large enough between efforts on a case that memory alone is not enough. The Method field tells you which searches you already ran, including the ones that found nothing, so you do not repeat them, and it lets you answer a supervisor who asks how you found a case. Chapter 9 ’s closing-out protocol asks you to document what you searched; a log with good Method entries has already done most of that work. Here is what a completed entry looks like on the page, using a definitional question you will meet again in the Types of Questions section below: what is the federal definition of “organic”? Field Entry Research Question What is the federal definition of “organic”? Question Type Definitional Method Found in Annotated United States Code (Westlaw) under general Findings Partially answers the question. The statute hands definitional authority for the organic program to the USDA; the authoritative definition lives in the agency’s regulation, not the statute. Source Consulted 7 U.S.C. § 6502 Next Question What is the USDA’s definition of “organic”? Notes Definitional question answered at two levels of authority. 7 C.F.R. Part 205 is likely the best next resource A full example is available in Appendix F . Now write one of your own. Use the question you are holding in whatever you are working on this week. The log belo

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: Reverse Engineering the Question: A Demonstration
t: Legal arguments are built by answering questions. Take a real paragraph from a federal opinion and turn each sentence back into the research question it answers. Read closely Four sentences, four questions In the vast majority of legal malpractice cases, the plaintiff was a client of the defendant-attorney, and the direct attorney-client relationship establishes the attorney’s professional duties to the client. Pelham v. Griesheimer , 92 Ill. 2d 13, 440 N.E.2d 96, 99 (Ill. 1982). There is a small corner of legal malpractice law, however, in which Illinois recognizes that attorneys owe professional duties to persons who are not their clients. In Pelham , the Illinois Supreme Court held that an attorney may owe a duty to a third party when “the primary purpose and intent of the attorney-client relationship itself was to benefit or influence the third party.” Id. at 100. Examples of third parties to whom attorneys owe a duty include third-party beneficiaries of wills, third-party beneficiaries of wrongful death actions, and third-party recipients of formal opinion letters. See In re Estate of Powell , 12 N.E.3d at 21; Geaslen v. Berkson, Gorov & Levin, Ltd. ( Geaslen II ), 155 Ill. 2d 223, 613 N.E.2d 702, 704 (Ill. 1993); McLane v. Russell , 131 Ill. 2d 509, 546 N.E.2d 499, 504 (Ill. 1989). Oakland Police & Fire Retirement System v. Mayer Brown, LLP , 861 F.3d 644, 649–50 (7th Cir. 2017). Notice that for several of these questions the answer comes from a single source, Pelham v. Griesheimer . That is common for settled points of law: elements, familiar principles, conclusions nobody is fighting about. The last sentence is different. It carries multiple citations because the answer requires a survey of different scenarios. When you see one point of law supported by a string of citations, that usually signals a survey question answered by looking across many cases. Making the questions explicit shows you why some propositions might only need a single citation while others need several. Here we worked backward from a finished paragraph. When you research, you work forward toward one. The paragraph as a whole serves the macro question of the appeal. Each sentence answers a single research question. Assembled, the small answers resolve the big one, and every piece of legal writing you produce has this structure under its skin. Finally, those four questions, in order, are a research map. The paragraph is the annotated outline written out in full sentences, each question replaced by its answer and its citation.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Naming the type of question you are asking is the diagnostic move that makes everything else more efficient. Once you know the type, you know where to look, which source will answer it best, and roughly how far into the cycle you are.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Definitional questions ask what a word, phrase, or concept means. For your own orientation, a legal dictionary usually does the job. When the definition is load-bearing for your argument, you need primary authority: the statute’s definitions section, case law construing the term, or agency regulations. The diagnostic question is whether you need a working definition or an authoritative one. “What is the federal definition of organic ?” leads you to the statute, which hands definitional authority to the USDA, so your next question becomes “What is the USDA’s definition of organic ?” and you turn to 7 C.F.R. Part 205.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Exploratory questions ask what the legal landscape of an area looks like. There are three kinds, and each points to a slightly different source. No-clue questions come up when you have no familiarity with the area at all. You do not know the relevant terms, the key cases, or even whether the issue is mostly statutory or mostly common law. Foundational questions come up when you have a general sense of the area but need to understand the general structure of the law: the elements of a claim, the factors in a test, the major debates, the terms of art Survey questions come up when you need to know how multiple jurisdictions have handled the same issue.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Focusing questions ask what the specific legal rule governing your issue is, moving you from the general landscape to the particular standard, test, or sub-rule. This is usually where you cross over from secondary to primary authority. If you have been using secondary sources to get oriented, a focusing question pushes you to go find the actual statute, regulation, or case that states the rule. Focusing questions also breed sub-rules. “What is the standard for reasonable accommodation under the ADA?” leads to “What counts as undue hardship under that standard?”, which is itself a focusing question one level deeper. Every layer of the rule you uncover can expose another layer that needs its own question.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Application questions ask how the rule works once you apply it to specific facts. Like exploratory questions, there are multiple kinds. Fact-finding application questions go looking for cases with facts like your client’s, where the rule was applied in analogous circumstances. Constructive application questions become necessary when no articulated rule yet governs your question, so the applicable rule itself has to be built from several sources, reasoning by analogy from related contexts. When the rule is articulated but no decision applies it to facts like yours, you are still fact-finding: gather the closest decided applications and argue the analogy. The four types are not a strict sequence. You might circle back to an exploratory question when a focusing question turns up an unfamiliar doctrine. You might answer a definitional question mid-stream when a regulation throws an unexpected technical term at you. Treat the taxonomy as a diagnostic, not a checklist. Its value is helping you recognize, at any moment, what kind of inquiry you are actually in, and therefore where the answer is likely to live. A real case shows how unceremoniously the types trade places. The Types in Motion: Nix v. Hedden In Nix v. Hedden, 149 U.S. 304 (1893), a produce importer sued the collector of the Port of New York to recover import duties paid on tomatoes. The Tariff Act of 1883 taxed imported “vegetables” and admitted “fruit” free, and the importer’s argument was that, botanically, a tomato is a fruit. The threshold question is: which tariff category covers a tomato? That turns on a definitional question: how does the statute define “fruit” and “vegetable”? And here the definitional question comes back empty. The Act uses both words and defines neither. The next question is a focusing question, one level up: how have courts defined the terms when applying the Act? The Supreme Court answered that absent some contrary indication, words in the Tariff Act carry their ordinary meaning in common speech, not their botanical or scientific meaning, and dictionaries may aid the court’s memory and understanding but do not control. Now we can ask a closing application question: in ordinary speech, is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? The Court held, unanimously, that tomatoes are vegetables, served at dinner in, with, or after the soup rather than as dessert, and the duty stood. The Court cited Robertson v. Salomon, 130 U.S. 412 (1889)(which found that beans are vegetables, not seeds, for the purposes of tariffs). Reflection Point. A botanist, a chef, and the Tariff Act of 1883 each answer “is a tomato a fruit?” differently. What does that tell you about where a legal definition’s authority comes from? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .) Sort it Name the type What does “curtilage” mean? Definitional It asks what a word means. A working definition is enough to keep researching. How does the law treat security deposits when a tenant moves out? Exploratory No rule is named and no standard is presupposed. It asks what the landscape looks like. What is the test for when a school official may search a student’s backpack? Focusing It asks for the specific governing rule. The word “test” is the tell. Is a dog owner liable when the dog bites a guest who was teasing it? Application Specific facts in the question (a bite, a guest, teasing) are the tell. It asks how a rule has operated on facts like these. How do the fifty states handle recording a phone call? Exploratory The survey kind of exploratory question: how many jurisdictions do what. What are the elements of adverse possession in Michigan? Focusing “The elements,” in a named jurisdiction: the governing rule itself. What does “employee” mean under this state’s wage statute? Definitional Still a what-does-it-mean question. “Under this statute” changes where you look (the statute’s definitions section, not a dictionary). It does not change the type. Have courts treated taping a notice to the door as “deli

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: Beginning Your Research: A Practical Start Protocol
t: Questions are a key part of the research process. Before you get to ask them, it is important that you thoughtfully prepare and plan your efforts. Every research project, simple or complex, begins the same way. Spending a few minutes up front to clarify the assignment and take stock of what you already know pays off enormously later, because it sets the type of your very first question, which sets the source you reach for first.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Before you open a database, make sure you understand what you are being asked to find. What is the scope? What will count as doing the job well? What are the deadlines, and what resources do you have? If the assignment comes from a supervisor, pin down the jurisdiction, the format they want (a quick email, a formal memorandum, a list of citations), and the depth of research expected. “Do some quick research on this” and “give me a comprehensive memo” are very different requests. This is also where the macro question gets written down. Capture the big question the finished document must answer, in one sentence, at the top of your research log. Also, make sure to note anything you are instructed to avoid. Managing attorneys will often split research tasks among a team of associates, and if you are not tracking the scope of your assignment, you are likely to waste time researching questions assigned to others.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Before you search, go through everything you already have. What do the documents tell you about the facts, the timeline, and the parties? It will not always be clear which facts are dispositive for your case. So capture the ones that are helpful to you now. You can revisit the case again as answers make it clear other facts matter. The legal terms you run across (the names of statutes, the titles of the parties, the types of claims) will seed your search terms and will often save you a no-clue exploratory step entirely.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Take a moment to be honest about what you already know. How familiar are you with this area? Do you know the relevant terms and claims? Are you an expert who just needs to confirm a couple of points, or someone meeting this area for the first time? That honest self-diagnosis decides what type your first question should be, and getting it right keeps you from wasting time at the wrong level of generality.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: With that assessment in hand, draft your first question. What is the very first thing you need to know? What in the file seems relevant to it? Where might that information live? If you are walking into unfamiliar territory, your first question should be exploratory. If you already have a handle on the landscape and just need a specific rule, it might be focusing. One move can come before even that choice. If you do not yet have the vocabulary the area uses, the terms of art you would need just to search, then your true first step is a plain-language or general search whose only job is to surface those terms. A term of art belongs in a question only after the file supplied it or an earlier step turned it up; it is something your research delivers, never something you assume at the outset. Writing that first question down is itself the first cycle of the method.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: When Is Your Research Done? Research Closure
t: Earlier in this chapter we saw that done usually means done for now. Here is how to make that judgment formally. Research closure is the professional judgment that your research is good enough for its purpose. It is a conclusion you can support with specific, documentable indicators, never just a feeling. Analytical closure means your research is substantively complete. You have identified the governing rule. You can explain how it applies to your facts. You have found the counterarguments and dealt with them. Your annotated outline covers the full scope of the issue. More research at this point would polish your writing but would not change your analysis. Practical closure means an external constraint forces you to stop: a budget cap, a client instruction, a supervising attorney’s direction. Practical closure is a fact of professional life. When it arrives before analytical closure, your job is to do three things: document where you stopped and what remains unresearched in your research log; tell your supervisor or client about the limitation; and flag any significant gaps that could affect the analysis. Practical closures are intentional, not a result of poor planning. Running out of time before a deadline is not a practical closure; it is potential malpractice One distinction keeps the judgment honest: running out of new sources is not closure. Closure arrives when your outline fully accounts for the legal question and more research would only change your wording rather than your analysis, and it gets finished off with a short ritual, a last sweep of the major sources, a citation update, and a check of the annotated outline for gaps. Chapter 9 builds that finish into a full closing-out protocol. Sort it Closure, or just stopping? Your map shows no open questions, the outline answers each one, and your last sweep turned up only authorities you had already read. Analytical closure The outline accounts for the legal question, and more research would change wording, not analysis. The client authorized five hours. At five you stop, log the two questions still open, and tell the supervising attorney what they are. Practical closure An external constraint, met deliberately: documented, communicated, gaps flagged. You cannot think of another search term to try. Not closure Running out of ideas, or of new sources, says something about your searching. It says nothing about whether the question is answered. The memo is due at nine and it is past midnight. Not closure A deadline you ran into is not a constraint someone set. The chapter’s word for it is blunter. The supervising attorney tells you to skip the federal claim and brief only the state one. You note the instruction and the unresearched issue in the log. Practical closure A supervisor’s direction is one of the constraints that properly ends research, so long as the gap is on the record. The method helps with both kinds of closure. Because each cycle is a recorded checkpoint—a question asked, a source consulted, an answer synthesized—you always know where you are. If you reach analytical closure, your research map confirms it by showing no open questions, your annotated outline shows an answer for each, and the judgment is defensible instead of intuitive, because you can point to a research log in which every question has been answered. If practical closure comes first, the questions still open on your map tell you exactly what is left.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
s: The Question Method in Action: A Full Demonstration
t: This demonstration runs the Question Method through a problem about student speech and the First Amendment. Read it for the thinking that drives the process, not just the sources consulted but the decisions made at each stage. One decision shapes the whole demonstration: a secondary source appears exactly once, at the start, to orient you and hand you a map. Every answer after that comes from primary authority.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: A supervising attorney asks: “Can a public high school principal remove articles he doesn’t like from the school-run student newspaper without violating the First Amendment?” You are a first-year law student. You know the First Amendment protects free speech, but you have never studied how it works inside schools.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Before drafting a question, you orient yourself. This is a constitutional issue (First Amendment) in a specific setting (a public school, a student newspaper). You do not know much about this area. You review the file and note that the newspaper is produced as part of a journalism class, that the principal removed several articles before publication, and that the articles do not seem to involve profanity, threats, or illegal activity. There is more detail about the article topics and the timing of the removal, but you are not yet sure which details would bear on the legal question, so you leave them where they are. That self-diagnosis tells you something useful: your first question has to be exploratory. You are not ready to ask what the legal standard is, because you do not yet know which standard governs.

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Question (Exploratory, No-Clue): How has First Amendment free speech protection been applied to students in school environments? You search the secondary sources in your database for “free speech” and students and schools. In your results, you find a legal encyclopedia entry titled “Students, Constitutional Rights.” The entry states that in Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District , 393 U.S. 503 (1969), the Supreme Court held that students still have free speech rights while at school, and that those rights may be restricted only if the expression materially and substantially disrupts school operations. The entry then surveys the cases marking where that standard does and does not reach. Two matter here. Bethel School District No. 403 v. Fraser , 478 U.S. 675 (1986), permitted a school to discipline lewd and vulgar speech that conflicted with the school’s basic educational mission. And Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier , 484 U.S. 260 (1988), governs school-sponsored publications, with the entry offering the example of a newspaper produced in a journalism class, and permits educators to regulate them when the regulation is tied to “legitimate pedagogical concerns,” a phrase the entry uses but does not define. Notice how much this single encyclopedia entry hands you beyond the question you are holding. Hazelwood is plainly the branch your facts sit on, and the temptation is to jump straight there. Resist it. The entry told you Tinker is the foundation the later cases build on, and a foundation you skip is a gap you will trip over the moment a later case assumes it. So you do two things at once: you keep one question open, and you map the routes you are not yet taking. Mapping adding the rest to your research map logging the rest as later questions, with their citations noted as leads, before you can answer any of them. Reading Tinker is clearly next. Hazelwood goes on the map too, but it is not next, because at least one question sits between the first question and the research question Hazelwood will puportedly answer. At least one does: the entry’s description suggests Hazelwood builds on Fraser , so Fraser will need a read after Tinker . You note that in the log. Example of what our research log entries look like at this stage: Cycle 1 Research Question: How has First Amendment free speech protection been applied to students in school environments? Question Type: Exploratory (No-Clue) Method: Searched the secondary sources in my database for “free speech” and students and schools; opened the encyclopedia entry. Findings: Tinker starts the student free speech case law: rights survive the schoolhouse gate, and restriction requires material and substantial disruption. Later cases set context-specific standards. Hazelwood governs school-sponsored publications like a curricular newspaper and ties regulation to “legitimate pedagogical concerns.” Fully answers the question, for orientation. It also identifies which branch of the doctrine governs our facts. Source Consulted: Legal encyclopedia entry, “Students, Constitutional Rights” [citation] (Note: The entry is a fictitional one for this example) Next Question: What are the bounds of student free speech rights in school? Notes: Tinker is the foundational case. Our newspaper is produced in a journalism class, so the school-sponsored branch (Hazelwood) is the thread to pull, but Hazelwood seems to build on Fraser, so Fraser gets a read after Tinker. The entry used “legitimate pedagogical concerns” without defining it; that is a future definitional question. Those later questions go on your research map, which you keep as a separate document from the log. Here is the map at this stage, with the leads the entry gave you. Your annotated outline is still empty. The exploratory answer does not make it into the outline because the answer came from a secondary source, not a primary one. As you answer each map question from primary authority, its synthesized answer mo

p: Chapter 3: The Question Method of Legal Research
t: Question (Focusing): What are the bounds of student free speech rights in school?
