Learning Objectives Describe how statutes are enacted and organized at the federal and state levels Locate statutes using annotated codes in print and electronic databases Read and interpret statutory text, including definitions, cross-references, and exceptions Apply basic canons of statutory construction to resolve ambiguous language Use annotated code features (case notes, cross-references, historical notes) to research a statutory question Update statutes to confirm they remain current and valid law Integrate statutory research into the Question Method framework

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Statutes are where focusing questions about codified law get answered, and the Question Method shapes both how you reach the statute and how you read it once you arrive. It shapes how you reach the statute because the first fork comes before any searching at all: if you already have a citation, from a secondary source, a case, or the assignment itself, you retrieve rather than search, exactly as Chapter 2 ’s known-source rule says. When you do not have one, the question type tells you the fastest route to a citation. If your question is “what law governs this regulated activity?”, the quickest path is rarely a keyword search of the code; it is a secondary source or the annotated code’s index naming the controlling section and handing you the citation. Either way, naming the question keeps you out of the frustrating experience of keyword-searching a code and drowning in scattered, decontextualized sections. It shapes how you read the statute because a statute almost never answers your question in one self-contained sentence. Reading a statute to answer a focusing question means reading the operative provision, the definitions section that controls its terms, the exceptions that might remove your client’s conduct from its reach, and the cross-referenced sections it incorporates. The method’s habit of asking “did this fully answer my question?” is what stops you from relying on a subsection you read in isolation, which is the single most common statutory research error. The occasions when a statute does answer your application question are those where legislatures draw bright lines, and a bright line performs the application step on its own. Three forms show up constantly. Numeric thresholds: was the complaint filed within the limitations period? Enumerated lists and schedules: is this substance on the controlled-substances schedule? Deeming provisions and safe harbors: a statute voiding any covenant longer than a stated term has already applied itself to every longer covenant. Each of these closes a genuine application question on the statutory text, without a case. Call these self-applying rules, and read the form of a provision early, because its form tells you where the answer lives. A bright line closes your question only when every operative term is defined, and your facts map onto it without inference, and that condition fails more often than you would expect. A limitations period is a precise number, but whether the clock started is usually a case-law question. A coverage threshold of fifteen employees is precise, but whether a particular worker counts as an “employee” is not. So a self-applying rule does one of two things: it closes the question, or it hands you a candidate answer plus a fresh definitional question, which is the same two-level move that runs from statute to regulation in the organic thread below. Chapter 3 ’s tariff case shows the failure mode. The Act named its categories and defined neither, so the statute could not close anything, and the answer had to come from a court. Had the schedule listed tomatoes by name, the research would have ended at the statute. Same facts, same question type, a different source, because the drafting changed. Sort it Does the statute apply itself, or do you need cases? Is this substance listed on the controlled-substances schedule? Statute answers it An enumerated list. Find the entry and the application is done. Did the landlord make the repair within a “reasonable time”? Cases needed A vague standard. Only decided cases show what courts have treated as reasonable. Is a five-year covenant void under a statute voiding any covenant longer than two years? Statute answers it A numeric threshold applies itself to every covenant that exceeds it. Was the employee “substantially limited” in a major life activity? Cases needed An undefined standard that courts and regulations have had to fill in. Was the complaint, filed 25 months after an undisputed injury date, within a two-year

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Statutes are the right starting point when your question asks what the law requires, prohibits, or permits in a legislatively regulated area. If you need the elements of a federal employment discrimination claim or the procedures for filing a patent application, you begin with the statute. Focusing questions (“What does Title VII require of an employer who receives a complaint of religious discrimination?”) are the most common type you will answer with statutes. Definitional questions come up constantly too (“The statute uses the term employer , so how does it define that term?”). Each annotated-code feature generates potential sub-questions that become entries in your Research Log. Reflection Point. Why might a statute be a poor source for answering a no-clue exploratory question, even when the area turns out to be statutory? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
s: How Statutes Are Made and What That Means for Research
t: A statute begins as a bill introduced in a legislative chamber. It is assigned to a committee, marked up, reported for floor consideration, passed by both chambers in identical form (sometimes requiring a conference committee to reconcile differing versions), and signed by the President or Governor. Every stage produces documents that may help you understand what the statute means; these legislative history materials are covered in Chapter 10 . The two relevant artifacts that are created in the lawmaking process are session laws and codes.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Session laws are statutes published chronologically as enacted, like the United States Statutes at Large . Codes reorganize session laws by subject into a unified collection, like the United States Code . Annotated codes, such as the United States Code Annotated (U.S.C.A.) published by Westlaw and the United States Code Services (U.S.C.S. ) published by Lexis, are the most useful research tools, because they pair the statute text with editorial enhancements such as case annotations, cross-references, and research aids, turning bare text into a hub that connects to the rest of the legal landscape. Explore One statute, five publications The same enacted words appear in several forms. Select each to see when a researcher reaches for it. Bill | before enactment. The proposal as introduced and amended. Not law. You return to it only when a later question asks how the language changed on its way to passage (Chapter 10 ). Slip law | first publication. The act as a standalone document, issued shortly after enactment and identified by its public law number. The first official text of a brand-new statute. Session laws | by date. Every act of a legislative session, in the order passed: the Statutes at Large for Congress. This is where you find the text exactly as enacted at a point in time, and provisions that were never codified, such as effective dates and findings. Code | by subject. The session laws in force, rearranged by topic and updated as amendments pass. This is what you cite and where you read the law as it stands, with each section sitting beside its definitions and exceptions. Annotated code | with apparatus. The code plus a publisher’s research layer: case notes, cross-references, history, and secondary sources. The text is identical. The annotations are not law, and they are where your next questions get their leads.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Start from a citation, drawn from a secondary source or a case, and look it up directly in an annotated code. Without a citation, work through the code’s own finding aids before you reach for a search box. The Popular Name Table locates statutes by their common names (“Clean Air Act,” “Americans with Disabilities Act”) and is often the fastest route when you know what a law is called but not where it is codified. The subject index and table of contents, in print or online codes, sort the code by topic and reward the vocabulary your secondary sources handed you. Keyword searching within statutory databases comes last, not second: statutory drafting is technical and rarely matches the words a searcher would guess, so the search box misses provisions the finding aids surface easily. Save it for when the finding aids fail or when you are hunting a phrase you know the statute uses.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
s: Answering Questions with Statutes: Using Annotated Codes
t: An annotated code is the statute plus a research apparatus. Beneath the official text, editors stack everything the provision has touched: the cases construing it, the statutes and rules it connects to, its amendment history, the secondary sources discussing it, and citator links. That is why the annotated code, not the bare statutory text, is where statutory research happens; one page holds the law and every pathway out of it. Each annotation type answers a different kind of question, so read what follows as a menu keyed to the question you are holding. Case Notes / Notes of Decisions. Brief summaries of cases interpreting the statute. Read several to spot leading cases or conflicting interpretations. Each is a focusing question a court has already answered about the provision: “how did the court read this element in this context?” Cross-References. Links to related statutes, regulations, or court rules. Each one is a potential research pathway and a potential next question. Historical Notes and Amendments. The legislative evolution of the statute. Critical for figuring out which version was in effect when the relevant events occurred. Research References. Pointers to secondary sources discussing the statute, a shortcut back to treatises and law review articles that may supply the interpretive context you need. Citator Links. Subsequent amendments, cases interpreting the statute, and pending legislative changes. Always run a citator check on any statute you plan to rely on. A brief worked thread shows the annotations in motion. Suppose your question is the definitional one this book has carried since Chapter 3 : What is the federal definition of “organic”? The annotated code’s index points you to the Organic Foods Production Act. The next move is the one experts stop noticing: pull up the code’s table of contents for the Act, chapter 94 of Title 7, and scan its structure. Near the front, where definitions almost always sit, is a section titled “Definitions,” 7 U.S.C. § 6502, and it supplies the program’s defined terms. Reading the operative provisions in context, you find the statute directs the Secretary of Agriculture to establish the certification program, which hands definitional authority to the agency. That delegation is your next question: what does the USDA’s regulation require? The annotations’ implementing-regulations note points you to 7 C.F.R. Part 205, and the cycle crosses into Chapter 7 . One statute, read in context, answered the question you brought and told you exactly where the next one lives. Sort it Which part of the annotation holds the lead? How have courts read the word “dwelling” in this section? Case notes Notes of decisions summarize the cases interpreting the section. They are leads to opinions, not substitutes for them. Did the section read this way when the lease was signed in 2019? Historical notes Amendment history tells you which version governed on a given date. Has an agency issued a regulation under this section? Cross-references Related statutes, regulations, and rules are linked here. Is there a treatise discussion of this provision? Research references The route back to secondary sources when the text and the cases leave you unsure. Is “tenant” defined somewhere else in the chapter? Cross-references A definition elsewhere in the code controls this section’s terms, and the cross-reference is how you find it.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: The most damaging statutory error is reading a single subsection in isolation and missing the definitions, exceptions, or cross-referenced provisions that change what it actually requires. Read the section in context every time. The second pitfall is citing the wrong version, since statutes are amended and the language in force when your client’s events occurred may differ from today’s text; the historical notes are there to keep you honest. A third is treating an ambiguity as a dead end rather than as your next question, when in fact an undefined term or vague standard is exactly where the research goes next, into case law, legislative history, or agency interpretation. And do not skip the citator check, because a statute can be amended or held unconstitutional and still sit unchanged in an older database copy.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Statutes often delegate implementation authority to agencies. The annotated code’s “Implementing Regulations” notes are your pathway to the Code of Federal Regulations, covered in Chapter 7 . The full picture of what the law requires usually emerges only when you read the statute alongside its implementing regulations: the statute sets the framework, the regulation supplies the operative detail. Chapter 8 covers researching across sources in more depth.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: When statutory text is genuinely ambiguous, courts may look to legislative history (Chapter 10 ). Identifying and articulating the ambiguity is itself an important skill, because before you can argue that legislative history resolves an ambiguity, you first have to show the text is ambiguous. A court committed to plain meaning will never reach the legislative history at all.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: When a federal statute preempts state law, the state statute is invalid to that extent. Always consider preemption when you research a state statutory issue in a federally regulated area. The bounds and application of preemption are the subject of a doctrinal course, as it is too complex for the scope of this textbook.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: When statutory text is ambiguous, courts do not just guess. They reach for the canons of construction , a toolbox of reading rules courts have relied on for centuries, and knowing the handful that do most of the work helps you predict which reading a court will pick. The plain meaning rule says unambiguous text gets applied as written. Expressio unius says that when a statute lists some things, it probably meant to leave out the rest. Ejusdem generis says a catch-all phrase at the end of a list only catches things like the ones listed. And the rule against surplusage says every word is presumed to be doing a job. (Your legislation or statutory interpretation course will hand you the full toolbox and the fights over when each tool applies. For research purposes, recognizing them is enough.) Treat the canons the way this chapter has taught you to treat every interpretive tool: as generators of next questions. If two canons point in different directions, which one your jurisdiction’s courts favor is itself a researchable question. Appendix C ’s How to Read a Statute carries the full working list with examples; that appendix is where the skill gets its reps. The canons also have a secondary source dedicated to them: Sutherland Statutes and Statutory Construction , the treatise courts themselves cite. Even a browse through its table of contents will give you a sense of the range of canons courts use, and it is the place to turn when a canon starts to matter in your case.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Statutes are binding expressions of legislative will. The annotated code is the researcher’s primary statutory tool, connecting legislative text to judicial interpretation, scholarly commentary, and procedural rules. Always read statutes in context, consult the annotations for interpretive case law, and verify currency. And every ambiguity you find is simply your next question. Key Takeaways Statutes are organized chronologically (session laws) and by subject (codes); annotated codes are the best research tool. Read statutory text in context: neighboring sections, definitions, and exceptions all matter. Annotated code features connect the statutory text to its full legal context. Ambiguous statutory language generates the next Question Method cycle: check case law, legislative history, and agency interpretation. Always update statutes using citator tools.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
s: Reviewing Through Practice: Can the Podcaster Record the Call?
t: The following exercises test your ability to map a statute’s anatomy and to use annotations as research pathways, followed by the statutes drill from the single-source set.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: Take a statute your instructor assigns, or choose any substantive section of your state’s code that regulates conduct. Map its anatomy: the operative provision (who must or must not do what), every defined term it uses and where the definition lives, every exception and where it lives, the penalty or consequence provision, and the currency information telling you the text is current. Some of these will live in neighboring sections rather than the one you started in; finding them is the exercise. Deliverable: a labeled anatomy map of the section, with a citation for each component you located outside it. Self-check: if your map shows no defined terms and no exceptions, one of two things is true: you chose an unusually self-contained section, or you did not look in the neighboring sections. It is almost always the second. Statutes are schemes, and reading one section alone is how their traps get sprung.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
t: In an annotated code, take any substantive statute (your instructor may assign one, or reuse a statute you have already read this term) and use its Notes of Decisions or case annotations to identify two cases interpreting the section’s most important term. Do not read the cases yet. Log each in your Research Log as a pathway: the question it appears to answer, the citation, and where the annotation pointed you. This is the discipline of the Chapter 5 protocol’s fourth move, applied from the statute side: annotations hand you leads, and a lead recorded is not an answer synthesized. Deliverable: two Research Log entries, each honestly marked as a lead: the Findings field opens with the words lead only and attributes the claim to the annotation. Self-check: if either entry’s Findings field states what the case held, you exceeded the exercise. All you know is what the annotation claims, and an annotation is an editor’s summary, not the case.

p: Chapter 6: Statutes Research
s: Exercise 6.3 — The Chapter 6 Drill (Statutes Only): Can the Podcaster Record the Call?
t: This is the statutes drill from the single-source set introduced at the end of Chapter 4 . Same rules: one source type only, every question drafted, every answer logged. The scenario. A client runs a small podcast and wants to record phone interviews with sources. Some sources are in California. The client asks: can I record a phone call with a California source without telling them I am recording? The supervising attorney tells you the governing law is California’s recording-consent statute and asks you to answer from the statute. Run the chain yourself. When you have it, check your work against the walkthrough in Appendix E . Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Statutes create broad rules, but much of the law that affects people day to day comes from administrative agencies. Agencies like the EPA, the SEC, and the Department of Labor write the detailed rules, or regulations, that put statutes into practice. Once properly adopted, regulations carry the force of law. You need to be able to locate, read, and update them, because for many regulated activities the regulation, not the statute, is the rule your client actually has to follow. Learning Objectives Explain the rulemaking process and how regulations acquire the force of law Locate federal regulations using the Code of Federal Regulations and eCFR Read and interpret regulatory text, including authority and source notes and preambles Trace the rulemaking history of a regulation through the Federal Register Update regulations to confirm currency Locate basic state administrative materials Integrate regulatory research into the Question Method framework

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: Regulations, Administrative Materials, and the Research Cycle
t: Regulations are where focusing and definitional questions about implemented statutory mandates get answered. A focusing question that begins with a statute (“the statute requires X, so what does compliance actually look like?”) is answered by following the annotated code’s “Implementing Regulations” note straight to the relevant CFR part. A definitional question about a term the statute delegated to the agency (“what does the agency mean by this term?”) is answered by the regulation’s definitions section. And, like statutes, regulations generate new questions at every turn. An authority note raises the question of whether the regulation stays within its statutory grant. A cross-reference raises the question of what the referenced section requires. An incorporated external standard raises the question of what that standard says. Each becomes a Research Log entry and a next cycle.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Regulations are your primary tool for Focusing questions about how a broad statutory mandate operates in practice (“What specific requirements must a food manufacturer meet to label a product organic?”) and Definitional questions about terms statutes delegate to agencies (“What is the federal definition of waters of the United States under the Clean Water Act?”). You will also use regulations for Application questions when a client’s conduct is governed by specific regulatory requirements. As you research any regulatory issue, the Federal Register preamble often supplies the interpretive context the regulation’s text alone cannot. Reflection Point. Why might a regulation be a poor source for answering a no-clue exploratory question, even in a heavily regulated area? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: How Regulations Are Made and What That Means for Research
t: Before a regulation becomes law, it typically goes through a notice-and-comment process governed by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 551 et seq. Understanding the process tells you where to look for interpretive context. Statutory Authorization. Congress passes a statute delegating authority to an agency. The regulation is valid only if it falls within the scope of the authorizing statute, a point that is frequently litigated. Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM). The agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register, explaining what it intends to do and why. The NPRM includes the proposed text and a preamble laying out the agency’s reasoning. Public Comment Period. The agency takes written comments from the public, including individuals, companies, and advocacy groups. Comments come in through regulations.gov and become part of the rulemaking record. Final Rule. After considering comments, the agency publishes the final rule in the Federal Register with binding text, a detailed preamble responding to significant comments, and an effective date. Codification. The final rule is codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), organized by subject. Every stage produces documents you can use. The NPRM shows original intent. The comments show what stakeholders objected to. The final rule’s preamble explains why the agency made specific choices. That preamble is often your single best interpretive resource, the regulatory equivalent of legislative history, and overlooking it is the most common way researchers misread what a regulation requires. A shorthand worth keeping: NPRM = intent; comments = objections; final-rule preamble = the agency’s answers. Put it in order From delegation to codified rule Put the life of a regulation in order, first to last. Congress passes a statute delegating authority to the agency No delegation, no rule. This is why you read the authority note first. The agency publishes a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in the Federal Register The proposal and the agency’s first explanation of it. The public submits written comments The record of what regulated parties and the public objected to. The agency publishes the final rule, with its preamble, in the Federal Register The preamble answers the comments and is the best evidence of what the agency meant. The rule is codified in the Code of Federal Regulations The operative text, arranged by subject, without the explanation.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Federal regulations move through a fixed set of official publications, and each answers a different question about the same rule: what has been proposed, what is codified, and what is current today. Knowing which publication holds which answer is most of regulatory search strategy. Federal Register (FR). The daily publication of proposed rules, final rules, notices, and executive orders. Best for tracing recent or proposed regulatory action. Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The annual codification of all effective regulations, organized into 50 titles by subject. The official source for existing federal regulations. Structure: Title, then Chapter (agency), then Part, then Section. For example, 40 C.F.R. § 50.8 is Title 40 (Protection of Environment / EPA), Part 50 (National Ambient Air Quality Standards), Section 8 (carbon monoxide standards). List of CFR Sections Affected (LSA). A monthly record of which CFR sections have changed since the last annual update. Use it to verify currency when you are working from a print or annual edition. Two small features of every CFR part deserve attention now, because later chapters lean on them. The authority note cites the statute that empowers the agency to issue the part. The source note cites the Federal Register document that created or last amended it, which is the thread you pull to reach the preamble. Appendix D ’s How to Read a Regulation shows both in context. Sort it Which publication answers it? What does the rule require today? CFR The codified, operative text. The eCFR is the current version. Why did the agency reject a commenter’s proposed exemption? Federal Register The final rule’s preamble answers the comments. The CFR carries none of that reasoning. Has this section changed since the annual volume on the shelf was printed? LSA The List of CFR Sections Affected exists for exactly this question. Is an amendment to this rule currently proposed? Federal Register Proposed rules appear here and nowhere in the CFR. Where do all of the agency’s rules on this subject sit together, with their definitions? CFR Codification arranges rules by subject. The Federal Register arranges them by date.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: If you already hold a CFR citation, retrieve it directly in the eCFR and skip the search. Otherwise, start from the statute or topic: use the annotated code’s “Implementing Regulations” notes to locate the relevant CFR part. If you know which agency regulates your issue, browse that agency’s chapters in the CFR or check the agency’s website, which often links directly to its regulations. Keyword searching, in the eCFR (free, updated daily), Westlaw, Lexis, or GovInfo.gov, comes last here too, and only with the precise terms the regulation uses, identified through secondary sources or the statute itself; regulatory drafting is at least as technical as statutory drafting, and the CFR’s structure is the better guide.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: Answering Questions with Regulations and Updating for Currency
t: Regulations can be amended, suspended, or invalidated at any time. Currency checking matters even more for regulatory research than for statutory research, because agencies revise regulations far more often than legislatures amend statutes. Checklist Is this regulation current? Five checks The eCFR (ecfr.gov). Updated daily; the most current freely available source. Each title carries a note indicating the date through which it has been updated. List of CFR Sections Affected (LSA). Use it when you are working from the annual CFR edition to catch any intervening amendments. Federal Register. Check for recent proposed rules, interim final rules, and final rules that may affect your regulation. The Unified Regulatory Agenda, published twice a year, lists the rules agencies plan to propose or finalize. Citators. Run KeyCite (Westlaw) or Shepard’s (Lexis) on your CFR section. Regulatory citators identify decisions that have interpreted, applied, challenged, or invalidated the regulation. A regulation struck down by a court is no longer enforceable, even if it still appears in the CFR text. Agency websites. Some agencies post compliance bulletins, guidance updates, or enforcement-policy changes that effectively change how a regulation operates in practice before the CFR text is formally amended.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Each state has its own administrative code and rulemaking process. State registers publish proposed and final rules; state codes compile them by subject. The research process mirrors the federal model: locate the authorizing statute, find the implementing regulation, and check for updates. Westlaw and Lexis often provide better search functionality than state agency websites do.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Stopping at the CFR text without checking the Federal Register for the preamble and context is the most common regulatory research error, because the agency’s explanation of what its rule means lives in the preamble, not the codified text. The next is ignoring amendments, since agencies revise regulations frequently and an older copy can be silently out of date. Watch too for overlooking related parts that hold the definitions and exceptions controlling the section you are reading. And keep guidance documents in their place; treating a non-binding guidance document as if it were a binding regulation can lead you to tell a client something is legally required when it is only the agency’s preference.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: Guidance Documents: Influential but Not Binding
t: Policy statements and guidance documents do not go through notice-and-comment and lack the force of law, but they are highly influential as statements of how agencies interpret and enforce their regulations . Chapter 11 covers these materials, the weight courts give them, and the case law that governs that weight, in depth. One more development belongs on your radar now: in 2024 the Supreme Court ended the longstanding practice of courts deferring to an agency’s own reading of an ambiguous statute. The doctrinal ins and outs belong to your admin law course. What the shift means for how you weigh administrative authority is addressed in Chapter 11 .

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Regulations implement statutory mandates through the APA notice-and-comment process and carry the force of law once properly promulgated. The Federal Register records rulemaking; the CFR organizes final rules. The preamble is often as important as the regulation text itself. Always trace a regulation’s statutory authority, rulemaking history, and currency, and let your unanswered questions, not the bare CFR text, tell you when you are done. Key Takeaways Regulations implement statutory mandates through the APA notice-and-comment process. The CFR codifies current federal regulations; the eCFR provides the most current free version. The Federal Register preamble is the most important interpretive resource for understanding regulatory intent. Authority notes link regulations to enabling statutes; source notes link them to Federal Register history. Always verify currency using the eCFR, LSA, Federal Register, and citators. Post- Loper Bright , courts independently interpret ambiguous statutes rather than deferring to agency interpretations.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: Reviewing Through Practice: Does the Roofer Need Fall Protection?
t: The following exercises test your ability to locate a regulation, verify its currency, and trace its statutory authority, followed by the regulations drill from the single-source set.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Chapter 3 ’s Research Log example asked what the federal definition of “organic” is. Finish the job properly. Locate the current federal regulation governing organic labeling in the eCFR, and then run the full five-check currency checklist from this chapter on the section you found: the eCFR check with its updated-through date, the LSA if you touched an annual edition, the Federal Register sweep for pending or recent rules, a citator run, and a pass through the agency’s website for guidance that changes how the rule operates in practice. Deliverable: the regulation’s citation, and a currency note recording what each of the five steps found, including the exact date the eCFR title had been updated through on the day you checked. Self-check: a currency note with five entries reading “nothing found” is possible but should make you suspicious. At minimum, the eCFR step always yields a date, and the Federal Register step nearly always yields activity somewhere in the part. If your note is empty, your searches were too narrow.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
t: Every regulation exists because a statute told an agency to write it. Find the authority note for the federal organic-labeling regulation ( Appendix D shows you where the authority citation lives in a regulatory section), name the delegating statute, and write two sentences: one on what the statute itself decided, and one on what it left for the agency to fill in. This is the statute-to-regulation joint that Chapter 8 will build on, met here for the first time in the wild. Deliverable: the authority citation and your two sentences. Self-check: the two sentences should describe genuinely different things. If they blur together, you have not yet located the line between the legislature’s judgment and the agency’s detail, and that line is the whole reason this source type exists.

p: Chapter 7: Regulations and Administrative Research
s: Exercise 7.3 — The Chapter 7 Drill (Regulations Only): Does the Roofer Need Fall Protection?
t: This is the regulations drill from the single-source set introduced at the end of Chapter 4 . Same rules: one source type only, every question drafted, every answer logged. The scenario. Our client is a small residential roofing contractor. A new hire will be working on a two-story house, roughly twenty feet up. The client asks: am I legally required to provide fall protection, and if so, at what height does the requirement kick in and what counts as acceptable protection? The supervising attorney tells you this is governed by the federal OSHA construction regulations and asks you to answer from the regulations. Run the chain yourself. When you have it, check your work against the walkthrough in Appendix E . Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Research is rarely a tidy matter of finding one statute and a few cases. Often the law governing a client’s issue is spread across many sources: a federal statute, a state common law rule, agency regulations, local ordinances, decades of judicial interpretation. To research efficiently, you have to understand how those sources intersect and when to move from one to another. To research completely, you have to do something more: identify every authority type that governs the issue, reach each one, and read it directly rather than through another source’s description of it. A researcher who treats each source type as a separate, sealed exercise produces a fragmented analysis. A researcher who lets one source type stand in for the others produces something worse, a confident analysis with a hole in it. This chapter teaches both skills: moving fluidly among sources while keeping a single legal question in view, and knowing, at the end of a complex project, that your coverage of the governing authority is complete. Chapters 4 through 7 treated each source type on its own. This chapter shows how they work together in practice, with the Question Method as the organizing framework. Learning Objectives Recognize when a legal issue is governed by multiple overlapping sources of law Build a research map that identifies every authority type in play, and maintain it as a coverage checklist Apply the Question Method to move across source types as each answer hands off to the next question Read statutes and regulations directly, including their definitions and related sections, rather than only as other sources characterize them Recognize and document research gaps Use a return pass through secondary sources to confirm coverage on complex, wide-ranging projects

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Researching Across Sources and the Research Cycle
t: In single-source research, the Question Method tells you which source to consult and how to read it. In multi-source research, it does something more: it tells you when to switch sources and why. The mechanism is the “Next Question” field of your Research Log. Each source you consult answers your current question and, in doing so, generates the next one, and the next question may be answered best by a different source type. A secondary source orients you and points you to the governing statute. The statute states the framework and, through an undefined term or a delegation of authority, points you to the regulation. The regulation supplies the operative detail and, through its ambiguities, points you to the case law interpreting it. The case law applies the rule to facts and may send you back to a secondary source to make sense of a confusing line of decisions. Each handoff is a question type changing: exploratory to focusing, focusing to definitional, definitional to application. Being explicit in your method lets you flag when you have gotten all you can out of a source and need to move forward. The method also decides which source comes next. The question in front of you picks the source, and the discipline of asking “did this fully answer my question, or only partially?” after every cycle keeps you moving wherever the answer actually lives. What the full landscape of authority contains, and how to be sure you covered all of it, is the work of the rest of this chapter.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: In many areas of law, statutes, regulations, and case law all together set the law. The statute sets the framework and delegates authority to an agency. Regulations implement the statute’s mandate with technical and procedural detail. Case law interprets both the statute and the regulations, resolving ambiguities and setting their scope. Your research has to engage all three to give a complete answer. Missing any one of them leaves a gap, and often an error, because the missing source is frequently the very one that would have changed the conclusion. Explore Three sources, one rule Select a corner to see the question that source answers and what it cannot tell you alone. Statute | the framework. Answers: what does the law require, prohibit, or permit, and whom does it reach? It cannot tell you the technical detail it delegated to an agency, or how courts have read its undefined terms. Regulation | the detail. Answers: how does the agency put the statutory mandate into operation? It is valid only within the authority the statute gave, so it cannot be read without the statute behind it. Case law | the operation. Answers: how have the statute and the regulation worked on real facts, and are they valid? An opinion’s quotation of a statute or rule is a pointer to the text, never a replacement for reading it. Reflection Point. Chapters 4 through 7 walled you into one source type at a time. Why does that discipline make multi-source research easier rather than harder? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Go to the Source: Reading Primary Authority Directly
t: Multi-source research creates a temptation that single-source research never did. When the cases you are reading quote the statute, it begins to feel as though you have read the statute. When a guidance document walks through the regulation, it feels as though you have read the regulation. You have not. You have read someone’s excerpt, selected for someone else’s purposes, and building your analysis on an excerpt is one of the quietest ways a multi-source project goes wrong. Consider what an opinion’s quotation of a statute actually gives you: the language that mattered to that dispute, and nothing more. The definitions section that controls the operative terms almost never makes it into the quote. Neither do the exceptions, one of which may remove your client’s conduct from the statute’s reach entirely, nor the cross-referenced sections the provision incorporates. The quoted text may not even be current. Statutes get amended, and an opinion faithfully quoting the pre-amendment version will mislead you without containing a single inaccurate word. And a court’s paraphrase is not text at all; it is interpretation, valuable for what it is and dangerous the moment you mistake it for the thing interpreted. Regulations invite the same shortcut and punish it the same way. Guidance summarizes. Preambles explain. Opinions excerpt. The operative CFR text is what binds your client, and the sections surrounding it in the same part, the definitions, the exemptions, the compliance detail a neighboring section supplies, are part of the rule whether or not any other source thought to mention them. So adopt a bright-line habit: the moment a statute or regulation becomes load-bearing in your analysis, open it in the code and read it the way Chapters 6 and 7 taught. For a statute, that means the operative provision, the definitions section, the exceptions, and the cross-references. For a regulation, it means the section itself, the part’s definitions, the authority note, and the adjacent sections of the part. (Appendices C and D walk both reading protocols step by step.) Then make your Research Log honest about what happened. An entry that records the statute as a case quoted it is a case-law entry. The statute gets its own entry when you have read the statute.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Open your Research Log and suppose you find five consecutive case-law entries. Is something wrong? Quite possibly not. If your question is a common-law question, the elements of negligence, the formation of a contract, the cases are where the rule lives, and a long run of case entries is the research working exactly as designed. The same is true when you are deep in application questions, comparing your client’s facts against a line of decisions, or following a citation trail through the cases that built a doctrine. A streak in the log measures the rhythm of your research. By itself, it tells you nothing about whether the research is complete. The failure that deserves a name is a coverage failure: an authority type that governs your issue and that you never looked for, never found, or never read directly. Call it the single-source trap, and notice that it comes in two forms. In the first, a governing authority type is missing from the research altogether. The agency’s regulations sit unread while you work through a sixth case, or a local ordinance controls the client’s conduct and never appears in your log. In the second, subtler form, the authority type appears in your log but only secondhand: every statutory point you hold arrived through a case’s characterization, every regulatory point through a guidance document, and the primary text itself was never opened. That is the failure the last section taught you to correct. You will see the trap again in Chapter 9 ’s diagnostic toolkit and in Chapter 14 ’s practice contexts. Check yourself Audit this log Five consecutive entries in a Research Log on a wage claim list these as the source consulted: a court of appeals opinion; a second opinion from the same court; a district court opinion quoting the statute’s overtime exemption; a state supreme court opinion; a district court opinion summarizing the Department of Labor’s rule. What is the problem? Nothing. Five cases on point is thorough research. It may be thorough on one side of the triangle. Count the authority types this project is governed by, then count the ones in the log. The log relies too heavily on district court opinions. Weight matters, but it is not the gap here. Something that governs the claim was never opened at all. The statute and the regulation appear only secondhand, through what courts said about them. The subtler form of the single-source trap. Two governing authority types are in the log only as quotations and summaries. Open both and read them directly, or record why you are not.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Each source type answers a different kind of question about the same issue. The statute tells you the framework. The regulation tells you the technical detail. The case law tells you how both operate in practice. Your annotated outline should reflect all three, and your Research Log should track when you shifted from one source type to another and why. Worked example: ADA website accessibility. Must a business make its website accessible under the ADA? One question, three source types, each answering what only it can. A secondary source orients and points to 42 U.S.C. § 12182, Title III’s public-accommodations provision; the statute, read directly, supplies the framework but never mentions websites, because it was enacted in 1990; the DOJ’s Title III regulations, 28 C.F.R. Part 36, turn out to contain no web-accessibility rule, only guidance and proposals, which makes the guidance’s weight its own question; and the case law reveals a circuit split on whether websites are “public accommodations” at all. The synthesis is an annotated outline holding all four findings, framework, regulatory gap, guidance and its weight, split, which is what an accurate answer to a genuinely contested question looks like. The full walkthrough appears in Appendix G . Sort it A leave dispute under the FMLA: where does each answer live? How many weeks of leave may an eligible employee take in a year? Statute The entitlement itself is the framework, set by Congress. What information must a medical certification contain to be sufficient? Statute A fair trap. The Act itself lists what a sufficient certification states. The regulation then elaborates. Read the statute before the rule that implements it. How many days of incapacity and how many treatment visits make a condition “serious” through continuing treatment? Regulation Technical detail the statute left to the Department of Labor. Have courts treated a text message to a supervisor as adequate notice of the need for leave? Case law An application question: how the rule has operated on facts like yours. Is the Department’s notice rule a valid exercise of the authority Congress delegated? Case law Only a court decides whether a regulation is within its statute.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Managing the Research Log Across Multiple Sources
t: When you research across sources, the Research Log becomes especially important. Each source type may generate a new sub-question that leads down a different path, so record each question, source, and finding to keep track of how the sources connect. Two small habits make the log do coverage work for you. First, note the authority type of each entry (statute, regulation, case, secondary source, guidance), so that you can quickly see if you have yet to directly engage with a source. Second, when you switch source types, record why in the Next Question field. That “why” is the record of your research judgment, and it is what lets you, or the colleague who inherits the project, reconstruct the movement across sources later.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: When a federal statute and a state common law rule appear to cover the same conduct, ask first whether the federal statute preempts state law expressly or impliedly. If it does not, both may apply, and your analysis has to address each. The priority rules in practice: the U.S. Constitution overrides all other authority; federal statutes and treaties override conflicting state law; regulations are valid only if within statutory authority; and case law interprets all of the above and cannot contradict clear statutory, regulatory, or constitutional text.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Confidence on a Complex Project: The Return Pass
t: There is a question every new researcher asks on a big project, usually late at night: how can I know I have found everything? The issue sprawls across a statute, two sets of regulations, a stack of guidance, and case law from three jurisdictions. The log runs to dozens of entries. No search can prove a negative. The anxiety is reasonable. Confidence on a complex project is something you build, with specific moves. Audit the research log, authority type by authority type, direct engagement or explicit ruling-out, as the trap section described. Consider going back to the secondary source that opened the project and reread the relevant sections now, at the end, with everything you have learned. Call it the return pass. Now you know the legal points, so additional sections might prove relevant where they were not before. Looking at these sections will hopefully confirm what you have found in your research. If nothing new surfaces, that silence is affirmative evidence that your coverage is complete, and it belongs in your Research Log as exactly that: “return pass through [the treatise], §§ [sections]; no new threads.” Checked and found nothing missing is a finding. It is what earned confidence looks like on paper. In the worst case, if you find another authority you did not realize was implicated or new research questions you had not asked, you have highlighted a gap in your research and you address it the same way you would any gap you surface, regardless of when you find it. Whatever the result, you will be more confident when you reach the close out phase of your research process.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Complex research projects are subject to more error not because they are necessarily novel problems, but rather because the size of the project leads to more moments for small failures to compound. You did not validate a point of law and traced backward to other cases that cited that faulty point of law. Or you took a case’s overview of a statute as good enough, and in failing to look at the statute directly, did not find critical language in the section that changes the application of the law to your case, leading you to continue down a line of cases that are not on point for your purposes. The solution is to research thoughtfully and not to skip your research pauses . By engaging in this way, you are more likely to catch a misstep, misinterpretation, or gap that would cause you trouble later unchecked. Another trap of complex projects is losing yourself in the research. There are so many authorities across various source types that you may continue searching for more and more to feel as though you have truly ‘completed’ the research. To avoid this, stick to the method and synthesize what you find into your outline. In the same way you would not look for 5 cases to cite to establish the elements of negligence in a common law research problem, more is not always better in a complex research project. By synthesizing as you go, you can best assess if you need more sources to either securely support a legal claim in your writing or address a gap in your argument.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Multi-source research is the same cycle with two added judgments: when to switch sources, and how to know your coverage is complete. The research map supplies the checklist, and the statute-regulation-case law triangle is its regulatory core. Read every load-bearing statute and regulation directly, related sections included, because an excerpt is not the law and a paraphrase is someone’s interpretation of it. The single-source trap, properly scoped, is a coverage failure, a governing authority type unreached or reached only secondhand, and its diagnostic is the map, not the streak. On sprawling projects, build confidence structurally: audit the log against the map, run the return pass through your secondary sources, and triangulate your finding tools. The line between “the law is unsettled” and “I have not finished looking” remains the difference between a finding and a confession. Key Takeaways Most real legal issues are governed by an overlapping combination of statutes, regulations, case law, and constitutional or local provisions. The research map identifies every authority type in play and, kept current, becomes the coverage checklist you audit against. Read statutes and regulations directly, with their definitions, exceptions, and related sections; never rely on another source’s excerpt or paraphrase for a load-bearing rule. The single-source trap is a coverage failure, an authority type unchecked or checked only secondhand; a streak of same-type log entries is not by itself a problem. The return pass, rereading your orienting secondary source at the end with expert eyes, catches unpulled threads cheaply and turns “nothing new” into documented evidence of coverage. Research gap identification, distinguishing “the law is unsettled” from “I haven’t found the answer yet,” is a critical professional skill.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Reviewing Through Practice: The Drone Capstone
t: The following exercises test your ability to map the relationships among source types and to distinguish unsettled law from incomplete research, followed by the capstone of the drill set.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: Return to the organic-labeling question that has run through this book since Chapter 3 , and build its research map as a statute-regulation-case-law triangle. At the statute corner, record what the delegating statute decided, located through the regulation’s authority note. At the regulation corner, record what the regulation itself supplies, located through the eCFR. At the case-law corner, identify at least one decision interpreting either, located through an annotated code or a citator. Then annotate each edge of the triangle: what question sends a researcher traveling from this corner to that one? Deliverable: a one-page triangle map, corners filled, edges annotated with the traveling questions. Self-check: the edges are the exercise. If your map has three full corners and empty edges, you have catalogued sources without mapping the movement between them, and movement between sources is what this chapter teaches.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
t: From any research question you have worked in this course (any of the Part I drills works, or your instructor may assign one), write two findings: one that honestly reads “the law is genuinely unsettled on this point,” and one that honestly reads “I have not yet found the answer.” Defend each in two sentences, naming what you searched and why that search entitles you, or does not, to the stronger claim. “The law is unsettled” is a professional conclusion; “I could not find any law” is a confession. Knowing which one you are holding is the skill. Deliverable: the two findings with defenses. Self-check: the unsettled finding must rest on a search thorough enough that a supervisor would accept it, and its defense should say so specifically. If both of your findings could trade labels without the defenses changing, neither defense is doing its job yet.

p: Chapter 8: Researching Across Sources
s: Exercise 8.3 — The Capstone: The Drone Question
t: This is the capstone of the single-source drill set introduced at the end of Chapter 4 , and it is the exercise this whole chapter has been building toward. Run the chain yourself first, from the scenario alone: draft every question, log every answer, and decide where closure is. Then, and only then, check your work against the walkthrough in Appendix E . The scenario. Our client runs a small real-estate marketing business and wants to start flying a camera drone to shoot aerial photos and video of listed properties, for paying clients. The client asks: what do I have to do to operate the drone legally for this commercial work, and what legal exposure should I worry about? You do not yet know the area, and no one has narrowed it for you. Map and answer the question across whatever sources govern, using the Question Method to move among them. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
s: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Chapter 2 introduced the opening phase of search: natural language searching, synonym mapping, and the core Boolean connectors. This chapter picks up where that process leads, at the moment your questions become specific and your goal shifts from discovery to precision. At this stage you know the legal terminology and you know which sources govern. Your remaining questions are targeted: Does the rule apply in this specific factual context? Is there a circuit split on this point? Has this particular statutory phrase been interpreted by courts in my jurisdiction? Those questions call for search tools built for precision, not exploration. This chapter also takes on the question every new researcher struggles with: when am I done? The narrowing tools and the closing-out protocol are two halves of the same final phase. One finds the right authority, the other confirms you have all of it. Learning Objectives Construct precise Boolean searches using proximity, exclusion, and frequency connectors Transition from broad orientation searching to precise, targeted retrieval as your questions narrow Apply a systematic closing-out protocol to confirm research is complete, current, and gap-free Diagnose and respond to common research problems: no results, too many results, conflicting authority, circular trails Document the research closure decision in a defensible, professional manner

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
s: The Full Connector Set: Proximity, Frequency, and Exclusion
t: Building on the core connectors from Chapter 2 , this chapter adds the precision tools that make Boolean searching a real narrowing instrument. Proximity connectors specify how close together terms must appear, which dramatically cuts false positives. /n requires terms within n words of each other in either order (landlord /5 heat, within five words). /s requires terms within the same sentence. /p requires terms within the same paragraph. Be aware that /s and /p do not look for terms within sentences or paragraphs as we think of them structurally. They are database shorthand for a default number. For example, /s might be shorthand for /14. What the actual number is a database-specific artifact they don’t share. Databases also allow you to determine distance between terms as well as the order. pre/n requires the first term to appear before the second within n words (reasonable pre/3 accommodation). Platforms also allow you to use connectors to exclude results where terms are within a distance from each other (e.g., cases where medical is within three words of liability), but the syntax is not uniform. At the time of publication, Lexis uses term NOT /n term while Westlaw uses BUT NOT (or %) term /n term . Check the system’s documentation before attempting to use proximity exclusion. Frequency connectors. ATLEAST n(term) requires the term to appear at least n times in the document. ATLEAST3(preemption) retrieves only documents where preemption is discussed substantively rather than mentioned in passing. This helps you find documents where a concept is a major focus rather than a stray reference. The practice database below shows the difference. It holds eight invented case summaries. Four are on point for the question the next section works through, whether remote work can be a required accommodation for an employee with an anxiety disorder; four are not. Run the presets in order and watch the off-point results fall away. Search lab AND, then closer, then closer still Ibarra v. Meridian Health Plans | on point. The employee, who has an anxiety disorder, asked to work from home three days a week. The court held that a reasonable accommodation may include telecommuting where physical presence is not an essential function of the job. Novak v. Brightline Analytics | on point. Plaintiff’s panic disorder, a mental health condition, worsened in the open office. Her request for remote work as a reasonable accommodation under the ADA should have triggered the interactive process. Osei v. Great Basin Credit Union | on point. Anxiety and depression limited the analyst’s ability to commute. The employer refused telecommuting without considering whether it was a reasonable accommodation, and summary judgment was improper. Pruitt v. Tri-County Dispatch | on point. The court found that permitting a dispatcher with post-traumatic stress to perform her duties off-site was a reasonable accommodation under the statute. Quintana v. Atlas Warehousing | off point. The ADA requires reasonable accommodation of known disabilities. Here the warehouse employee sought a modified lifting schedule after a back injury, which the employer granted in part. In a remote part of the record, a supervisor mentioned the plaintiff’s anxiety about an upcoming audit. Rowe v. Harborview Hotels | off point. A customer alleged the hotel’s website was inaccessible under Title III of the ADA. The hotel offered remote booking by telephone as an accommodation, and the customer’s anxiety about travel was not at issue. Salas v. Pine Ridge School District | off point. The teacher requested a classroom aide as a reasonable accommodation for a hearing impairment. The district’s remote learning program ended the following year, and the court expressed no anxiety about mootness. Tran v. Lakeshore Logistics | off point. The employer’s telecommuting policy applied to all staff during an office renovation. No disability was alleged, and the claim concerned unpaid overtime. The first sear

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
s: Translating Your Research Question into a Precision Search
t: The discipline of the Question Method pays off here, because a precisely stated question already contains the terms and relationships you need for a Boolean search. This is the most direct link between the method and the mechanics: a well-drafted question is, in effect, a Boolean search waiting to be formatted. Example. Your question is “Have Ninth Circuit courts held that remote work is a required reasonable accommodation under the ADA for employees with anxiety disorders?” Extract the components: core concepts (ADA, reasonable accommodation, remote work / telecommute / work from home, anxiety); the relationship (accommodation and remote work should be close together); the jurisdiction (Ninth Circuit filter). The resulting search: “reasonable accommodation” /10 (remote! OR telecommut! OR “work from home”) AND (anxiety OR “mental health”), with the Ninth Circuit filter applied. Now look at the same question translated badly: ADA AND accommodation AND remote AND anxiety. Every concept is welded to a single word, so the telecommuting cases vanish, and nothing requires the concepts to appear anywhere near one another, so a passing mention of anxiety in an unrelated ADA opinion still qualifies. Set the two side by side and you can see what the good version is actually doing: synonyms gathered with OR, concepts bound with proximity, jurisdiction filtered. A bad example next to a good one is the fastest way to learn the difference. The general principle: find all synonyms for a concept using OR and the expansion operators; require concepts to co-occur using AND; specify how close together they must appear using proximity connectors; find specific legal tests using quotation marks; exclude irrelevant context using NOT; require substantive treatment using ATLEAST; and require term order using pre/n.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law use similar but not identical syntax. Westlaw uses /n for proximity; Bloomberg uses W/n; Lexis uses /n but with slightly different behavior for /s and /p. Always check the syntax documentation for the specific database before you run precision searches. A misread connector can produce a radically different result set, and worse, it can silently exclude the very authority you are looking for. You can find each database’s terms and connectors in their help file.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: For any substantial project, record each search string, the database used, the number of results, and whether the search was productive. A search log keeps you from repeating yourself, provides evidence of thoroughness, and supports your research closure documentation. It works hand in hand with the Research Log: the Research Log tracks the questions and answers, the search log tracks the exact queries that produced them. As your research log evolves with your the growth of your research skills, so too will your search log.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Precision searching narrows your results; closing out confirms that what you found is complete and current. Notice that this is the Question Method’s Checkpoint again, run at full scale: where the checkpoint asks whether one answer was sufficient, the protocol asks whether the whole project is. Checklist The closing-out protocol Run a final sweep. Before you declare research complete, run at least one more search using different terms than the ones that produced your best results, and at least one search aimed deliberately at authority that cuts against your position, the adverse-authority question Rule 3.3 will hold you to (Chapter 12 ). These additional searches, even when they turn up nothing new, create a documented record that you searched comprehensively. Update every case and statute. Run KeyCite or Shepard’s on every primary authority you plan to cite, and read each one for the specific proposition you cite it for, because you never cite what you have not read. For cases, check for negative treatment in your jurisdiction, and note which points of law it reaches. For statutes, check for pending amendments and recent session laws. For regulations, check the eCFR effective date and the LSA. Evaluate the outline for gaps. Every legal proposition should be supported by primary authority, and every ambiguous term should have a source addressing it. A gap is either a remaining research question or a genuine area of legal uncertainty your analysis must acknowledge. Document the closure decision. Record that you completed the protocol. Note the databases searched, the final search strings, the dates you verified authorities, and any open questions. This protects you professionally; if your research is ever questioned, you can show exactly what you did and why you concluded it was enough. Reflection Point. Your annotated outline already answers the question. Why does the closing-out protocol still make you run a search aimed at authority that cuts against you? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
s: The Difference Between No Results and No Law
t: A search that returns nothing means one of two things: there is no authority on the point, or your search was too narrow. Before you conclude the law is silent, try alternative terms, remove proximity constraints, expand to persuasive authority from other jurisdictions, and check secondary sources for discussion of the issue. Only after you have exhausted the alternatives is a “no results” conclusion defensible, and the difference matters enormously, because “there is no law” is a powerful argument while “I could not find any law” is a confession. (This is the same line Chapter 8 drew for research gaps; here it becomes a closing-out discipline.) Sort it No results: is the law silent, or is the search? One search, three terms joined by /5, zero results. Keep searching A single narrow search proves only that those words do not sit that close together. Zero results in your state’s cases. You have not looked at statutes, regulations, or a secondary source. Keep searching You may be in the wrong source type. That is the single-source trap, not silence. Alternative terms tried, proximity removed, other jurisdictions checked, and a leading treatise says the question is open in your state. Defensible to report no authority You exhausted the alternatives and a secondary source confirms the gap. Now “there is no law” is a finding, and your log proves it. Zero results for the statute’s exact phrase, because the statute was amended last year and courts have not yet construed the new language. Defensible to report no authority A real gap with an explanation. Say so, and turn to analogous authority and the prior version’s cases. Zero results, and you used only the client’s own word for the problem. Keep searching Courts may call it something else. Find the legal term in a secondary source and search again.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
s: When Research Goes Wrong: Diagnosing Common Problems
t: Every researcher hits moments when the research is not working. What sets competent researchers apart is that they diagnose the problem accurately and apply a specific correction instead of just searching harder. Explore What symptom are you seeing? No results. Check whether your terms are too specific, and broaden with OR and synonyms, remove proximity constraints, or reduce the number of terms. Check whether the issue is genuinely novel and may call for analogous authority. Check whether you are in the wrong source type, the single-source trap from Chapter 8 , and should return to a secondary source. Too many results. The search is probably too broad. Add a proximity connector, add a third term, apply jurisdiction and date filters, or use ATLEAST for substantive treatment. Remember that you are looking for the answer to a specific question, not every possibly relevant document. Conflicting authority. Diagnose whether the conflict is jurisdictional, factual, temporal, or doctrinal. Apply the hierarchy of authority. Address the conflict honestly in your analysis; a genuine split is itself a research finding, not something to hide. No authority in your jurisdiction. Confirm the silence first: other source types, other terms. Then widen deliberately to persuasive authority from other jurisdictions, an ALR annotation or fifty-state survey, and analogous rules at home. Report it as what it is: an open question here, with the direction the persuasive weight runs. You cannot follow the source. You have probably skipped a question. Step back to the exploratory or definitional question the source assumes you already answered, take it to a secondary source, and return once you have the vocabulary. The law is genuinely uncertain. Before you conclude the law is unsettled, verify with secondary sources, search for analogous authority, and check persuasive authority from other jurisdictions. Law review articles, Restatement provisions, and legislative history give you the analytical framework for genuinely open questions.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: The temptation at the finish line is to declare victory the moment you find your best authority, but skipping the final sweep with alternative terms is how a controlling case slips past you. A quieter danger lives in the syntax itself: a mistyped connector does not error out, it simply returns the wrong set, sometimes excluding the very authority you needed, so verify the database’s connector rules before you trust a precision search. Be careful, too, not to read an empty result list as proof the law is silent; “I could not find it” and “it does not exist” are very different claims, and only the second is an argument. Finally, do not leave closure undocumented. The note explaining what you searched and why you stopped is what protects you if the work is ever questioned.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Narrowing and closing out are the final phases of every research cycle. Precision Boolean searching converts broad orientation results into a targeted, comprehensive authority set. The closing-out protocol confirms that every authority is current, every gap is identified, and the research decision is documented. Together they convert “I think I’m done” into “I can demonstrate that I’m done.” Key Takeaways Proximity connectors (/n, /s, /p), platform-specific exclusion operators, ATLEAST, and the exact-phrase quotation are the primary precision instruments. Translate your research questions directly into Boolean searches: key terms become search terms, and the relationship between them determines the connectors. Closing out requires a final sweep with alternative terms, citator updates on all primary authority, gap analysis against the annotated outline, and documentation of the closure decision. Document the closure decision in your Research Log. No results is not the same as no law; exhaust alternative search strategies before concluding the law is silent.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: The following exercises test precision search construction and the discipline of documented closure. Each one writes to the Search Log.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Take three research questions from a current project, or from your instructor’s set, or from your own completed drills, and translate each into a precision search: synonyms gathered with OR, concepts bound with proximity connectors rather than bare ANDs, jurisdiction and source type filtered before the search runs. Record every search in your Search Log as you go: the query as entered, the filters, the result count, and one line on result quality. Deliverable: three Search Log sequences, one per question. Self-check: every search string should use at least one proximity connector doing real work. If AND is the only connective tissue in all three strings, you translated the Chapter 2 way, and this chapter existed to upgrade you.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Take this question: is a landlord liable when a tenant’s guest is injured on a broken staircase? Translate it twice. First, deliberately badly: all ANDs, single words, no synonyms, no proximity, no filters. Then properly, with the full Chapter 9 toolkit. Run both versions back to back and write two sentences on what the two result sets tell you. Contrast is the fastest way to sharpen the discrimination this chapter teaches, and building the bad version yourself teaches more than being shown one. Deliverable: both strings, both result counts, and your two sentences. Self-check: your sentences should name a specific difference, in volume, in relevance of the first page, in what floated to the top, not a generic “the good one was better.” If you cannot name the specific difference, look at result ten in each list and start there.

p: Chapter 9: Narrowing and Closing Out Your Research
t: Run this chapter’s closing-out protocol, every step, on any research chain you have completed in this course (a Part I drill works well), and document the closure decision in your Research Log: the final sweep with alternative terms, the citator updates, the check against the original question, and your explicit finding of analytical closure or a named remaining gap. Deliverable: the documented closure decision. Self-check: one test, and it is the chapter’s test. If you cannot document why you stopped, you have not closed. You have just stopped. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: When courts interpret statutes, they often confront a question about what the legislature meant when it wrote or amended the law. Statutory language can be ambiguous or broad, and judges sometimes look beyond the text to find its intended meaning. Legislative history is the record of materials produced as a bill moves through the legislative process, from early drafts to floor debates. These materials help uncover legislative intent: why the law was enacted, what problem it sought to solve, and how lawmakers expected it to operate. One important caveat: legislative history is persuasive, not binding. The first step is always the statute’s plain language; only if genuine ambiguity remains do interpreters look to legislative intent, and even then courts may consider it but are never required to follow it. Learning Objectives Explain the role of legislative history in statutory interpretation Identify the types of documents that comprise legislative history and their relative weight Conduct a complete federal legislative history research project using multiple databases Locate basic state legislative history materials Integrate legislative history research into the Question Method framework

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
s: Legislative History and the Research Cycle
t: Legislative history is unusual among research sources, because you should almost never start a project here. The Question Method tells you precisely when to arrive and when to stay away. You arrive at legislative history only when a prior cycle has produced a specific kind of question: a focusing or definitional question about an ambiguous statutory term that the text itself, the case law, and the regulations have all failed to resolve. That ordering is not arbitrary. Because legislative history is merely persuasive and many courts discount it heavily, consulting it before you have established that the text is genuinely ambiguous is wasted effort, since a court committed to plain meaning will never reach your findings. The method’s discipline of naming the question type protects you here.
