Only a question that begins “the statute is ambiguous as to X, and no higher-authority source resolves it” justifies opening the legislative record. Sort it Is it time for legislative history? You have read the operative subsection but not the chapter’s definitions section. Not yet The text may answer the question itself. Legislative history comes after the statute, never before it. The term is undefined, the text supports two readings, and no court in your jurisdiction has construed it. Yes, now Ambiguity that the text and the cases leave open is exactly the gap legislative history exists to fill. Your state supreme court construed the term last year. Not yet A binding construction answers the question. History matters only if you intend to argue the court was wrong. The annotated code shows the disputed phrase was added by amendment, and the question is what the amendment was meant to change. Yes, now A question about why language changed is a question about the documents that record the change. Once you are properly here, the method shapes how you engage with the materials by keeping the originating question in view. You are not reading the entire legislative record of a major statute. You are searching it for the specific provision or term your question concerns. That focus tells you which documents to prioritize, the committee and conference reports discussing your provision and the bill versions showing whether your specific language was added or changed, and it lets you skim past the vast bulk of the record that does not touch your question. And because legislative history so often raises as many questions as it answers, a committee report silent on your term, a floor statement that contradicts the report, each finding feeds back into the cycle as a new question about weight and reliability rather than a final answer.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Legislative history research usually arises from Focusing questions generated during statutory research: “The statute uses the term significant risk , so what did Congress mean by that?” It may also arise from Exploratory questions about a statute’s purpose (“Why was this law enacted?”) or Application questions about congressional expectations (“Did Congress intend this statute to cover independent contractors?”). If your question can be answered by the statute’s plain text, you do not need legislative history. If the text is ambiguous, legislative history is your next source. Different materials answer different question types at different stages: committee reports answer foundational questions about purpose; hearings answer background questions; bill versions answer focusing questions about why specific language was chosen; and floor statements may answer application questions about how sponsors expected the law to operate. Reflection Point. Why is legislative history a poor first stop even when your question is about what the legislature meant? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
s: How Legislative History Is Made and What That Means for Research
t: Each stage of the legislative process produces distinct documents, and understanding each stage’s typical output tells you where to look and what to expect. Explore A bill's journey, and the paper it leaves behind Bill introduction | bill versions. The original bill, subsequent amendments, and bill versions, useful for comparing language changes over time to determine whether specific language was added or removed intentionally. Committee review | reports, hearings. Committee reports, hearings, committee prints, and markups. Committee reports are the most authoritative evidence of legislative intent; courts cite them frequently and give them substantial weight. Hearings include expert testimony and public comment, which reveal policy concerns and factual context, though they reflect individual viewpoints rather than legislative consensus. Floor debate and passage | Congressional Record. The Congressional Record contains sponsor statements and debate context. Statements by bill sponsors and floor managers carry more weight than other members’ remarks. One caution: members may insert statements into the Record that were never actually spoken on the floor, and these carry reduced interpretive weight. Conference committee | conference report. When House and Senate versions differ, a conference committee produces conference reports reconciling the two. These carry high interpretive weight, because they represent both chambers’ final agreement on disputed provisions. Presidential action | signing statement. Signing statements or veto messages give the executive perspective, though they carry lower interpretive weight, since the President is not a legislator.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
s: The Most Important Sources and Their Weight
t: You have now seen these documents once, in the order Congress creates them. Here they are again, reranked in the order courts trust them. Committee reports. High. Reflect the drafting committee’s collective explanation; courts cite them frequently. The committee reports on the Civil Rights Act of 1964 are a classic example, providing extensive discussion of key provisions that courts later relied on. Conference reports. High. Represent both chambers’ final agreement on disputed provisions; often the definitive source on compromised language. Bill versions and amendments. Moderate. Evidence of how language evolved. If “knowingly” was added to a criminal statute late in the process, that likely signals an intent to require proof of mental state. Hearings. Moderate to low. Informative, but they reflect individual viewpoints rather than consensus. Floor debates. Variable. Value depends on the speaker’s role (bill sponsors and floor managers carry more weight) and the clarity of the intent expressed. Presidential statements. Low to moderate. Provide the executive perspective, not legislative intent. Check yourself Four documents, one ambiguous word A statute bars “vehicles” from a wilderness area. Your client rode an electric bicycle. Which of these is the strongest evidence of what Congress meant? The committee report’s section-by-section analysis, which says the bar reaches “motorized conveyances of any kind.” The drafting committee’s collective explanation, written to tell the full chamber what it was voting on. A floor statement by a senator who voted against the bill, warning that it would ban bicycles. An opponent has every reason to overstate a bill’s reach. Floor statements carry weight in proportion to the speaker’s role, and an opponent’s role is the weakest. Testimony from a cycling association at a subcommittee hearing. Informative about the problem Congress heard about. It reflects a witness’s view, not the legislature’s. The President’s signing statement praising the protection of “quiet places.” The executive’s perspective on a bill Congress wrote.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Identify the law. Start with the statute’s credit line in the annotated code: the Public Law number, the Statutes at Large citation, and the enactment year. For the ADA, that is Pub. L. No. 101-336, 104 Stat. 327 (1990). Find the bill number and Congress. Use Congress.gov or USCCAN to identify the bill number (for the ADA, S. 933) and the Congress (the 101st). Check for compiled legislative histories first. Before you build your own, see whether someone has already done it. The Union List of Legislative Histories, Nancy Johnson’s Sources of Compiled Legislative Histories , ProQuest Legislative Insight, and HeinOnline’s compiled histories catalog thousands of them. Starting with a compiled history can save enormous time on significant public laws. If no compiled history covers your law, locate the documents yourself across multiple databases. Each database has its own coverage and strengths: Congress.gov: free; comprehensive for modern legislation; includes bill summaries, status, texts, Congressional Record and committee reports ProQuest Congressional: the single most comprehensive database; committee reports, hearings, prints, and the Congressional Record. HeinOnline U.S. Federal Legislative History Library: compiles materials by Public Law number. Westlaw: Congressional Record and committee reports. Lexis: Congressional Record, bill tracking, and committee reports. GovInfo.gov: free; official GPO PDFs of committee reports, hearings, bill versions, the Congressional Record, and the Statutes at Large. Coverage continually changes as more information becomes digitally available, so be sure to check the coverage dates for any database you use to ensure you are getting all the relevant information. Read in chronological order. Trace the bill’s journey: introduction, then committee reports, then floor debates, then the conference report, then the presidential statement. Analyze and synthesize. Identify recurring themes across sources. Note language changes. Weigh source credibility. Use committee and conference reports as your foundation, and use the other sources for supporting context. Put it in order The route, start to finish Arrange the steps of a federal legislative history search in the order you would run them. Identify the law from the statute’s credit line: Public Law number and Statutes at Large citation Everything else is indexed to the public law, so this is the key that opens the rest. Find the bill number and the Congress Committee reports, hearings, and debate are filed under the bill, not under the code section. Check for a compiled legislative history Someone may already have gathered every document. Look before you build. If none exists, locate the documents yourself Reports, bill versions, debate, hearings, across the databases that hold them. Read the documents in chronological order You are tracing how the language changed and why, so the sequence is the evidence. Synthesize: recurring themes, changes in language, and what each source is worth The answer goes in the outline with its weight stated honestly.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: State legislative history varies widely. Some states, with California and New York the most notable, maintain extensive archives of committee analyses, bill versions, and legislative journals. Others, like Arizona, provide limited access, often only to session laws and committee minutes. The general strategy: start with the annotated state code’s history line, check the state legislature’s website for bill tracking, committee materials, and session archives, and use state law library research guides for whatever is available. When state legislative history is genuinely unavailable, which is the reality in many states, courts in those states tend to rely more heavily on the statutory text itself and on canons of construction. That is not a research failure. It is a reality of state-level documentation practices, and recognizing it keeps you from burning hours hunting for documents that were never created or preserved.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Legislative history rewards restraint, and most of its pitfalls come from forgetting that. Leaning on a single legislator’s floor statement is the first, because one member’s comment rarely speaks for the whole legislature, and courts know it. Overlooking later amendments is the second, since a law’s meaning can shift when Congress revises it, so always check whether the provision you are reading was amended after the original enactment. A third, easy to make, is confusing legislative with administrative history; an agency’s interpretation belongs to administrative history, not to the record of what the legislature intended. And citation precision matters more here than almost anywhere else: legislative documents are numbered in sequence by Congress or session, so a cite has to name the specific document, page, and year, as in H.R. Rep. No. 101-485, pt. 2, at 67 (1990).

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Some judges and scholars, most prominently associated with the late Justice Scalia, argue that legislative history should play no role in statutory interpretation, because only the enacted text has the force of law. Understanding this debate matters for assessing how much weight a particular court is likely to give legislative history. Before you invest significant time, check whether the court that will hear your case follows a textualist or a purposivist approach. That affects whether your findings will be useful in your argument, and it is itself a research question worth answering early, because the answer determines how much of this chapter’s machinery you should deploy at all.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Legislative history helps interpret ambiguous statutory language by revealing lawmakers’ intent. Committee and conference reports carry the most interpretive weight. Always start from the Public Law citation in your annotated code, locate the relevant bill number and Congress, and read the sources in chronological order. Legislative history is persuasive. It supports the statutory text, but it never replaces it. Key Takeaways Legislative history illuminates legislative intent when statutory text is ambiguous. Committee and conference reports are the most persuasive sources; individual floor remarks are the least. Always begin from the Public Law citation in the annotated code’s credit line. Read sources chronologically to follow how the bill evolved and how language was added, removed, or changed. Legislative history is persuasive, not binding; always anchor arguments in the statutory text. Check for compiled legislative histories before building your own from scratch.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: The following exercises test the discipline of legislative history research: when the record may be opened, how a law’s documents are identified, and how they are weighed.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: Take a statutory term from your instructor’s set, a current project, or any statute you have read in this course, and try to write the one sentence that justifies opening the legislative record: “the statute is ambiguous as to X, and no higher-authority source resolves it.” Before you write it, document what you checked: the text, the definitions section, the interpreting cases, the regulations. If you cannot honestly finish the sentence, stop. Stopping is the exercise, and it is the discipline that separates researchers who use legislative history from researchers it uses. Deliverable: either the completed sentence with your documentation, or a short note explaining which source resolved the term and why the record stays closed. Self-check: both outcomes pass. The failing answer is a completed sentence sitting on top of an empty documentation list, because an undocumented ambiguity claim is just an unread statute.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: For the ADA, or a statute your instructor assigns, extract the Public Law number, the Statutes at Large citation, and the enactment year from the annotated code’s credit line. Use Congress.gov to find the bill number and the Congress. Then, before building anything yourself, check whether a compiled legislative history already exists, using the compiled-history sources this chapter listed. Deliverable: the full identifier set, and a note on what compiled history you found or that none exists. Self-check: for the ADA, this chapter already printed the answers; the exercise is producing them from the sources rather than from the page, and the compiled-history check is the step that saves the most time on any significant public law, so skipping it fails the drill even if everything else is right.

p: Chapter 10: Legislative History Research
t: For the ADA, or a statute your instructor assigns, gather one committee report passage, one floor statement, and one bill-version change that touch a single provision. Rank the three by interpretive weight, with one sentence of justification each. Deliverable: the ranked three with justifications and full citations in this chapter’s precision format, document, part, page, year. Self-check: if your ranking matches this chapter’s weight hierarchy, you understood the chapter. If it does not, your three sentences will show you exactly where, and check one more thing before you trust the floor statement: whether it was actually spoken on the floor or merely inserted into the Record, because the chapter told you those are not worth the same. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Chapter 7 introduced the basics of regulatory research: locating regulations in the CFR and tracing their rulemaking history. This chapter extends that foundation to the full range of materials agencies produce, including guidance documents, policy statements, opinion letters, and adjudicatory decisions. You need these materials, because agencies often clarify, and sometimes change, their positions through guidance rather than rulemaking, and the practical answer to a client’s question frequently lives in these materials rather than in the CFR itself. Learning Objectives Distinguish rulemaking, guidance documents, and administrative adjudication as sources of agency law Locate and evaluate agency guidance documents, policy statements, and opinion letters Research administrative adjudication decisions and agency enforcement actions Describe the current framework for judicial deference to agency interpretations post- Loper Bright Integrate advanced administrative research into the Question Method framework

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
s: Advanced Administrative Materials and the Research Cycle
t: Advanced administrative research is what the Question Method points you toward when the formal regulation answers your question only partway. Chapter 7 ’s regulatory cycle ends with a recurring kind of next question: the CFR text states a standard but does not tell you what it means in practice, or how the agency actually enforces it. That residual question is the entry point to this chapter’s materials. The method shapes how you find these materials, because the type of unanswered question tells you which agency product to seek. A question about what a vague regulatory term means in operation (“what does adequate ventilation actually require?”) points to interpretive guidance, compliance manuals, and opinion letters. A question about how the agency has applied the regulation to specific facts (“has the agency found conduct like my client’s to be a violation?”) points to administrative adjudication decisions, the agency’s equivalent of case law. A question about enforcement priorities points to enforcement guidelines and recent actions. Each question type maps to a different agency output, and naming the question keeps you from treating all “agency stuff” as interchangeable. The method also shapes how you weigh what you find, which matters more here than almost anywhere else in research. Because guidance documents are influential but not binding, every finding from this chapter’s materials has to be logged with an explicit note about its authority level: binding regulation, persuasive guidance, or merely advisory. In practice, that adds one required clause to the Chapter 3 Research Log entry. Open the Findings field with the authority level, before you say what the document says, so that no finding sits in your log without its weight attached. If an administrative project needs more, add an Authority Level field of your own; either way, the tool Chapter 3 handed you and the tool this chapter assumes should stay the same tool. The method’s habit of recording whether a source fully answers your question, partially answers it, or only redirects you becomes, in administrative research, a habit of recording “and how much legal weight this answer actually carries.” Skipping that step is how researchers end up advising clients that something is legally required when it is only the agency’s non-binding preference.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Advanced administrative research typically arises from Focusing questions that formal regulations do not fully answer (“The regulation requires adequate ventilation , so how does OSHA define adequate in practice?”) and Application questions about agency enforcement (“Has the FTC taken enforcement action against this type of marketing claim?”). These questions push past the CFR text to the full range of materials agencies produce. Reflection Point. If guidance documents are not binding, why does this chapter treat finding them as a required step rather than an optional one? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
s: Guidance Documents: Influential but Not Binding
t: Guidance documents, including agency manuals, policy statements, interpretive rules, compliance manuals, FAQ documents, staff memoranda, and enforcement guidelines, do not go through notice-and-comment and do not have the force of law. They are enormously influential anyway. Regulated entities follow them, enforcement decisions reflect them, and courts give them some deference. Skidmore v. Swift & Co. , 323 U.S. 134 (1944), established that courts may give guidance documents persuasive weight proportional to the agency’s expertise and the thoroughness of its reasoning. Always distinguish a binding regulation from a guidance document when you advise a client, because that distinction can decide whether the client is legally required to do something or merely advised to.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Many federal agencies resolve disputes through their own administrative processes. An administrative law judge (ALJ) hears cases; parties may appeal to the agency head and then to federal court. Administrative decisions are published and may function as precedent within the agency. They are often the most detailed interpretations of a regulation available, because they apply the regulation to specific factual patterns—exactly the application analysis a bare regulation cannot give you.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
s: Post-Loper Bright: No More Chevron Deference
t: Under the former Chevron framework, courts deferred to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo , 603 U.S. 369 (2024), the Supreme Court overruled Chevron . Courts now independently determine the best interpretation of ambiguous statutes rather than simply accepting the agency’s view. This does not eliminate Skidmore deference for informal guidance, but it fundamentally changes how courts evaluate regulations that reach beyond clear statutory text. For researchers, agency guidance still tells you how the agency will enforce the law, but it carries less guaranteed judicial weight than it once did. Always check how courts in your jurisdiction have treated the specific guidance document you are relying on. Two refinements matter in practice. First, the deference question changes when the ambiguity sits in an agency’s own regulation rather than in a statute. Courts apply a separate and narrower doctrine there, associated with Auer v. Robbins , 519 U.S. 452 (1997), as limited by Kisor v. Wilkie , 588 U.S. 558 (2019), which asks whether the regulation is genuinely ambiguous and whether the agency’s reading is authoritative, reasonable, and grounded in its expertise. That is the doctrine you will meet when you search for how an agency defines a vague regulatory term. Second, Loper Bright did not reopen every earlier decision that had applied Chevron ; those holdings keep their force as precedent. Check yourself Which deference question is this? An agency regulation requires “prompt” reporting of a spill. The regulation does not define “prompt.” The agency’s opinion letter says prompt means within 24 hours. A court must decide what the word means. Which framework governs how much the court defers to the letter? Chevron : defer to the agency’s reasonable interpretation. Chevron concerned ambiguous statutes, and Loper Bright overruled it. Loper Bright : the court decides independently, giving the agency’s view no special weight. Loper Bright addressed an agency’s reading of a statute. Here the ambiguous word is in the agency’s own regulation. Auer , as limited by Kisor : is the regulation genuinely ambiguous, and is the agency’s reading authoritative, reasonable, and grounded in its expertise? The ambiguity sits in the regulation, so the separate and narrower doctrine applies. Your next research question is how courts in your circuit have applied it. Chapter 10 raised a parallel question about legislative history: how much weight should a court give an account of what a statute means that the court did not write and that the enacted text does not itself contain? After Loper Bright , an agency’s reading arrives in a similar posture. It is something a court may find persuasive, not something it must accept. Check which way the court in front of you leans before you decide how hard to lean on the agency.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Agency websites and electronic reading rooms. Most agencies publish guidance documents in dedicated Guidance or Policy sections. The quality and organization of these repositories varies dramatically by agency. Regulations.gov. The federal rulemaking portal includes guidance documents in the docket alongside formal rulemaking materials and provides access to public comments on proposed rules. Federal Register. Some guidance documents are published as “notices” even though they are not regulations. Commercial databases. Westlaw, Lexis, and Bloomberg Law include selected agency guidance documents and adjudicatory decisions, though coverage is not comprehensive. Agency-specific sources (the SEC’s website for no-action letters, the NLRB website for board opinions, the EEOC for enforcement guidance) are often more comprehensive for their respective agencies. FOIA requests. The Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552) can be used to request unpublished agency documents, internal guidance, and enforcement records. Responses can take months or years, so factor that into your timeline.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Administrative materials answer the questions that formal regulations leave open. If your question asks what an employer must do to accommodate an employee’s religious practice, the binding regulation (29 C.F.R. Part 1605) provides the framework, but the EEOC’s Compliance Manual and enforcement guidance explain how the agency applies that framework in practice. Administrative adjudication decisions show how the agency has ruled on specific fact patterns. Each answers a different level of question about the same issue, and your annotated outline should keep them visibly distinct so the binding framework is never confused with the persuasive gloss.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Binding authority includes regulations properly promulgated through notice-and-comment and administrative adjudication decisions (binding within the agency, subject to judicial review). Non-binding but influential authority includes guidance documents, policy statements, and interpretive rules ( Skidmore deference), along with no-action letters and informal opinion letters (advisory only). When you cite administrative materials, always characterize their authority level accurately. Representing a guidance document as binding law is a professional error, and after Loper Bright , an increasingly consequential one. Sort it Must the client comply, or is the agency advising? A rule adopted through notice-and-comment and codified in the CFR Force of law Properly promulgated regulations bind regulated parties. An FAQ page on the agency’s website Persuasive only Guidance. It tells you how the agency reads its rule and will probably enforce it. It is weighed under Skidmore , not obeyed as law. The agency’s enforcement manual for its own inspectors Persuasive only Guidance again, and often the best window into enforcement priorities. An interpretive notice the agency published in the Federal Register Persuasive only Publication in the Federal Register does not turn guidance into a rule. Ask how it was made, not where it was printed. A no-action letter issued to a different company Persuasive only Advisory, and addressed to someone else’s facts. A published decision of the agency’s appeals board, cited in a later proceeding before the same agency Force of law Adjudication decisions bind within the agency, subject to judicial review. Outside the agency, a court reads them as the agency’s view.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: The error that matters most in administrative research is treating a guidance document as binding law, because the line between “legally required” and “the agency’s preference” is exactly the line a client is paying you to draw, and Loper Bright has made that line sharper. A related slip is failing to record an authority level for each finding, which is how a persuasive gloss quietly migrates into your outline as if it were the binding rule. Watch, too, for stopping at the CFR when the real answer lives in the agency’s adjudication decisions or compliance manual, the materials that show the regulation applied to facts like your client’s. And do not lean on FOIA when the clock is running, since responses can take months or years and are no help on an urgent matter.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: The Freedom of Information Act requires federal agencies to disclose most records on request. FOIA requests can surface internal agency documents, unpublished guidance, enforcement records, and decision-making processes not otherwise available. Responses can take months or years, which makes FOIA impractical for urgent matters but valuable for thorough compliance or scholarly research.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: States have their own administrative court systems, varying widely in organization and availability. Check your state’s administrative procedures act and the relevant agency’s website. Some states publish ALJ decisions in comprehensive searchable databases; others provide only limited access.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Administrative agencies produce a range of materials beyond formal regulations. Guidance documents are influential but not binding; administrative adjudication decisions interpret regulations in specific factual contexts. Post- Loper Bright , courts independently evaluate agency statutory interpretations. Effective advanced administrative research means identifying not just what an agency has enacted but what it has said through guidance and decided through adjudication, and recording, for each, exactly how much weight it carries. Key Takeaways Guidance documents are influential but not legally binding; only formally promulgated regulations carry the force of law. Administrative adjudication produces decisions that function as precedent within an agency’s domain. Post- Loper Bright , courts determine the best interpretation independently, without automatic deference to agency statutory interpretations. FOIA requests can uncover otherwise unavailable agency documents. Always distinguish the type of administrative material and represent its authority accurately.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: The following exercises test your ability to distinguish binding regulations from agency guidance and to record an authority level for everything you find. All three work the same area this chapter opened: religious accommodation in employment.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Locate the binding framework at 29 C.F.R. Part 1605, one EEOC guidance document interpreting it, and one adjudication decision applying it to facts, or, where the agency’s decisions prove hard to access, an adjudication from another agency your instructor designates, logged the same way. Log all three, each with an explicit authority level: binding regulation, persuasive guidance, or advisory. Deliverable: three Research Log entries, each with the authority level stated at the start of the Findings field. Self-check: the log entry is the exercise. If any entry’s authority level is missing from the start of Findings, or hedged, redo it, because skipping that clause is precisely how a persuasive gloss migrates into an outline dressed as the rule.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Pick the vaguest operative term you met in the regulation and ask how the agency defines it in practice. Find the answer, and note which agency product answered you: a compliance manual, an opinion letter, an adjudication. The question type told you where to look; this pass tests whether you heard it. Deliverable: the term, the practical definition with its source, and one sentence naming which of this chapter’s question-to-product mappings your search followed. Self-check: if your answer came from the CFR text itself, the term you picked was not vague enough to need this chapter. Pick again. The drill only works when the regulation genuinely runs out.

p: Chapter 11: Advanced Administrative Research
t: Take any agency guidance document in this area and search a case-law database for opinions that cite it by name or title, and check what your citator does and does not cover for agency guidance, to find how courts have actually treated it. Deliverable: a short note: what weight, if any, courts have given the document, with citations, or a documented finding that no court has addressed it. Self-check: “legally required” versus “the agency’s preference” is the line a client pays you to draw. Your note should let a reader place your guidance document on the correct side of that line without reading anything else. Draw the line three times here, cheaply, before you ever have to draw it for real. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
s: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Legal research is a professional obligation, not just a technical skill. The quality of your research bears directly on your clients’ outcomes, the integrity of legal proceedings, and your standing as a licensed professional. A missed case is not just a lower grade. In practice it can be a forfeited argument, a sanctioned attorney, and a harmed client. When an appellant provides no citation to legal authority supporting his contentions, those contentions are waived. Shields v. Town of Perrysville, 136 N.E.3d 309, 312 n.2 (Ind. Ct. App. 2019). Learning Objectives Identify the professional responsibility rules that govern legal research obligations Recognize the consequences of inadequate legal research for clients, courts, and counsel Apply the duty of competence and the duty of candor to common research scenarios Evaluate the ethical dimensions of using AI and emerging technologies in legal research Describe the standards courts use when sanctioning attorneys for research failures

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
s: The Duty of Competence: Model Rule 1.1
t: ABA Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 requires lawyers to provide competent representation, which includes “the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.” Comment 8 speaks directly to technology: a competent attorney must keep abreast of “changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks of relevant technology.” Competent legal research means knowing which sources govern, locating them efficiently, reading and synthesizing them accurately, and updating them to confirm they are still valid. Failing to find controlling authority is a breach of the duty of competence, not merely an oversight. Relying on outdated or overruled authority can amount to incompetent representation. The duty demands the current, controlling answer. Recall the following excerpt from Chapter 5 . [H]e did not conduct legal research beyond [an older decision on the issue], nor did he reread any of the cases cited to or relied on in . . . the most recent First Circuit decision addressing the contours of [the issue]. Thus, I conclude that [his] erroneous interpretation of the controlling law at the time constituted a breach of the professional duty. ST Engineering Marine, Ltd. v. Thompson, MacColl & Bass, LLC, 633 F. Supp. 3d 354, 361 (D. Me. 2022), aff’d, No. 22-1844 (1st Cir. Dec. 6, 2023) . This case shows the core competence failure: the attorney relied on outdated authority without checking whether the law had moved. The closing-out protocol’s second step—updating every case and statute through a citator (Chapter 9 )—is designed to prevent exactly this. And the finding held up: the First Circuit affirmed, so the competence holding is not one trial court’s view of how much research is enough. The habit the method builds is the same habit the rule requires.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
s: The Duty of Candor Toward the Tribunal: Model Rule 3.3
t: Rule 3.3 prohibits false statements of law to a tribunal and requires disclosure of directly adverse controlling authority the opposing party has not cited. That creates an affirmative research obligation: you must search for controlling adverse authority, not only authority that helps you. Rule 3.3 also prohibits citing false or fabricated authority, a concern of heightened urgency in the era of AI-generated research. The rule reaches authority that is in the controlling jurisdiction (not just persuasive authority from elsewhere), directly adverse (not merely unfavorable or tangential), and known to the lawyer, which includes authority you should have found through competent research. Ignorance born of inadequate research is no defense. The duty of candor therefore reaches back into the quality of your research. You cannot disclose adverse authority you never found, and “I didn’t find it” is no answer when competent research would have. Sort it Does Rule 3.3 require you to tell the court? A decision of your state’s supreme court squarely against your position. Opposing counsel has not cited it. Disclose Controlling jurisdiction, directly adverse, not disclosed by the other side: every condition is met. A neighboring state’s supreme court decision squarely against your position. No duty under the rule Not from the controlling jurisdiction. You may still choose to address it before your opponent does. A controlling decision that criticizes arguments like yours in passing while deciding a different issue. No duty under the rule Unfavorable is not the same as directly adverse. A controlling, directly adverse decision that opposing counsel has already cited and discussed. No duty under the rule The court has it. Your job now is to distinguish it honestly. A directly adverse decision of the intermediate appellate court whose decisions bind the trial court you are in. Opposing counsel missed it. Disclose It controls the tribunal you are before. That your opponent researched poorly does not relieve you.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
s: The Duty to Supervise: Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3
t: Supervising attorneys are responsible for making sure subordinate lawyers and non-lawyer staff comply with the conduct rules. In research, that means senior attorneys must review delegated research for accuracy, completeness, and proper citation. The Research Log serves a professional function here. It documents what was searched, what was found, and why the researcher concluded the research was complete. If a supervisor questions your work, the log gives a complete, defensible record. If you are the supervisor, the log is what lets you actually evaluate a subordinate’s research rather than simply trusting it. Reflection Point. The Research Log is a research tool. Why does this chapter also call it a professional record? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .) Sort it Which duty did the lawyer breach? Relied on a twenty-year-old decision without checking whether it was still good law. 1.1 Competence Stale authority is the core competence failure. Found a controlling, directly adverse case the other side missed and left it out of the brief. 3.3 Candor The research was competent. The filing was not candid. Signed and filed a junior associate’s memo with no way to see what she searched or read. 5.1 and 5.3 Supervision Delegated research no one can review. The Research Log is what makes review possible. Adopted a new research tool for the office without learning how it produces its answers. 1.1 Competence Competence includes understanding the benefits and risks of the technology you use. Filed a paralegal’s case summaries without any attorney reading the cases. 5.1 and 5.3 Supervision Responsibility for a nonlawyer’s work stays with the supervising lawyer.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Sanctions by courts. Courts have broad sanctioning authority when counsel fails to research adequately. Sanctions include monetary penalties, attorney fee awards, adverse rulings, and public reprimands in published opinions. [B]ecause I find that Defendants incurred these unnecessary fees in major part due to inadequate legal research on the part of Plaintiffs’ counsel, I find that both Plaintiffs and their counsel are jointly and severally liable to Defendants. Royal Oak Ent., L.L.C. v. City of Royal Oak, 486 F. Supp. 2d 675, [ pincite ] (E.D. Mich. 2007). Waiver of arguments. Courts routinely hold that arguments unsupported by citation to legal authority are waived. Inadequate research does not merely weaken an argument. It can forfeit it entirely, as the Shields court’s note at the opening of this chapter makes plain. Malpractice exposure. An attorney who fails to find controlling authority and thereby harms a client’s case may face a legal malpractice claim. The competence failure that begins as a research shortcut can end as a civil judgment against the lawyer.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: [A]t this point, no lawyer should be using ChatGPT or any other generative AI product to perform research without verifying the results. Period. In re Martin, 670 B.R. 636, 649 (Bankr. N.D. Ill. 2025). Generative AI tools produce output that can look authoritative but may contain fabricated case citations, incorrect legal propositions, and misattributed quotations. Courts have sanctioned attorneys for submitting briefs citing AI-generated, nonexistent cases. The professional responsibility implications are clear: the duty of competence requires verification of all research, whatever its source. AI tools do not relieve attorneys of the obligation to confirm that cited authorities exist, say what they are claimed to say, and remain valid law. Emerging court rules and bar guidance increasingly require disclosure when AI tools are used to generate any part of a brief or memorandum. Watch your jurisdiction’s developing rules. Chapter 15 addresses AI tools and legal research in depth; this section supplies the ethical framework that governs their use. Read closely Pull every citation before you sign A residential landlord must provide adequate heat during the cold months. Marsh v. Golden Rentals . A tenant left without heat may withhold rent at once, without notifying the landlord. Prewitt v. Stonegate LLC . And a tenant who goes thirty days without heat is entitled to treble damages. Hollis v. Ironwood Residential .

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
s: Build Verification Into Your Research Workflow
t: As you research, keep a running citation log: every source you intend to cite, with its full citation and the database where you verified it. Before you finalize any document, run every case citation through KeyCite or Shepard’s to confirm that the points of law you cite it for remain valid. Before you finalize any statute citation, verify the current text against the eCFR or the official code and check for pending amendments. If you used any AI tool at any stage, independently verify each source it identified before it goes into your work product. These are not separate ethics chores bolted onto research. They are the closing steps of the Question Method, performed with the awareness that the rules of professional conduct require them. The chapter in one glance: Rule The research failure it targets The method step that prevents it Rule 1.1 (competence) Stale or overruled authority; citations that do not support the claim they are offered for; inadequate or no research at all The citator update and the read-before-you-cite check in the closing-out protocol Rule 3.3 (candor) A one-sided search that misses adverse authority The adverse-authority search in the closing-out protocol’s final sweep (Chapter 9 ) Rules 5.1 and 5.3 (supervision) Delegated research no one can review The Research Log as the reviewable record

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: The competence failures that get lawyers sanctioned tend to share a shape: relying on the first answer rather than the current, controlling one. Leaning on an old case without running it through a citator is the classic version, and ST Eng’g Marine is what it looks like in a published opinion. A second pitfall is researching only your own side; Rule 3.3 obligates you to find and disclose directly adverse controlling authority, so a one-sided search is not just weak advocacy, it is an ethics problem. A third is trusting AI output without verification, since a fabricated citation is a Rule 3.3 violation whether it came from a chatbot or anywhere else. And do not treat the Research Log as busywork; it is the record that protects you and your supervisor if the quality of the research is ever questioned.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Research quality is an ethical obligation with names attached. Rule 1.1 demands competent, current research; Rule 3.3 demands candor about adverse authority; Rules 5.1 and 5.3 make supervisors answerable for research they delegate. Courts enforce all of it through sanctions, waived arguments, and malpractice exposure, and AI has raised the stakes on verification rather than lowering them. And here is the good news: the citator step, the adverse-authority question, the Research Log—the habits this book has been building in you all along—are exactly the habits the rules require. Key Takeaways Legal research is a professional obligation, not merely a technical skill. Model Rule 1.1 (competence) and Model Rule 3.3 (candor) are the primary rules governing legal research. Courts sanction attorneys for inadequate research; arguments unsupported by authority may be waived. AI tools create heightened verification obligations; they do not substitute for professional research judgment. Supervising attorneys are responsible for the research quality of their subordinates. The Research Log documents your process; it is your professional record of diligence.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: The following exercises test your ability to connect the professional conduct rules to specific research practices: verification, adverse-authority searching, and documentation.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Pull ST Engineering Marine ; the competence excerpt in this chapter gives you the citation. Read the court’s account of what the attorney failed to do, and then rebuild this chapter’s closing table from the opinion itself rather than from memory: for each failure the court names, write the rule it violates and the method step that would have prevented it. Deliverable: your rebuilt three-column table, failure, rule, preventing step, with a pincite to the opinion for each failure. Self-check: compare your table against the chapter’s. Where they differ, the difference is the finding: either you caught a failure the chapter’s table generalized over, which is good reading, or you attributed to the opinion something it does not say, which is the exact error the autopsy exists to catch.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Return to any completed drill from Part I and run the one question your first pass almost certainly skipped: what controlling authority cuts against my conclusion? Draft the question, run the search, and log the result in your Research Log even if the search comes back empty, because Rule 3.3 does not accept “I didn’t look” as an answer. Deliverable: the Research Log entry, including the searches run. Self-check: an empty result logged with its searches is a passing answer. An empty log is not. The difference between those two is the whole of the candor duty’s research obligation.

p: Chapter 12: Ethics and Professional Responsibility in Legal Research
t: Run a full verification pass on any completed drill from Part I: build the citation log, one line per source you would cite, run every case through a citator, and confirm every statute and regulation’s currency against the official or current source. Deliverable: the citation log with a verification status for every line. Self-check: every line has a status and a date. The log you produce is not homework. It is the record that answers for you when someone asks whether the research was done, and Rules 5.1 and 5.3 mean someone is allowed to ask. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
s: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Court documents give you a window into how the law operates in practice. Judicial opinions tell you what courts decided; the pleadings, briefs, and motions show you how lawyers argued, what facts they marshaled, and how courts reasoned through contested issues before issuing a published opinion. Court document research is especially valuable for finding arguments in cases with similar facts, understanding the procedural history of a precedent-setting case, locating unreported orders, and mining briefs for citation lists in novel areas. Court documents are a research tool, not a source of authority, and keeping that distinction clear is the first discipline of this chapter. Learning Objectives Explain what a court docket is and what types of information it contains Locate federal court dockets using PACER and free alternatives Identify and retrieve key court documents: complaints, briefs, motions, and orders Evaluate the research value of court documents and their limitations Locate state court documents using state-specific resources Integrate court document research into the Question Method framework

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
s: Court Documents and the Research Cycle
t: Court documents occupy an unusual place in the Question Method. They are almost never the answer to a research question, but they are one of the most efficient accelerators of the research cycle. Understanding how the method treats them prevents the beginner’s error of citing a brief as if it were authority. The method shapes how you find court documents, because they are most useful once a specific question has already narrowed your inquiry. Early exploratory questions are answered by secondary sources, not dockets; reaching for PACER before you know the governing standard wastes money and time. But once a focusing or application question is in front of you (“what is the full range of arguments on this contested point?” or “how have lawyers in my circuit framed this exact claim?”), a well-researched brief in a major case becomes a shortcut, because its author has already done the work of assembling the leading authorities on the point. The citations in that brief become candidate answers to your next several questions. The method shapes how you engage with court documents, because it forces you to treat them as leads, not findings. A brief tells you what one party argued, not what the law is. The method’s Step 3, “write down what you found,” applies with a twist: what you found in a brief is a set of citations and a framing, both of which have to be independently verified against the primary authority before anything enters your annotated outline as an answer. A docket entry that looks like an answer is really a new question: “does the authority this brief cites actually say what the brief claims?” Running that verification is the cycle continuing, not concluding.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Court document research answers Application questions about how lawyers have argued specific issues (“How have attorneys framed Eighth Amendment cruel-and-unusual-punishment claims in conditions-of-confinement cases?”), procedural questions (“What motions have been filed in this case, and when?”), and strategic questions (“What evidence did the opposing party rely on in similar cases?”). Briefs in major cases are particularly efficient for identifying leading authorities on contested points; the citations in a well-researched appellate brief can accelerate your research substantially. Reflection Point. A well-researched brief seems like a shortcut to everything at once. Why does the method still send you to dockets only after your question has narrowed? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
s: How Dockets and Court Documents Are Created
t: When parties file documents in court, each one is assigned a number and recorded on the docket , the official log of all filings. The federal courts use CM/ECF for filing, accessible through PACER (pacer.uscourts.gov). Document types include pleadings (complaints, petitions, answers), motions and responses, briefs, amicus briefs, orders and opinions, and judgments.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Each PACER entry shows the date, docket number, document type, and filer. Key information includes party names and counsel, the assigned judge, the case number and district, and the filing sequence from complaint to judgment. The documents most worth locating are the complaint (the scope of the dispute), the dispositive motions and supporting briefs (the legal arguments), and the court’s orders resolving those motions (the court’s reasoning, sometimes more detailed than any published opinion). Do not confuse docket entries with the documents themselves. The docket lists filings; you have to open each entry to read the actual document. Example What only the docket holds. The sanctions decision in Mata v. Avianca (Chapter 15 ) is a single document. The docket runs to dozens of entries, and it is where the research actually lives: the order to show cause, the affidavit attaching the fabricated opinions, the transcript of the June 8 hearing where the lawyer explained what he had assumed about the tool, and the letters the court later required. A researcher who reads only the published decision knows the holding. A researcher who pulls the docket knows how the failure unfolded, which is the part that answers “how do I keep this from happening in my office?” Explore Read a docket, newest entry first A fictional federal docket, Marsh v. Golden Rentals, LLC , shown the way a docket is displayed: latest filing at the top, the complaint at the bottom. Select an entry to see what it tells a researcher. 12 | Minute order. Minute order setting oral argument on [8] Motion for Summary Judgment. Short, procedural, and often published nowhere else. It answers “what happens next in this case?”, which is why the freshest fact sits at the top. 11 | Reply. Reply in support of [8] Motion for Summary Judgment, filed by Golden Rentals. The reply closes the briefing sequence: motion, response, reply. Entries cross-reference one another by number. Following the bracketed numbers is how you reconstruct which paper answers which. 10 | Response. Response in opposition to [8] Motion for Summary Judgment, filed by Marsh. For a researcher with a similar case, the opposition brief is often the best free collection of contrary authority available. It is advocacy, so it is a list of leads to read, not a statement of the law. 8 | Motion. Motion for Summary Judgment. Attachments: (1) Memorandum in support; (2) Statement of facts; (3) Exhibits A–C; (4) Proposed order. One entry, five documents. The motion itself is often a two-page formality. The argument lives in the memorandum, the evidence in the exhibits, and the proposed order shows exactly what relief is sought. Stop at the entry line and you miss all of it. 7 | Scheduling order. Scheduling order: discovery closes 04/24; dispositive motions due 05/01. The case’s calendar. It tells you when a ruling you could use is likely to issue. 6 | Order. Order denying [4] Motion to Dismiss. An order with reasoning, and quite possibly unreported. It decided a real legal question and may never appear in a reporter. The docket is how you find rulings the published record does not show. 2 | Answer. Answer to [1] Complaint, filed by Golden Rentals. Admissions, denials, and defenses, paragraph by paragraph. Read against the complaint, it maps what is actually in dispute. 1 | Complaint. Complaint with jury demand, filed by Marsh. Where the case begins, at the bottom of the display. Allegations are unproven assertions, not findings. They are still the best single statement of what the plaintiff says happened and how counsel framed the claims.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Federal courts, PACER. Comprehensive; charges per page, though if your quarterly charges stay under the current threshold the fees are waived automatically, so most light users never owe a dime; separate research exemptions exist but are narrow and granted court by court; requires account registration. CourtListener (free). Free access to many federal court documents, and home to the RECAP archive, a freely accessible repository of PACER documents uploaded by users. Justia and Google Scholar. Partial free coverage, especially of published opinions. Bloomberg Law and Westlaw. Comprehensive commercial docket access for many jurisdictions. State courts. Each state runs its own electronic filing system. Accessibility varies a lot; most state appellate courts offer more comprehensive online access than trial courts.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Complaints answer “How have lawyers framed similar legal theories?” Briefs answer “What is the full range of arguments on this issue?” Amicus briefs answer “What perspectives do non-parties bring?” Orders and unpublished opinions answer “How has the court reasoned through procedural or preliminary issues in similar cases?” Each document type has a distinct research use. Use briefs to identify authority, complaints to understand factual framing, and orders to understand procedural reasoning. Record your findings in your annotated outline: the case, the document type, the key argument or passage, and the docket entry number. Court documents are also valuable in several practical situations: to review filings in a pending or recent case that has not yet been fully reported; to run due diligence on a client, company, or opposing party; to research procedural history and understand all prior proceedings before an appeal; and to find expert reports, deposition transcripts, or exhibits attached to filed motions. Sort it Authority, or a lead? The argument section of a party’s summary judgment brief A lead to follow Advocacy. Its citations tell you what to read. Its characterizations tell you what one side wanted the court to believe. The factual allegations of a complaint A lead to follow Unproven assertions. Useful for seeing how counsel framed a theory. The judge’s unreported order denying the motion to dismiss, with reasons A court’s ruling A decision, even though no reporter printed it. Weigh it as what it is, a trial court’s ruling, and check the court’s rules on citing unreported orders. An expert’s declaration attached as Exhibit B A lead to follow Evidence in that case. It is not law in any case. The appellate opinion the winning brief relied on, once you have read it yourself A court’s ruling The brief was the accelerator. The opinion is the authority, and you cite it only after reading it.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: The error this chapter exists to prevent is citing a brief or a complaint as though it were authority; it records what one side argued, and the proposition it asserts is only as good as the primary source behind it, which you have to verify yourself. A second is going to PACER too early, before a secondary source has told you the governing standard, which spends money and time chasing documents you cannot yet evaluate. And do not blur published opinions, which carry binding or persuasive weight, with the unpublished orders and filings around them, which are research tools and nothing more.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Court documents are created under the authority of court rules, and those rules are themselves an essential research target. Before you file anything, research the applicable rules at every level. The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Criminal Procedure, Evidence, and Appellate Procedure govern federal practice nationwide and are available at uscourts.gov. Advisory Committee Notes function as legislative history for procedural rules. Local court rules supplement the Federal Rules and govern page limits, formatting, scheduling, and much more, available on each court’s website. Judge-specific standing orders supplement local rules further. Work through the rules hierarchy top to bottom before filing, because a perfectly researched motion filed in violation of a local formatting rule can still be rejected.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: In landmark or frequently litigated areas, searching the briefs filed in major cases, including amicus briefs, is an efficient way to canvass the whole debate on an issue. Many law school libraries and commercial databases maintain brief banks.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Searching dockets for pending cases on the same issue can reveal that the law is about to change. A case on appeal or pending certiorari may overrule current law. Always check whether any leading case in your research has been granted certiorari or is on appeal. A citator check accomplishes part of this, but a docket search can surface a challenge before any citator flag appears.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Dockets and court documents are accelerators, not authority. A docket is the map of a litigation; the filings on it show how lawyers actually argued, and a well-researched brief can hand you the leading authorities on a contested point in minutes. But every proposition you take from one is a lead to verify, and the reframing to remember is that a docket find is a new research question: does the authority this brief cites say what the brief claims? Come here after your question has narrowed, not before. Key Takeaways A docket is the official log of all filings in a case; PACER provides federal access, and CourtListener provides free partial coverage. Briefs, complaints, amicus filings, and orders each provide different research value. Brief mining is an efficient strategy for identifying leading authorities on contested issues. Court rules research is mandatory before any filing: Federal Rules, then local rules, then judge standing orders. Always distinguish published opinions (binding or persuasive authority) from unpublished orders and briefs (research tools, not authority).

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: The following exercises test your ability to read a docket, verify claims made in briefs, and trace the court rules that govern filings. All three run in free sources.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Choose a recent federal civil case, filed within the last few years so its docket lives in the electronic systems this chapter covers; your instructor may assign one, or take one from recent legal news. Find its docket on CourtListener. Read the docket as a map, and identify, by entry number, the complaint, the dispositive motion with its supporting brief, and the order resolving that motion. Do not open the documents yet. The point of this pass is learning to read the log itself. Deliverable: the three entry numbers with one line each on how you recognized them. Self-check: if you had to open documents to find them, note where the docket text alone failed you; on a metered system, every one of those opens would have cost money, and the skill of reading the log is the skill of not paying for what the log already says.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: Locate a brief supporting a dispositive motion in any recent federal case on CourtListener, or use a brief your instructor assigns. Harvest three authorities it cites for its central argument, and pick one to run this chapter’s defining question on: does the authority this brief cites actually say what the brief claims? Read the primary source and log the verdict. That verification is the cycle continuing, not concluding. Deliverable: the three harvested authorities, and one Research Log entry recording the claim as the brief made it, what the primary source actually says, and your verdict. Self-check: your entry must quote or pincite both the brief’s characterization and the source’s own language. A verdict without both sides on the page is an impression, and impressions are what got the brief’s author into the habit you are checking.

p: Chapter 13: Dockets and Court Document Research
t: For any federal district court (the one nearest you works well), trace a single filing requirement, page or word limits work well, down the ladder: the governing Federal Rule, the district’s local rule, and any judge-specific standing order. Note where each level lives and what each adds or tightens. Deliverable: the three-rung ladder with citations and locations. Self-check: if two rungs say the same thing, read again; local rules and standing orders exist to add or tighten, and finding the delta is the exercise. And where a judge has no standing order on the point, record that finding; knowing a rung is empty is knowing something. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: Everything you have learned so far applies across all areas of practice. But how you apply it, the sources you prioritize, the questions you ask, the closure criteria you use, varies depending on whether you are litigating a case, closing a transaction, advising on regulatory compliance, or doing something else. The NextGen Bar Exam recognizes this; it is built to balance the skills and knowledge needed in litigation and transactional practice. This chapter prepares you for that balance by showing how the Question Method adapts to different contexts. Learning Objectives Identify how research strategies differ across litigation, transactional, and regulatory practice contexts Adapt the Question Method to the distinct research demands of each practice area Recognize the source types and databases most relevant to each practice context Apply different research closure criteria depending on the professional context

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
s: Practice-Specific Research and the Research Cycle
t: The Question Method is deliberately context-neutral: question, research, synthesize, next question, repeat. That neutrality is its strength, because the same disciplined cycle survives the move from a litigation file to a merger to a compliance audit. What changes from one context to the next is not the cycle but the parameters the cycle runs with. Three parameters shift. First, the default question type shifts: litigation runs heavily on application questions (how do these facts compare to the controlling cases?); transactional work runs on focusing questions about requirements and risks (what does this deal type require?); regulatory work spans all four types. Second, the first source shifts: litigation starts in case law, transactional work starts in statutes and standardized forms, regulatory work starts in the CFR and agency guidance. Third, and most important, the closure criterion shifts: what counts as “research sufficient” in litigation (controlling authority for each issue, adverse authority identified) differs from what counts as sufficient in a transaction (all applicable requirements and risks identified) or in compliance work (all obligations mapped). This is why the method is worth learning as a method rather than as a set of source-specific recipes. A lawyer who has internalized the cycle can walk into an unfamiliar practice area and immediately ask the right meta-question, “in this context, what is my default question type, where do I start, and what will tell me I’m done?”, and then run the same five steps they have always run. The Research Log even changes function accordingly: in litigation it documents the authority behind each argument; in transactional practice it tracks requirements and risk factors; in regulatory practice it maps compliance obligations. Reflection Point. When the practice context changes, why does the closure criterion matter more than the question type or the first source? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: A court will sometimes chastise counsel whose motion ignored a settled body of case law: In this case, for example, plaintiff ignores basic principles and long standing consistent case law covering motions for reconsideration and fails to make the showing required under that consistent body of case law. Kiss Pharm LLC v. Becker Prof’l Dev. Corp. , No. 18 C 7848, 2021 WL 3207822, at * (N.D. Ill. July 29, 2021). The research context. Litigation research supports the prosecution or defense of claims in court. The goal is to find controlling authority governing the disputed issues, identify and address adverse authority, and build a framework for persuasive argument. Case law is the dominant source, because the arguments you make to a court have to be supported by judicial authority. Statutes and regulations provide governing rules, and the case law interpreting them is equally important. Court rules and local rules govern procedural requirements, and failing to follow them can be dispositive. Characteristic questions. Application questions dominate: “How do the facts of my case compare to the leading cases?” “Does the statute of limitations bar my client’s claim given these specific dates?” “What standard of review applies to this issue on appeal?” Research closure in litigation. Controlling authority identified for each issue; adverse authority identified and addressed; procedural requirements confirmed; all cited authorities updated and validated. Specialized databases. Docket research: PACER (federal), state court electronic filing systems, Bloomberg Law. Judicial analytics: tools tracking individual judges’ rulings and citation preferences. Brief banks: Westlaw, Lexis, Bloomberg Law.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: The research context. Transactional research supports the negotiation, drafting, and closing of deals: mergers, acquisitions, financings, real estate transactions, corporate formations, and commercial contracts. The goal is to identify the legal requirements, risks, and market practices that should shape the structure and documentation. Statutes and regulations are typically dominant, because transactions have to comply with governing law. Characteristic questions. Focusing questions about requirements and risks dominate: “What approvals are required for this type of corporate acquisition in Delaware?” “Are there regulatory restrictions on this type of financing arrangement?” “What representations and warranties are market-standard for this deal type?” Research closure in transactional practice. All applicable regulatory requirements identified; tax implications analyzed; comparable transactions reviewed for market terms; risk factors identified and addressed in the deal documentation; due diligence complete. Specialized databases. SEC EDGAR (essential and free for federal securities research; public company filings, prospectuses, precedent transaction documents). Practical Law (Westlaw) and Lexis Practice Advisor (market-standard forms, checklists, and practice notes organized by transaction type). Bloomberg Law (transactional intelligence tools, deal analytics).

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: The research context. Regulatory research supports clients navigating the requirements of administrative agencies. The goal is to identify all applicable requirements, understand how the agency interprets and enforces them, and assess the client’s compliance status. Regulations (the CFR) are the primary source, and agency guidance documents are essential for understanding enforcement in practice. Characteristic questions. Definitional, focusing, and application questions all arise: “What does the EPA consider a point source under the Clean Water Act?” “What reporting obligations apply to this facility?” “Does my client’s waste management process comply with RCRA Subtitle C?” Research closure in regulatory practice. All applicable regulations identified (federal, state, local); agency guidance consulted for interpretive questions; recent enforcement actions reviewed for current priorities; compliance status assessed against each applicable requirement; pending rulemaking checked for upcoming changes. Sort it Which practice context is asking? Does the two-year limitations period bar the claim when the injury was discovered eighteen months after it occurred? Litigation A rule applied to specific dates in a live dispute. What consents does the buyer need before it can assume the seller’s commercial leases? Transactional A focusing question about requirements, asked before anything has gone wrong. Which recordkeeping rules apply to a brewery that begins shipping across state lines? Regulatory Mapping the obligations that attach to an ongoing activity. Is a non-compete of this length enforceable against the client’s former sales director, on these facts? Litigation Application to facts, with an adversary. What indemnification terms are standard in agreements of this kind? Transactional “Market standard” is answered by comparable deals, not by cases.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
s: Adapting the Question Method Across Practice Contexts
t: The five steps and intermittent checkpoints stay the same regardless of context; only the parameters move. You have now seen that shift played out three times: a different default question type, a different first source, a different closure criterion, and a Research Log doing a different job in each. Sort it Is the research sufficient for this context? Litigation. Controlling authority found and updated for every issue. You have not searched for authority against your position. Not yet Closure in litigation requires adverse authority identified and addressed. Transactional. Every required approval is identified and the tax treatment analyzed. You have not looked at how comparable deals allocated the risk. Not yet Market terms come from comparable transactions, and closure here includes them. Regulatory. Federal rules mapped, guidance read, recent enforcement reviewed. State and local requirements are unchecked. Not yet Compliance closure means every applicable level of government. Litigation. Controlling and adverse authority identified and addressed, procedural requirements confirmed, every citation validated. Closed Each element of the litigation criterion is met. Regulatory. Obligations mapped at all three levels, guidance consulted, enforcement actions reviewed, pending rulemaking checked. Closed Including the forward look. In compliance work, a rule about to change is part of the answer.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: The most common practice-specific mistake is importing one context’s habits into another, like running a litigation-style case-law-first search on a transactional problem whose answer lives in statutes, regulations, and standardized forms. Closing out by the wrong criterion is a close relative: “I found controlling authority for each issue” is the right finish line in litigation but not in a transaction, where the question is whether you have identified every applicable requirement and risk. New lawyers also tend to reach reflexively for the source type they trained on rather than asking the meta-question first: “in this context, what is my default question type, where do I start, and what will tell me I’m done?” In an unfamiliar practice context, that reflex ripens quickly into Chapter 8 ’s single-source trap—a governing authority type never reached, or reached only through another source’s description of it—because the authority types that govern the new context are exactly the ones your old habits never taught you to open. And in any context, do not forget the procedural layer; in litigation especially, a substantively perfect argument can still be undone by a missed court rule.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: Research strategies differ across practice contexts, but the Question Method provides a consistent framework that adapts to each. Litigation research prioritizes case law and adversarial analysis. Transactional research prioritizes statutory requirements, regulatory compliance, and market practices. Regulatory research spans the full range of agency-produced materials. Understanding these differences prepares you for the NextGen Bar Exam’s balanced testing approach and for the varied demands of professional practice. Key Takeaways Litigation research prioritizes case law and adversarial analysis; closure requires controlling authority for each issue and identification of adverse authority. Transactional research prioritizes statutes, regulations, forms, and market practices; closure requires identification of all applicable requirements and risks. Regulatory research spans formal regulations, agency guidance, and enforcement actions; closure requires mapping all compliance obligations. The Question Method adapts to each context through different question types, source priorities, and closure criteria.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: The following exercises test your ability to adapt the method’s parameters, question type, first source, and closure criterion, to different practice contexts.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: Reread the drone scenario printed in Chapter 8 , same client, same facts, and research it three times without researching it once. Everything you need is the scenario itself and this chapter’s parameters.
