From the litigation posture, a neighbor has sued over the flights; from the transactional posture, the client is selling the business, drone operation included; and from the compliance posture, the client wants an audit of everything the operation must do to stay legal. For each posture, write only the first three research questions you would draft. Then label each question’s type, name the source you would open first, and state the closure criterion that would tell you the research was done. Nine questions, three postures, one page. Deliverable: that one page. Self-check: now read the page. The facts never changed, but the question types shifted, the first sources shifted, and the finish lines shifted. If any two postures produced the same three questions, you researched the file instead of the posture, and this chapter’s entire argument is that the posture sets the parameters.

p: Chapter 14: Practice-Specific Research Strategies
t: Pick a practice context this chapter never mentions, immigration, tax, family law, anything, and answer the meta-question cold: in this context, what is my default question type, where do I start, and what will tell me I am done? Write your three answers, then spend fifteen minutes in a secondary source checking them, and revise. Deliverable: both versions, cold and checked, with a line on what the check changed. Self-check: you will not know the sources before the check, and that is fine. The lawyer who can ask the meta-question walks into any unfamiliar area already oriented, and if the check changed nothing at all, you either guessed remarkably well or checked remarkably little. Be honest about which. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: [A]t this point, no lawyer should be using ChatGPT or any other generative AI product to perform research without verifying the results. Period. In re Martin , 670 B.R. 636, 649 (Bankr. N.D. Ill. 2025). Generative AI tools promise to speed up legal research. The reality is more complicated. General-purpose large language models can produce fluent, confident-sounding legal summaries, and they can also fabricate case citations, misattribute quotations, and state legal propositions that are simply wrong. Courts have sanctioned attorneys for relying on such fabrications. The Question Method is your best safeguard. Apply the same question-by-question, synthesize-and-verify discipline to AI-assisted research that you apply to everything else, and you can capture AI’s efficiency while still meeting your professional obligations. Learning Objectives Describe how generative AI tools work and why they produce unreliable legal citations Apply the Question Method framework to AI-assisted research to minimize error Evaluate AI-generated legal research output for accuracy and reliability Apply professional responsibility obligations governing AI use in legal practice Distinguish general-purpose generative AI tools from the generative features integrated into verified legal databases

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: Generative AI Tools and the Research Cycle
t: Generative AI does not change the Question Method. It slots into it as a particular kind of source, one with an unusual reliability profile that the method is well suited to manage. The method shapes how you use generative AI, because it forces the work into small, discrete, well-specified questions, which is exactly the shape of task these systems handle best and you can verify most easily. A vague mega-prompt (“research my whole case”) produces fluent output that is nearly impossible to check. A single Question Method cycle (“what is the governing standard for X in the Ninth Circuit?”) produces a narrow claim you can verify against one or two primary sources. The iterative structure that makes the method good pedagogy also makes it good AI hygiene: one question, one checkable answer, one verification, then the next question. The method also fits how these systems actually behave. A complex legal issue has many moving parts, and when you hand a generative system all of them in one sweeping question, its statistical predictions start to drift: each small inaccuracy feeds the next, and by the end of a long answer the errors have compounded. Small, single-issue questions keep the model on firmer ground, and they give you a natural checkpoint after each one, so a hallucination gets caught before it propagates into everything built on top of it. That is why Step 3 of every cycle, “write down what you found,” becomes, for generative output, “write down what you found and independently confirmed.” Nothing from a generative tool enters your annotated outline until it has been checked against the primary source, because the model cannot tell a real citation from a plausible fabrication. If you cannot find and read the source the system named, the answer does not exist and the cycle is not complete. And the method shapes which questions you bring to a generative system at all. Generative AI is strongest on exploratory and focusing questions (orientation, terminology, explaining a concept you can then verify) and weakest on application questions (which specific cases match these specific facts), where its tendency to retrieve the plausibly-related-but-wrong is most dangerous. Knowing the question type, the method’s core diagnostic, tells you in advance how much to trust the output and how hard to verify it. Reflection Point. A generative tool answers your narrow question and cites a case that looks perfect. What does the method have you do before the answer goes anywhere, and why does keeping the question narrow help? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: How Generative AI Works and What That Means for Research
t: Generative AI tools are powered by large language models: computer programs trained on enormous amounts of text that respond to a prompt by predicting, word by word, what is most likely to come next. They do not look information up. They generate text that statistically resembles the kind of response that would follow the prompt. That is why LLMs hallucinate : they produce citations that look real because authentic legal citations have similar statistical patterns. The model cannot tell the difference between generating a true citation and generating a plausible-sounding false one. Watch it work Prediction without retrieval Press the button and watch a legal sentence get finished one piece at a time. At every step the highest-probability candidate is appended. The names and numbers are invented for illustration. The mechanism is not. implied 71%; lease 14%; covenant 9% “implied” wins because it most often follows words like these in the text the model learned from. Nothing has been looked up. warranty 83%; covenant 11%; duty 4% Still pattern completion. So far the pattern happens to track real doctrine. of habitability. 94%; of fitness. 4%; of quiet enjoyment. 1% A correct statement of a familiar rule, produced without consulting a single source. See 62%; Courts 21%; In 9% Legal sentences like this one are usually followed by a citation, so a citation signal is the likely next piece. Hollis 34%; Trammel 29%; Whitfield 22% A plausible surname, chosen the same way “implied” was chosen. The close percentages are the tell: no name is more true than another. v. Ironwood Residential, 58%; v. Northgate Flats, 27%; v. Stonegate LLC, 9% A landlord-sounding defendant, because that is what follows a tenant-sounding plaintiff. 412 P.3d 1187 38%; 398 P.3d 960 33%; 421 P.3d 77 21% Numbers shaped like the numbers in real citations. (Ariz. 2018). 57%; (Ariz. Ct. App. 2019). 31%; (Ariz. 2016). 8% Read what was built: a fluent, confident, fully cited sentence. The proposition is sound. The citation is fiction, chosen because it was likely, exactly like every word before it. The model cannot tell the two apart, and at no step did it check. Example What a fabricated citation costs. In Mata v. Avianca, Inc. , 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), a lawyer preparing an opposition brief on a Montreal Convention question asked ChatGPT for supporting authority and got six decisions that did not exist, complete with quotations and reporter cites. When opposing counsel could not find them, he asked the tool whether the cases were real; it said yes, and told him they were on Westlaw and Lexis. He never looked. The court imposed a $5,000 sanction under Rule 11, and its opinion located the fault precisely: not in using the tool, but in the failure to verify and then in defending the fabrications once challenged. Read the case as a demonstration of the principle above. The system was not looking anything up. It was predicting what a supporting citation looks like, and it is very good at that. The AI research features built into Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law operate differently. They work within verified databases and can ground responses in actual documents, which limits, though it does not eliminate, the hallucination risk. Understanding that distinction is the first step in using AI responsibly.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: Running the Cycle Through an AI System
t: You already own the framework for working with these systems, and you do not need a second one. It is the cycle you have been running since Chapter 3 , the same five steps in the same order, with a single discipline added at the point where these tools fail: nothing enters your record unverified. Run the cycle as written, and treat the added step as non-negotiable. Step 1, write your research question. Unchanged, and it does most of the work. One question per prompt, scoped exactly as you would scope it for a database, with the role, the single task, and the format you want back stated plainly. The compound questions the method has trained you to split are the same ones that make a generative system drift, because a sprawling prompt licenses a sprawling answer, and sprawling answers are where fabrications hide. Step 2, research to answer it. Also unchanged, and it includes the choice these tools tempt you to skip: is this the right instrument for this question? The types diagnose it. Exploratory and focusing questions are where these systems currently help most, orienting you, surfacing vocabulary, and stating settled standards. Application questions, which turn on facts in decided cases, are where they fail most often and most convincingly. The verification step, before anything is recorded. This is the discipline the cycle did not need until now. Every case, statute, quotation, and holding gets checked against the primary source before it goes into your log, your outline, or your draft, and you never cite what you have not read. Note the cost while you are at it: if verifying an answer takes as long as finding it yourself would have, that is data about the tool, and it belongs in your Notes field. Read closely Verify before you record Once a landlord has notice that the heat has failed, repairs must be made within a reasonable time. Tinsley v. Vista Prop. Mgmt. A tenant left in the cold may recover damages for emotional distress as a matter of course. Delgado v. Mesa Verde Rentals . Where the outage exceeds thirty days, the tenant is entitled to treble damages. Trammel v. Northgate Flats . Step 3, write down what you found. The verified answer goes into the Research Log exactly as an encyclopedia entry or an opinion would, with one addition to the Source Consulted field, which is the system you used and the prompt you ran. Open the Findings field honestly: the answer fully answers your question, partially answers it, or not really, because a confident tone is not an answer. Step 4, identify your next question. Unchanged. The verified answer exposes the next gap, and the next gap becomes the next question, whether you take it to the AI system, a database, or a book. Step 5, repeat. Unchanged, and so is the checkpoint. Reflect and evaluate as you go, and ask the question this chapter exists to make habitual: is this tool still earning its place in this project?

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: AI in Practice: The Question Method Applied to an AI Research System
t: The First Amendment student speech problem from Chapter 3 shows how the Question Method structures AI-assisted research, including where it succeeds and where it breaks down. Prompt 1 (Exploratory). “How has First Amendment free speech protection been applied to students in school environments?” The AI returned an accurate chronological overview of the major cases: Tinker , Fraser , Hazelwood , Morse , Mahanoy . Assessment: useful orientation, all citations verified in Westlaw. Next question: focus on Hazelwood and school publications. Prompt 2 (Focusing). “How has balancing students’ free speech rights with the unique needs of the school environment been applied to school-run student publications?” The AI correctly identified the Hazelwood standard and distinguished it from Tinker . Assessment: exactly what a focusing question should produce. Limitation: the response could not catalogue cases on either side of the balancing test. Prompt 3 (Application, and a failure mode). “Provide a list of federal cases that utilize the Hazelwood balancing test and find that the school did violate the student’s First Amendment rights.” The AI identified Mahanoy (a student-speech case, but about off-campus social-media speech, not a school publication), Papish v. Board of Curators of the University of Missouri, 410 U.S. 667 (1973) (a student-newspaper case, but at a public university, decided without the Hazelwood framework), and also Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (a case about a teacher’s personal prayer that does not apply the Hazelwood test). This is the characteristic AI failure: the system loses sight of the specific question and retrieves results plausibly related to the general topic rather than precisely responsive to the inquiry. It is the same Kennedy v. Bremerton false hit a human researcher caught in Chapter 3 ’s full demonstration, which is exactly why the method’s precise question-framing catches it here too. By separating out the questions, you can more easily assess usefulness and accuracy. What the demonstration shows: precision prompting produces better output; generative AI handles exploratory and focusing questions better than application questions; and every output requires question-specific review. As you use these systems, you will develop a sense of where they help (today, exploration and orientation) and where your own research remains faster and safer (tailored, fact-specific results).

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: What Generative AI Can and Cannot Do for Legal Research
t: The scannable version, two columns you should internalize: Appropriate uses Inappropriate without independent verification Summarizing a case you have already read and verified Initial case law research Generating initial search terms and synonyms Stating what the current law is Explaining a legal concept you already broadly understand Citing any case, statute, or regulation Drafting questions for your Research Log Asserting what a statute says Formatting and editing tasks, if you instruct the tool to track its changes or list its edits separately (silent regeneration can quietly alter text you never asked it to touch) Predicting case outcomes

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: The duty of competence (Model Rule 1.1) requires understanding generative AI’s hallucination problem; Comment 8 to Rule 1.1 specifically addresses the obligation to keep abreast of changes in practice, including technology. The duty of candor (Model Rule 3.3) prohibits citing false authority, and whether you found it through Westlaw or a chatbot is irrelevant. Many courts now require disclosure of AI use in filings. Supervising attorneys (Rules 5.1 and 5.3) are responsible for ensuring that subordinates’ AI-assisted work is verified before submission. Chapter 12 develops this ethical framework in full; this chapter supplies the technical understanding that makes the framework operational.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: Every AI pitfall traces back to one habit: trusting fluent output you have not verified. A confident citation can be entirely fabricated, so nothing the model produces belongs in your outline until you have read the actual source and confirmed it says what the model claimed. The second pitfall is the mega-prompt, asking a generative system to “research the whole case,” which yields exactly the kind of sprawling answer that is impossible to check; small, discrete questions are both better suited to the tool and far easier to verify. The third is bringing AI to the wrong question type, leaning on it for application questions, where its habit of surfacing the plausibly-related-but-wrong does the most damage, rather than the exploratory and focusing work it does well. And do not assume the database-integrated tools are safe to cite unchecked; their risk profile is lower, but the verification obligation does not change.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
s: AI Tools Integrated Into Legal Databases
t: The AI research features built into Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law are more reliable than general-purpose LLMs, because they work within verified databases and can cite specific documents. They still require verification, but the risk profile is lower. As these tools evolve, the profession’s ethical obligations, competence, candor, diligence, do not change. Check yourself When the tool is built on a real database A commercial platform’s AI assistant answers your question and links each proposition to an opinion in its own database. What has changed from the general-purpose chatbot? Nothing. It is the same technology and equally unreliable. Grounding in a verified database is a real difference. The linked cases almost certainly exist. The cases exist. Whether each one supports the sentence it is attached to is still yours to confirm by reading. Grounding limits fabricated citations. It does not stop a real case from being summarized wrongly or cited for a point it does not hold, and it does not run the citator for you. Everything. Linked citations mean the answer has been verified. A link proves a document exists. It says nothing about whether the document says what the summary claims.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: Generative AI tools offer real speed and carry serious reliability risks, and the Question Method, run one small verified question at a time, is the framework that manages both. Professional responsibility obligations require that every cited authority be verified, whatever its source. Key Takeaways Generative AI tools hallucinate: they produce plausible-sounding but sometimes fabricated citations. The Question Method framework (small discrete tasks, verified output, iterative questions) minimizes generative AI risk. Model Rules 1.1 and 3.3 require verification of all AI-generated content before citation. Generative AI tools integrated into verified legal databases are more reliable but still require verification. Courts are sanctioning attorneys for citing AI-generated fake authority; the consequences are severe.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: The following exercises test your ability to use generative AI within the method’s verification discipline and to recognize when it is the wrong instrument for a question.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: Take a legal question you have already researched by hand; any completed drill from this book works, and the drone capstone works best. Put three prompts to a generative tool: one exploratory (orient me to this area), one focusing (what standard governs this specific situation), and one application (list authorities matching these specific facts). Verify every citation in every response against the primary source before anything touches your Research Log, and log each response with a verdict: confirmed, partially confirmed, or fabricated. Deliverable: the three prompts, the three verdicts, and the verification record behind each. Self-check: because you already know the ground truth, you will catch what a first-time researcher cannot, and the application prompt is where you should expect the cracks. If all three responses came back fully confirmed, your prompts were easier than your drill; tighten the application prompt until the tool has to reach, because watching it reach is the lesson.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: Feed a project you know well to a generative tool as one mega-prompt, “research my whole case,” and write two sentences on why that output is harder to verify than a set of small, single-question answers would be. Deliverable: the mega-prompt output and your two sentences. Self-check: your sentences should be about verifiability, not quality. The mega-prompt answer may read beautifully. The question is how many discrete claims it makes, and how many of them you could trace to a source you have read without spending the afternoon.

p: Chapter 15: GenAI and Legal Research
t: Whenever you work with a generative tool, in this chapter and after it, keep a running note: wherever confirming the tool’s answer cost as much as researching the question yourself would have, write it down. Deliverable: the note, even if short. Self-check: that note is the signal this chapter told you to watch for, the sign that a generative tool was the wrong instrument for that question. Nothing enters your outline unverified, and not only because Chapter 12 showed you a rule requires it. An answer you cannot trace to a source you have read is not an answer. It is a guess wearing a citation. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
s: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: The NextGen Bar Exam tests legal research skills as part of Foundational Skills Group C. The purpose of that group is to assess how well an examinee can identify and implement research strategies, including preliminary issue-spotting, working with provided resources, developing and refining a theory of the case, and reaching closure on research questions. The Question Method prepares you for exactly this, not as a separate exam-prep exercise but as the natural byproduct of practicing the method throughout law school. Learning Objectives Identify the legal research competencies tested in the NextGen Bar Exam’s Foundational Skills Group C Apply the Question Method to timed research tasks typical of bar examination formats Analyze provided legal materials to identify controlling authority, ambiguities, and research strategies Synthesize a collection of provided sources to resolve a legal issue under examination conditions Connect bar exam research competencies to the substantive chapters of this textbook

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: The NCBE competencies consolidate into five skills, which this textbook names as follows: Skill 1: Ambiguity spotting. Reading a legal text and identifying terms, phrases, or provisions whose meaning requires interpretive research. Look for undefined terms, vague standards, terms of art, structural ambiguities, and scope questions. Developed in Chapter 6 (Statutes) and Appendix C ; applied in Chapters 5 , 7, and 8. Skill 2: Intra-jurisdiction source ranking. Given a collection of authorities from a single jurisdiction, ranking them correctly by binding effect. A state supreme court decision ranks above a court of appeals decision. A statute controls over common law on the same subject. Developed in Chapter 1 ; applied throughout. Skill 3: Dispositive fact identification. Reading a judicial opinion to identify the facts that, if changed, would change the outcome, then comparing those facts to a client’s facts. Locate the court’s analytical reasoning and ask whether different facts would change the result. Developed in Chapter 5 (Case Law) and Appendix B . Skill 4: Research gap identification. Recognizing when a source set does not fully answer the question and articulating what would fill the gap. Distinguish “the law is genuinely unclear” from “I have not yet found the answer.” (This is the line Chapters 8 and 9 drilled.) Developed in Chapter 8 (Researching Across Sources). Skill 5: Research sufficiency and closure. Determining when research is complete, which is a professional judgment. Research is sufficient when all questions are answered or identified as open, all authorities are validated, the framework is consistent, and counterarguments have been addressed. Developed in Chapters 3 and 9. Reflection Point. Which of the five skills does a single Question Method cycle already exercise, even with no bar exam in sight? (A short answer appears in Appendix I .)

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
s: Practice Strategies for Bar Research Questions
t: Approaching provided-materials questions. Read all the provided materials before you attempt an answer, and call this move excerpt triage. Build a mental map of what each source provides. Identify binding versus persuasive authorities. Identify ambiguities and note whether the provided cases resolve them. Look for analogous and distinguishable facts. Note gaps. The exam, in effect, hands you a closed universe of sources and asks you to run a compressed Question Method cycle over them. Example Excerpt triage, run once. The item: a customer sues a convenience store after a parking-lot assault, and the provided materials are (1) the state supreme court’s decision adopting a special-relationship exception to the general no-duty rule, (2) an intermediate appellate decision applying that exception to a gas station with two prior robberies, (3) a neighboring state’s supreme court decision using a different foreseeability test, and (4) the state’s premises-liability statute, which addresses physical conditions of the property and says nothing about third-party crime. The triage pass, before writing a word: the supreme court decision controls and supplies the rule; the appellate decision binds and supplies the closest application; the neighboring state’s decision persuades only; and the statute, read for scope, does not reach the issue, which is a finding, not a discard. The ambiguity the item was built around: what makes third-party crime foreseeable enough to ground a duty, the point on which the two in-state decisions leave room. The compressed cycle then runs on the mapped materials: macro question (did the store owe this customer a duty?); its research questions (what is the rule; what makes crime foreseeable under it; how do these facts compare to the applied case); each answered from the source triage identified for it; and the sufficiency call, committed—the materials answer the duty question, and any element they do not address is named as the gap rather than papered over. Forty-five minutes of exam time is this whole cycle at compression, and every move in it is one you have already run at full size. Using the Question Method under time constraints. The framework applies in compressed form: What is the macro question, and what research questions does it break into? What authority controls? What does it say? How does it apply to these facts? Are the provided materials sufficient? Identifying the strongest authority. Rank the provided authorities by the hierarchy: mandatory authority from the highest court controls; persuasive authority supports. A clear statutory provision controls over case law interpreting a different statute.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: The exam hands you a small set of sources and a client problem, and everything you may rely on is on the page. Here is a universe of that kind. Every source in it is fictional. A client’s apartment has had no heat for three weeks in January. Read closely Skill 1: find the terms that will need research Residential Rental Standards Act § 12. (a) A landlord shall maintain every residential rental unit in habitable condition , including operable heating facilities capable of maintaining safe indoor temperatures during the heating season . (b) Upon written notice of a defect under subsection (a), the landlord shall repair within a reasonable time . (c) Remedies for violation of this section are as provided by law . The universe also holds three decisions. Marsh v. Golden Rentals (state supreme court): a residential landlord’s duty to keep a rental fit to live in includes providing adequate heat during the cold months. Okafor v. Canyon Ridge Apartments (state supreme court): a tenant facing an unrepaired habitability defect may repair and deduct, or may withhold rent, but only after written notice and a reasonable opportunity to cure; an earlier decision permitting withholding without notice is disapproved. Delgado v. Mesa Verde Rentals (court of appeals): damages for a habitability breach are generally limited to the loss in rental value, and emotional-distress damages require egregious conduct. Check yourself Skill 2: which authority controls? The client stopped paying rent yesterday without telling the landlord anything. Within this universe, which authority controls the conditions for withholding rent? Okafor , the supreme court’s rule, which fills in what § 12(c) leaves to “law.” The statute frames and the highest court fills. Okafor conditions withholding on written notice and a chance to cure, and the client skipped the condition. Section 12(b), because a statute outranks a case. A statute does outrank a case when they address the same thing. Section 12(b) governs when the landlord must repair. It says nothing about withholding, and § 12(c) points outward. Delgado , as the most specific decision on remedies. Delgado addresses damages, not withholding, and as a court of appeals decision it ranks below Okafor in any event. Check yourself Skill 4: is the answer in the universe at all? The client asks whether she can recover her moving costs if she has to relocate. Answer from the universe. Yes. Section 12(c) makes remedies available “as provided by law.” Section 12(c) points to law the universe does not contain on this point. A pointer to nothing is a gap. No. Delgado limits damages to lost rental value. Tempting. Delgado says “generally,” it was deciding an emotional-distress claim, and it never mentions relocation. Stretching a holding past its facts is the classic trap. The universe does not answer it. Say so, and say what kind of source would. Research gap identification. The competent answer names the gap and what would fill it, such as a statute or decision on consequential damages, and does not dress a guess as analysis.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: Under time pressure, the tempting mistake is to start writing before reading every provided source, which is how examinees miss the one authority that controls the answer. Close behind is misranking what they have read, treating a persuasive decision or an off-point statute as though it controlled; the hierarchy of authority is the whole game on “which source governs” questions. Another is failing to spot the ambiguity the question was built around, since the exam usually hides an undefined term or a scope question that the provided cases are there to resolve. And examinees often forget the closure step, declaring an answer without asking whether the provided materials are actually sufficient or whether a gap remains to be named.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: The NextGen Bar Exam’s Foundational Skills Group C assesses the same research competencies the Question Method develops: issue-spotting, source evaluation, analogical reasoning, and research closure. Consistent practice of the method’s five steps throughout law school is also bar exam preparation. Key Takeaways The NextGen Bar Exam tests legal research as a discrete skill, balanced between litigation and transactional practice. Five named skills are tested: ambiguity spotting, source ranking, dispositive fact identification, research gap identification, and research sufficiency. The Question Method provides a compressed but applicable framework for bar exam research questions. Ranking authorities by the hierarchy of legal authority is the core skill for “which source controls” questions. Research closure, knowing when the materials are sufficient, is both a Question Method skill and a bar exam competency.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
t: The following exercises test compressed research under time pressure and your command of the five named skills.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
s: Exercise 16.1 — The Clocked Cycle and the Five-Skill Audit
t: Step one, the clock. Take a closed universe of sources: a source set your instructor provides, or the Research Log from a Part I drill you completed, with the logged sources as the provided materials and nothing else allowed in. Put forty-five minutes on a clock and run the compressed cycle from this chapter: state the macro question, break it into its research questions, rank the provided authorities by binding effect, name the ambiguity the problem turns on, apply the controlling authority to the facts, and finish with the sufficiency call, either “these materials answer the question” or a named gap and what would fill it. Step two, when time expires, the audit: mark where each of the five named skills appears in your answer, ambiguity spotting, source ranking, dispositive fact identification, gap identification, and closure. Deliverable: the written answer produced inside the clock, with the five marks placed, or an honest note on any mark you could not place. Self-check: the sufficiency call must be present and committed; “probably enough” is not a call. And a skill you cannot point to in your own answer is a skill you skipped; an unplaceable mark is next week’s assignment, not a failure. Run the exercise again on different material next week, and once more the week after, because compression is a skill you build on material you already own.

p: Chapter 16: The NextGen Bar Exam and Legal Research
s: Exercise 16.2 — Break It Down, No Searching
t: A bar-style item, run entirely from this page. A client was fired for refusing Sunday shifts she says her religion forbids. The provided materials: the state’s employment-discrimination statute; two decisions of the state’s intermediate appellate court applying it; one decision of a neighboring state’s supreme court; and one law review article. In ten minutes and without searching: state the macro question; break it into the research questions the materials would need to answer; say which provided material would answer each; and rank the materials by binding effect for the state’s trial court. Deliverable: the breakdown and the ranking. Self-check: the neighboring state’s decision and the article belong at the bottom of your ranking, persuasive and secondary respectively; if either appeared as the answer to a controlling-rule question, revisit the hierarchy of authority, because ranking the provided materials is the core skill behind every “which source controls” question the exam asks. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Legal scholarship asks something different of your research. In practice, you find the controlling law and apply it to a client’s facts. In scholarship, you are trying to add an original argument to an ongoing conversation. That requires thorough doctrinal research and a survey of the scholarly landscape: who has written on this topic, what arguments have been made, and where genuine controversy or underdevelopment exists. A note on this chapter’s shape: scholarship is a context, not a source, so this chapter deliberately drops the source-chapter template you have followed since Chapter 4 . No Questions This Source Answers section, no source anatomy. That is on purpose. You will most likely return to this chapter when you write a seminar paper, a journal note or comment, or a moot court brief. Those are the occasions it is for. Learning Objectives Distinguish legal scholarship research from practice-oriented research in goals, sources, and methodology Recognize the many kinds of questions a scholarly paper can answer, and turn any of them into a research question Generate and narrow a viable paper topic Map the scholarly landscape on a legal topic: positions staked out, points of agreement and disagreement, and genuine gaps Run preemption checks at the right moments, from the first cursory search to the final pre-submission sweep Locate relevant interdisciplinary scholarship that bears on a legal question Use the Question Method to research and draft the paper section by section, one question at a time

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Where does a paper come from? Students tend to imagine there is one kind of scholarly paper, usually some version of “find a question nobody has answered.” The truth is roomier. A paper can explore an unsettled question, where the law genuinely has not decided and your paper works out what the answer is or should be. Does training an AI model on licensed stock photography exhaust the license? Nobody knows yet. A paper can wade into a live controversy, where courts or scholars are actively fighting, and pick a side, broker a peace, or show that everyone has been asking the wrong question. A paper can argue that a working system needs fixing. How might we fix the DMCA’s notice-and-takedown process to protect creator rights without stifling creation in the new social-media landscape? Notice what that question is doing. Nothing about the DMCA is unsettled; takedown notices go out every day. The paper’s claim is that the machine runs exactly as designed and the design is hurting people it was never built to see. And these are only the common shapes. A paper can synthesize a scattered body of law that nobody has pulled together, respond to a single important new opinion, predict where a doctrine is heading, or carry another field’s insight into legal territory. What every version shares is the ending: the topic resolves into a question, and your thesis is the answer you will defend. If you have been running the method, you already hold a supply of candidates. Every project leaves questions behind: the issue an opinion expressly reserved (“we need not decide today whether…”), the open question an article names in its final pages, the point two authors dispute without ever quite engaging, the framework a practitioner grumbles about because it makes her clients’ lives harder. In practice research you set those aside, because the client needs an answer, not an agenda. In scholarship they are the agenda. Get in the habit of writing them down as you read. Call this your question inventory, and a well-fed inventory means you may never face the blank page asking “what should I write about?” at all. If the inventory is thin, you can hunt. Circuit splits are the classic starting point, because a split is a controversy with the proof already assembled: the Congressional Research Service publishes a regular roundup of new splits, several blogs track them weekly, and a terms-and-connectors search like circuit /s split, filtered to the last two years, surfaces them on demand. New technology straining an old statute is another dependable well, and so is its mirror image, a new statute colliding with settled practice. Fifty-state surveys and ALR annotations show you where the law is in disarray. For the fix-the-system paper, look where the complaints pile up: chronic litigation over the same provision, agencies issuing guidance to patch a statute that no longer fits, compliance regimes everyone works around instead of through. And talk to people. Professors, former supervisors, and practitioners all carry questions they wish someone would answer. Come with the areas you are considering; leave with their sense of which problems actually hurt. Before you commit to a candidate, ask four things of it. Is it supportable? A literature has to exist for you to stand on and push against. Is it open or fixable? You need a question that has not been answered, or a system whose flaws have not been honestly reckoned with. Is it worth answering? Someone (a court, a legislature, a practice community, the next scholar) should be better off once your question is resolved. And can you live with it? You will spend a semester or more in this question’s company, so pick one you actually want to think about. Be realistic about scope while you test. The articles you admire in the journals are often the product of years, and your seminar paper cannot cover the same ground. It does not need to. A narrow question answered thoroughly is a contribution; a broad one gestured a

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: The Question Method changes shape slightly in scholarship, and the change is worth naming before you start searching. In practice, your questions come from the client’s problem, and you work one at a time until each closes. In scholarship you run two tracks at once. The first is the question you are working right now, and early in a project it is usually some version of “has anyone already made my argument?” The second is the collecting habit from the last section: as you read, you keep harvesting the questions the field is asking into your inventory. The two tracks feed each other. Today’s working question sends you into the literature, the literature restocks the inventory, and the inventory supplies next semester’s paper. Run a cursory preemption check before anything else. The temptation at the start of a project is the grand tour: every database, every article, a mountain of PDFs. Resist it, because there is a cheaper question to answer first. Does your argument already exist? Spend an hour, not a week: search the distinctive terms of your claim in HeinOnline, Westlaw or Lexis, SSRN, and Google Scholar, and read the abstracts of the closest matches. If someone has written your paper, you want to know before the outline exists, not after. If the claim survives the hour, proceed to the full sweep; the formal preemption protocol later in this section digs deeper, and it will run again. Searching for articles and working papers. HeinOnline is the most comprehensive full-text database, with strong historical coverage. Westlaw and Lexis offer sophisticated search tools. SSRN is free and carries cutting-edge working papers, often months or years ahead of publication. Google Scholar is free and useful for citation counts and finding key articles. And do not overlook bepress’s Digital Commons network and institutional repositories, where new scholarship often lands first, free to anyone. One more habit, and it matters: do not stop at the law reviews. Depending on your issue, the conversation you are joining may be running partly in another field’s journals (economics, political science, psychology, public health, history), and a landscape map that omits them is incomplete. The interdisciplinary section below tells you where those literatures live. Organizing the literature. Organize by doctrinal position (the dominant view, the competing minority, emerging positions); by theoretical approach (law and economics, critical theory, originalism, purposivism, empirical legal studies); and by chronology (foundational articles, significant responses, the most recent contributions). Conducting preemption research. Preemption in scholarship means checking whether your argument has already been made. The cursory check was your first pass. This one is deeper, and it recurs, because a preempting article can land on SSRN while you are writing. A contribution that has been fully preempted is not a contribution, and discovering that early, rather than after a semester of writing, is one of the highest-value research tasks in scholarship. The protocol, formatted like the book’s others: Step 1: Search the claims. Look for articles asserting your thesis or something near it: keyword searches on the claim’s distinctive terms, symposium issues on your topic, and student notes, which cluster around exactly the questions a note-writer would pick. Step 2: Read the closest matches for actual overlap. An article in the same area is not preemption; an article making your argument is. Read for the thesis, not the topic. Step 3: Differentiate or pivot. If the argument exists, name precisely what you add (new doctrine, new data, new mechanism, new implication) or choose a different focus. State, in one sentence, what your piece says that the existing piece does not. If you cannot write that sentence, pivot. Check yourself Someone got there first. Now what? Your thesis is that courts should apply doctrine X to gig workers. The preemption search turns up a 2022

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
s: Writing the Paper One Question at a Time
t: A scholarly paper looks like one long argument, and that is what makes it intimidating: forty pages, hundreds of footnotes, a thesis that has to hold from the first line to the last. Here is the reassuring secret. Underneath, most papers answer a short, recognizable sequence of questions. What is the current legal framework? What problem has emerged that the framework must face? Why does the framework fail to handle it? What should be done instead? And, running beneath all of it, what will the strongest objection be? Open the table of contents of almost any article you admire and you will find some version of that sequence: background, problem, critique, proposal. Each section exists to answer one big question, and each big question breaks down into the same kind of research questions you have been drafting since Chapter 3 . The question taxonomy travels with you, and scholarship stacks one more level on top of it. A scholarly project usually opens with a doctrinal question, the familiar kind: What does the law currently require on X? It then moves to a scholarly question: Is this rule defensible, and who has argued for or against it? And it matures into a normative question: What should the law be, and why? The destination differs from practice, because the goal is an original, well-supported argument rather than the controlling rule for a client. The engine, though, never changes. Each answer becomes a section of your annotated outline, and each gap you find in the existing literature becomes a potential contribution. In the Introduction’s vocabulary, the scholarly and normative questions are the macro questions of scholarship, and your thesis is the answer the paper exists to defend. The research questions are still the steps. That means you research a paper the way you research everything else: one question at a time. An exploratory survey of the whole issue is right at the start; that is how you found the topic and mapped the landscape. But once the outline exists and drafting begins, resist the urge to hold the entire argument in your head at once. Nobody can digest every part of a forty-page argument simultaneously, and the method does not ask you to. When you sit down to work on the framework section, run cycles on the framework: what does the statute actually require, how have courts read it, where are its edges? When you reach the problem section, the framework questions are closed and the problem gets your full attention. Each section is a small research project with its own chain of questions, its own Research Log entries, and its own closure. Your annotated outline is where this becomes concrete. Draft the outline as questions rather than topics: not “III. The DMCA framework” but “III. What does the DMCA’s takedown process actually require?” The difference matters, because a question can be answered, and answered means done. As each section closes, the outline fills with answers in your own words, anchored to authority in your Research Log, and the paper begins assembling itself from parts you have already verified. Drafting becomes what it should be: writing up answers you already hold, and noticing the gaps that send you back for one more cycle.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Legal questions often benefit from insights in other disciplines, and knowing where to look for them is its own research skill. Some examples are included below, but this is not an exhaustive list. Contract interpretation: cognitive linguistics and behavioral economics (JSTOR, SSRN, NBER working papers). Constitutional design: comparative political science (JSTOR political science journals, comparative politics databases). Criminal sentencing: criminology, psychology, sociology (SSRN, Sociological Abstracts, PsycINFO). Administrative regulation: public administration and organizational theory (JSTOR, Public Administration Review). First Amendment: philosophy of speech and sociology of media (PhilPapers, communication journals). Useful search tools include JSTOR (humanities and social sciences), PhilPapers (philosophy), PsycINFO (psychology), SSRN (economics, finance, social science), NBER (economics working papers), and Google Scholar (broad interdisciplinary coverage). Consider making an appointment with a law librarian to learn what relevant databases you might have access to.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: The pitfall that wastes the most time in scholarship is skipping preemption research and discovering, a semester in, that your “original” argument was published three years ago; running that first cursory check before anything else is what protects the whole project. A second is choosing a subject area instead of a question and calling it a topic: a subject area is a shelf to browse, not a paper to write. A third is mistaking a literature summary for a contribution, gathering what everyone has said without staking out what you will add. A fourth is reaching for interdisciplinary sources as decoration rather than support, citing an economics paper you have not actually integrated into the argument. If your paper argues that a system needs fixing, remember that a complaint is not a proposal: the paper needs the repair, not just the diagnosis. And be careful with working papers: SSRN puts you at the front of the conversation, but a paper that has not been peer-reviewed may change before publication, so rely on it with that caveat in mind.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
s: Citing Secondary Sources in Scholarly Writing
t: In law review articles, citing treatises, other articles, and Restatements is standard and often essential for establishing scholarly context. The goal is to join and advance the conversation. Unlike court filings, where secondary source citations are rare, scholarship depends on engaging the full literature.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: SSRN working papers represent the cutting edge, often months or years ahead of publication. Engaging with them ensures your scholarship responds to the most current conversation. When you rely on a working paper, note that it has not been peer-reviewed and its arguments may change before final publication.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Scholarship gives the method a wider field and a longer clock. A paper can explore an unsettled question, join a controversy, argue that a system needs fixing, or take another shape entirely; whatever the shape, the topic resolves into a question your thesis will answer. Check cheaply and early whether the argument already exists, then map the landscape, reaching past the law reviews whenever the issue does, and run the full preemption protocol when the thesis firms up and again before you submit. When the writing starts, the paper itself becomes a chain of questions (what is the framework, what is the problem, why does the framework fail, what is the fix), and you research each section’s question the way you have researched everything in this book: one at a time, to closure. And keep the question inventory restocked as you read. The working question finishes this paper. The inventory starts the next. Key Takeaways Scholarly research aims to contribute original analysis, not merely to find controlling law. A paper can answer many kinds of questions (an unsettled question, a live controversy, a system that needs fixing, a synthesis nobody has done, among others), and every kind resolves into a question the thesis answers. Run a cursory preemption check before the deep literature search; run the full protocol again when the thesis firms up and once more before submission. Mapping the scholarly landscape (who has written what, and where positions diverge) reaches beyond the law reviews whenever the issue does. The method runs two tracks in scholarship: the question you are answering now, and the question inventory you restock as you read.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: This chapter has no source-by-source drills, because scholarship is a context, not a source. What it has instead is a working method, and the checklist below puts that method in the order you will need it. Run it when the seminar paper, note, or comment actually arrives. (Adapted from the interactive companion’s Chapter 17 page.) Checklist The Scholarship Research Checklist Run a cursory preemption check before anything else. An hour, not a week. Search your claim’s distinctive terms in HeinOnline, Westlaw or Lexis, SSRN, and Google Scholar, and read the closest abstracts. If someone has written your paper, know it before the outline exists. Choose a question, not a subject area. A subject area is a shelf to browse, not a paper to write. The topic resolves into the question your thesis will answer. Map the scholarly landscape. Note the positions staked out, the points of agreement and disagreement, and the genuine gaps. Read the closest matches for actual overlap: an article in the same area is not preemption; an article making your argument is. Run the full preemption protocol when the thesis firms up. If the argument exists, differentiate your contribution or refocus. A fully preempted contribution is not a contribution. Write the contribution sentence. Say what you add beyond a summary of what everyone else has said. A literature summary is not a contribution. Research and draft one question at a time. Framework, problem, why the framework fails, the fix: take each section’s question to closure. Reach past the law reviews when the issue does, but integrate interdisciplinary sources as support, not decoration. If your paper argues the system needs fixing, the paper needs the repair, not just the diagnosis. Mind working papers. SSRN puts you at the front of the conversation, but an un-peer-reviewed paper can change before publication. Rely on it with that caveat. Run the final preemption sweep before submission. A preempting article can land while you are writing. Restock the question inventory as you read. The working question finishes this paper. The inventory starts the next.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: The following exercises, together called Map the Conversation , test topic generation, preemption checking, and question-form outlining. They begin an actual paper rather than simulate one.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Go back through the sources you read for any three drills in this book, the cases, the secondary sources, the guidance documents (any three substantial legal sources you have read this term work as well), and harvest the questions they left open: the issue an opinion expressly reserved, the point flagged as beyond an article’s scope, the term two authorities read differently without ever engaging each other. Deliverable: a question inventory of at least five entries, each logged with where you found it. Self-check: every entry should be a question someone else’s text left open, not a topic you find interesting. “AI and copyright” is a shelf. “The court expressly declined to decide whether X, so what is the answer?” is an inventory entry.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: Take a candidate paper question, the strongest entry in your question inventory or any thesis you are considering, and spend exactly one hour on the cursory preemption check: search the claim’s distinctive terms in HeinOnline, Westlaw or Lexis, SSRN, and Google Scholar, and read the abstracts of the closest matches. Deliverable: a Research Log record of the searches you ran, the nearest neighbors you found, and the verdict: survives, needs differentiating, or preempted. Self-check: the hour is a real constraint; honor it, because the check’s whole value is being cheap. And if the verdict is preempted, celebrate briefly. The check just saved you a semester, and your inventory holds four more candidates.

p: Chapter 17: Research for Legal Scholarship
t: For a candidate claim that has survived a preemption check, or any working thesis, draft a four-line mini-outline in question form, framework, problem, critique, proposal, each heading written as a question a section could answer. Add one line naming the non-law literature the paper would need and the database where that literature lives. Deliverable: the five lines. Self-check: each heading must be answerable, because answerable means a section can be finished, and finished sections are how forty pages get written by someone who can only hold one question at a time, which is everyone. A subject area is a shelf to browse. A question is a paper you can start, and after this exercise you have started one. Sample answers for this chapter’s exercises appear in Appendix H .

p: Inception of the Textbook
t: Good researchers do not work by the seat of their pants, even when it looks that way from the outside. They have run the planning and the process so many times that the steps have gone underground, below conscious thought. This book digs those steps back up so you can learn them on purpose. Here is what skilled researchers actually do. They ask a question. They find an authoritative source that answers it. They write the answer down in their own words. Then they look at that answer and notice the next gap in what they know, and that gap becomes the next question. Then they do it again. The question drives the whole cycle. The sources are just where you stop along the way. Most legal research textbooks are really source guides. They tell you what databases exist, how to read an annotated code, how to run a citator check. That is useful, and you will find all of it in this book too. But most of those texts treat the research question as a planning step, something you settle before you begin and then file away once the “real” research starts. That framing leaves out the most important part. It also blurs two different questions. The question those texts have you settle up front is the big one, the legal issue your finished document must resolve. The questions that drive the actual research are smaller, and there are many of them. Experts research in loops. Each answer raises a new question. Each source exposes a new gap. The inquiry keeps narrowing and deepening until it runs out of questions to ask. When this book says research question, it means those smaller, moving questions; the Introduction lays out the full vocabulary. This is also why you cannot fully plan a research question in advance when you are working in an unfamiliar area of law. You do not yet know which facts matter, or which sources will help, because you do not yet know what the law requires. Relevance is something the cycle uncovers as you go. You cannot load it in at the start. The Question Method is built on that idea. It puts the iterative question at the center of how you learn legal research, ahead of the database, the source type, and the Bluebook. You will learn to ask a question, find and synthesize an answer, write it down, and ask a sharper question next. You will still learn each of the legal research sources thoroughly, and I would argue you will come out knowing them better, because each chapter shows you how a particular source answers a particular kind of question. A case might give you the elements of a tort. A statute might hand you the definition of a term you have been chasing. A regulation will tell you how to certify produce as organic. A law review article might flag an emerging issue your lobbying clients need you to see coming. The book also tries to make the invisible visible. An experienced researcher makes dozens of small decisions every session. Which source do I check next? When do I stop reading this case and move on? Is this result actually useful, or does it just look useful? Has this promising lead turned into a dead end? Those decisions are hard to teach precisely because the people who are best at them have stopped noticing they make them. If you already have some research experience, you may make a few of these calls on instinct, and some of what I ask you to do here will feel like a step backward. Take the step anyway. The granularity is scaffolding, and scaffolding comes down. Work every step explicitly now, and you will compress the chain later, the way every expert eventually does, knowing exactly which steps you are skipping because you once performed each one on purpose. If you are new to this, the book will help you build that judgment one deliberate move at a time. Work through it carefully, and you will come away with more than a map of where the law lives. You will have a practiced way of thinking about how to find the law, how to use it, and how to know when you are finished.

p: Introduction
t: A few years ago, in the middle of a legal research class, a student asked me a question that changed how I teach. We had spent the session on secondary sources: how to find them, how to navigate a table of contents, how to scan a section’s footnotes for the citations that point to cases on your issue. We had even worked through a passage together and flagged the footnotes worth chasing. Then the student looked at the half-dozen cases those footnotes pointed to and asked, “But which one do I read first?” It was a simple question. It was also exactly the right one, because it exposed a gap, not in what the student understood, but in what I had taught. I had shown them how to find a secondary source, how to navigate it, and how to spot the passages whose footnotes led somewhere useful. I had not shown them how to decide which lead to follow first. I had assumed that choice was obvious. It is not, and it happens to be the judgment that separates a novice from an expert. Handed six plausible citations, a novice reads all of them and drowns, or picks one at random and hopes. An expert reads the one that answers the question they are holding right now. The footnotes do not put themselves in order. The researcher’s current question orders them. Knowing which gap to close next, and therefore which lead to chase first, is the skill that source-guide instruction tends to leave out. This textbook is what happened when I took that realization seriously.

p: Introduction
t: The Question Method is a structured, repeating approach to legal research. The cycle is simple. You define the question you are working on right now. You research to answer it. You write down what you found. Based on what you found, you identify the next question. Then you run the cycle again, and you keep going until no real question is left. None of this is new. It is what skilled researchers already do. The method just names each move so you can learn it on purpose instead of hoping to absorb it by osmosis. Naming each move is what makes it teachable. Because every step has a name, you can watch yourself do it, and you can catch yourself when it goes wrong. When the research starts to feel unproductive, you can stop and ask, “What kind of question am I actually asking right now?” More often than not you will find the question is poorly scoped, pointed at the wrong source, or already answered. Naming the moves also answers my student’s question. When a source hands you several leads at once, the one to follow first is the one that answers your current question. The rest become later questions, which you write down and come back to in turn. ( Appendix A returns to this exact moment when it shows you how to work a secondary source’s footnotes.) The method threads that discipline through every stage of research and writing, so the judgment an expert applies without thinking becomes a habit you build on purpose.

p: Introduction
t: Before the method gets to work, three terms need pinning down, because the rest of this book leans on them. The legal issue is the problem the law must resolve, the reason the file landed on your desk. The macro question is that issue framed as the single big question your document exists to answer: the question presented in a memo, the issue on appeal in a brief, the thesis of a seminar paper. A research question is the micro question you ask and answer along the way, one of the many subquestions whose answers, assembled, answer the macro question. When this book says research question, it always means the micro question. The distinction matters because the macro question is a terrible research companion. If it is the only question you hold, every source has to be weighed against all of it at once, and every passage looks potentially relevant, because everything ultimately bears on the macro question. That is not how brains process information. We work through one concept at a time. Nobody learns a dance routine by running the whole thing at every rehearsal. You drill it in sections, then you assemble the performance. Research questions are the sections. This is also why it is not enough to write a research question at the planning stage and never revisit it. A researcher who does that is really carrying the macro question through the whole project, trying to process everything a source says all at once, and feeling buried by it. The method asks for the opposite discipline: write the macro question down where you can see it, hold exactly one research question at a time, and let each answer hand you the next. The macro question is the destination. The research questions are the steps.

p: Introduction
t: If you are in a first-year legal research course, read Part I straight through, in order. The method shows up in Chapter 3 and runs through every chapter after it. Start each chapter with its Chapter Objectives. They tell you what you should be able to do by the end, not just what you should know. The Research Log is the single most useful practical tool in this book. Use it for every exercise here, and eventually for every research task you take on in practice. The habit you build in the safety of a course is the same one that will protect you and your clients later.

p: Use of AI in the Development of this Textbook
s: Use of AI in the Development of this Textbook
t: Generative AI was used in the development of this textbook. This section is my effort to disclose that use as transparently as possible, so you can be as informed as possible as you engage with the material. Please note, I reviewed and edited every chapter before publication, and I verified every statement of law and every citation against primary authority, the same rule Chapter 15 asks of you. Any errors that remain are mine. If you find one, tell me. That’s the beauty of a live, open-access textbook: I can fix it.

p: Use of AI in the Development of this Textbook
t: I used generative AI to help build this textbook and the accompanying interactive website and instructor edition, from early planning through final drafts. The ideas and frameworks are mine. The Question Method deviates sharply from the methodology most research textbooks describe. So, this textbook could not be created solely with a prompt and limited oversight. The book is built on a large body of my original work product: teaching notes, methodological descriptions, fully worked examples, chapter outlines, draft language for the core elements of each chapter, and samples of my writing so the drafting would sound like me. AI drafted from that foundation.I also matched the tool to the task rather than defaulting to the most powerful option: the smallest capable models for settled material and first drafts, larger models only where the work demanded them, for developing novel concepts at scale, for deep structural edits, and vibe coding to speed the development of the accompanying website.

p: Use of AI in the Development of this Textbook
t: I did not make the choice to utilize Generative AI lightly. I weighed the costs of using this tool, which I attempt to calculate below, against the value of a free, open textbook on a new method with a companion interactive website finished within a few months before the Fall 2026 semester. As with many libraries, our bandwidth is limited, and our desire to do the absolute best for the communities we serve is often bottlenecked by that bandwidth. As such, this tool gave me the ability to expand my internal teaching materials on this method into a full textbook that could better serve my students and hopefully students at other institutions.

p: Use of AI in the Development of this Textbook
t: It was my intention from the beginning to limit the use of genAI to initial development. Nothing about reading, hosting, or updating this book will utilize another large language model. The accompanying interactive website might, but only if there are major technological issues that must be addressed within a timeframe too short for me to programmatically solve myself in a timely manner (e.g., a major accessibility concern). I can and intend to update the content and code myself as needed. Below are my best estimates of the environmental impact from the development of this textbook and accompanying resources. These numbers are in flux as people continue to do research, so I used the high end for my textbook and the median of ranges for the conventional textbook. Using the high end of available estimates, developing this book and companion materials consumed roughly 12 kWh of energy (up to 12 kg of CO2, depending on the grid) and about 100 liters of water. Digital hosting adds an estimated 3 to 7 kWh and 1.3 to 3.1 kg of CO2 per gigabyte per year, and this book is a fraction of a gigabyte (I only know the size of the downloadable files, not the actual size of all code on the Pressbooks site). For comparison, a conventional 400-page print textbook is estimated to consume 400 liters of water (over 5,000 at the high end), about 2 kg of timber (roughly a twentieth of a tree), and 2.7 to 7.5 kg of CO2 across its life cycle. This is per textbook. What is harder to quantify, and deeply important to me, is the positive impact from students who pay nothing for their class materials, and, I hope, students who learn legal research better from the question method and more than one way to learn it. The development costs for this textbook were paid once, for every reader. At least 40 students will be using this textbook this year between my fall and spring classes. To me, if this textbook can improve legal research comprehension, even among this small a cohort, the positive impact outweighs the negative externalities. Should it be adopted by others, which is the hope of any textbook writer, the cost per user shrinks, meaning the positive impact begins to exponentially outweigh the negative externalities.

p: Part I: Foundational Legal Research Topics
s: Part I: Foundational Legal Research Topics
t: Part I is the complete foundation: everything you need to complete most basic research projects from first question to documented closure. Chapter 1 maps where the law lives, because you cannot decide where to look until you know what is out there. Chapter 2 introduces the platforms and search mechanics you will use every working day. Then Chapter 3 introduces the Question Method itself, the engine the rest of this book runs on. Read those three in order. Everything after them assumes you have. Chapters 4 through 7 each take up one major source type: secondary sources, case law, statutes, and regulations. They share a deliberate template. Each shows you how the source fits the research cycle, what kinds of questions it answers, how it is made and what that means for your research, and how to search it. The repetition is the point. By the fourth pass, the questions you ask of a new source will start to feel automatic, and that is the habit forming. Chapters 8 and 9 put the pieces together. Real projects rarely live in one source; Chapter 8 shows you how statutes, regulations, and cases interlock, and how to run the cycle across all of them at once. Chapter 9 teaches the endgame: precision searching once your questions have narrowed, and the closing-out protocol that lets you say, with a documented basis, that the research is done. Between the macro question you write down at the start and the closure you document at the end, every move in this part is one you will use for the rest of your career. A word on how to work through it. The chapters include drills, and Appendix E holds the model walkthroughs, kept apart so you cannot read an answer by accident. Attempt every drill before you look. The method only becomes yours through repetition, and Part I is where you get them. Do the reps.

p: Part II: Advanced Legal Research Topics
s: Part II: Advanced Legal Research Topics
t: Part I introduced the process. Part II provides the knowledge to apply everything you have learned to more complex and varied legal research processes. The sources get more specialized, the contexts more demanding, and the stakes more explicitly professional. Part II opens where Part I left off, with statutes and regulations. Chapter 10 takes up legislative history, the record of what a legislature said while it was writing the law. Chapter 11 takes up the materials agencies produce beyond the regulations themselves, including where agency interpretations stand after Loper Bright . Both answer the question Chapters 6 and 7 leave behind: the text is on the page, so what does it mean in practice? Each follows the familiar template, so you will know exactly what to ask of it. Chapter 12 then turns to the rules that govern all of it. Research quality is not a private matter between you and your grade. It is a professional obligation with rules attached, and lawyers are sanctioned for failing it. The chapter shows that the verification habits, the citator checks, and the Research Log as a reviewable record are the method’s own closing steps, performed with the rules of professional conduct in view. Read it as the frame for everything else in Part II, and return to it whenever the stakes rise. Chapter 13 adds the last source most first-year courses never reach: dockets and court documents. Chapters 14 through 17 then shift from sources to contexts. Litigation, transactional, and compliance practice each bend the method to their own rhythms. Generative AI tools demand the cycle’s verification discipline more than any source before them. The NextGen bar exam tests the skills this book has been naming all along. And scholarship hands you a new kind of macro question, one where the thesis is the answer your paper exists to defend. Unlike Part I, this part does not need to be read straight through. After Chapter 11 , take the chapters as your coursework or your practice demands them, but read Chapter 12 before you rely on any of them in practice.

p: Appendix A: How to Read a Secondary Source
s: Appendix A: How to Read a Secondary Source
t: Secondary sources are the ones that talk about the law rather than being the law: encyclopedias, treatises, Hornbooks, Restatements, ALR annotations, practice guides, and law review articles. They are usually where a research project should start, especially in an unfamiliar area, because a good secondary source hands you the landscape and the citations to the primary authority all at once. The thing to keep in mind while you read one is that it is a map, not the territory. You use it to find and understand the law, but with rare exceptions you do not cite it as the law itself. And reading one is the method you have been practicing, applied to a page. Every source exists to answer certain kinds of questions. A secondary source exists to answer the exploratory and definitional questions that open a project, so you read it holding the question you brought. Read closely One encyclopedia paragraph, read for one question § 3. Duty; status of the entrant. Since 1967 Arizona has fixed the possessor’s duty by the entrant’s status as an invitee, a licensee, or a trespasser , and Arizona courts have declined invitations to abandon the categories. To an invitee the possessor owes an affirmative duty to use reasonable care to make the premises safe, which includes discovering and correcting, or warning of, hazards the possessor should foresee as dangerous to the invitee. A lessee, an occupant, or a public body operating land it does not own can each be a possessor; in the leading Arizona park case the State was held to the possessor’s duty for a recreation area it leased from the federal government. Modern Arizona decisions treat obviousness as a factor bearing on breach rather than as a bar to duty.

p: Appendix A: How to Read a Secondary Source
t: Finding Aids. The table of contents and index are how you locate the right discussion inside a long work. Learning to navigate them quickly is half the skill of using treatises and encyclopedias well. The Narrative Text. The author’s explanation of the doctrine: how the area is structured, what the elements and tests are, where the debates lie, and which terms of art you need to know. This is what orients you and supplies the vocabulary your later questions will require. Footnotes and Citations. The most valuable part for a researcher. The footnotes point you to the primary authority (the cases, statutes, and regulations) that the narrative is describing. A single well-placed footnote can hand you the leading case on your issue. Currency and Supplementation Information. Print treatises and encyclopedias update through pocket parts and supplements; online versions show a “current through” date. Knowing how a source updates, and when it was last updated, tells you how far to trust it before you verify against primary authority. Editorial Apparatus. Cross-references to related sections, research references to other secondary sources, and (in annotated works like ALR) summaries organized by jurisdiction or by factual scenario.

p: Appendix A: How to Read a Secondary Source
s: How to Engage With the Source
t: Match the source type to your question type. A no-clue exploratory question wants an encyclopedia. A foundational question wants a treatise. A survey question across jurisdictions wants an ALR annotation, a Restatement, a CRS report, or a 50-state survey. Choosing the right secondary source for the question you are holding is the first efficiency the method buys you. Navigate, do not read end to end. Use the table of contents and index to jump to the relevant section. You are looking for the discussion that answers your current question, not trying to absorb the whole treatise. Mine the footnotes for primary authority, in the order your question dictates. This is where my student’s question comes back.
