When a passage’s footnotes point to half a dozen cases, you do not read all six. You read the one that answers the question you are holding right now, and you log the rest as later questions with their citations noted. The narrative tells you what the law is; the footnotes tell you where to confirm it. Confirm against primary authority, and check currency. A secondary source can be out of date, can oversimplify, or can simply be wrong. Use it to find and understand the law, then go read the primary authority it points to and verify the rule yourself. Note the source’s “current through” date or check its pocket part, because doctrine described in an older edition may since have changed. Cite primary authority, not the secondary source. With narrow exceptions (a Restatement section a court has adopted, a leading treatise on an unsettled point), you build your argument on the primary authority the secondary source led you to, not on the secondary source itself.

p: Appendix B: How to Read a Case
s: Appendix B: How to Read a Case
t: Reading a judicial opinion is harder than it sounds, and it helps to say that out loud. Opinions are written by judges for other lawyers and judges, who are assumed to already know the terminology, the procedural context, and the analytical conventions. The disorientation you feel at first is normal, and it passes. Once you can recognize the parts, you can move through any opinion efficiently, reading for the components that answer your question and moving quickly past the rest. That is the Question Method restated for opinions. Reading a case is answering the questions the opinion exists to answer: what was the dispute, what rule resolved it, and which facts the resolution turned on. Bring your current research question to every opinion, and let it tell you which components deserve the close read. Read closely The parts of an opinion, on a real one Markowitz v. Arizona Parks Board , 146 Ariz. 352, 706 P.2d 364 (1985) (en banc). The state, the only defendant remaining, moved for summary judgment, primarily claiming that it had breached no duty owed to David. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the state and the court of appeals affirmed, one judge concurring specially and the other judge dissenting. No signs prohibiting diving or warnings of any kind were posted in the area or at the park entrances. David described the path leading to the diving spot on the cliff as “well worn.” […] David then dived from the same spot and hit his head on a shallow ledge or sandbar below the surface. The first question presented, therefore, is whether the state as a possessor of land is under any duty of care with respect to the safety of those it has invited to use the particular parcel of state land. [W]e cannot posit a rule of law that the state is relieved from all duty to those invited to use particular portions of public land, no matter what the hazard, simply because the state’s parks are large and their terrain often inhospitable. When the government invites citizens onto public land — and this opinion has no application to areas where the public is not invited — it is under a duty to take some precautions to avoid injury to those invited. The summary judgment granted by the trial court is reversed. The opinion of the court of appeals is vacated. The case is remanded for further proceedings.

p: Appendix B: How to Read a Case
t: Caption. The case name, court, date, and citation at the top of the opinion. It tells you who is suing whom, which court decided the case, and when. In appellate opinions, the first-named party is usually, though not always, the appellant (the party who lost below and is asking the higher court to reverse). The citation tells you where to find the opinion in a reporter. Procedural History. How the case got to the court writing the opinion. Was it appealed from a trial court? Is this a ruling on a motion to dismiss, a summary judgment decision, or an appeal after a full trial? The posture controls what standard the court applied and how broadly you can read the result. Facts. The events that gave rise to the lawsuit. Courts present facts selectively, including what is relevant to the legal question and leaving out the rest. Read them carefully, because they are the foundation for everything that follows. Issue(s). The legal question or questions the court has to decide. Sometimes the issue is stated outright (“The question before us is whether . . .”). Sometimes you have to infer it from the discussion. Identifying the issue is one of the most important reading skills you will build, and it is the court’s version of Step 1 of the Question Method. Holding(s). The court’s answer to the issue, and the part with precedential effect. When you record a case in your Research Log, the holding belongs at the center of your Findings entry. Reasoning. The court’s explanation of why it reached its holding. This is where the analytical work happens, and it is what you will use most often in your own writing. A holding gives you the rule; the reasoning shows you how the court applied it. Two cases can reach the same holding through different reasoning, and the reasoning is what tells you which case is more useful for your facts. Disposition. What the court actually orders: affirmed, reversed, remanded, vacated, or some combination. “Affirmed” means the lower court’s decision stands. “Reversed” means it is overturned. “Remanded” means the case goes back down for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. Two further distinctions that go deeper than reading mechanics, the difference between a holding and dictum, and how to read concurrences and dissents, are covered in Chapter 5 , Beyond the Basics.

p: Appendix B: How to Read a Case
s: How to Engage With the Source
t: Determine the weight before you invest the time. Start with the caption. The jurisdiction and court level tell you whether the case is mandatory or persuasive authority in your matter, which decides whether the opinion is worth a close read at all. Read with your research question as the lens. Research reading is strategic, not cover to cover. Use your current question as a filter. If your question is “What are the elements of a breach of fiduciary duty claim in Delaware?”, you are reading for the court’s statement of those elements. Note other useful passages, but do not chase them now; log them as next questions instead. Identify the dispositive facts. Dispositive facts are the ones the court actually relied on, the facts that, if changed, would change the outcome. This skill matters enormously for predicting how a precedent applies to your client. The question is not “is this case in the same area of law?” but “are the facts the court relied on close enough to my client’s facts to expect the same result?” Read the court’s analysis and watch for signal phrases like “critically,” “because,” “here,” “in this case,” and “unlike,” which mark the court telling you which facts mattered. Confirm the points you rely on are still good. Run the case through a citator (KeyCite or Shepard’s) before you rely on it, and read the citing opinions rather than trusting the flag alone. A negative flag may reflect a treatment that has nothing to do with your point. Treatment attaches to specific points of law, never to the opinion as a whole. Record and move on. In your Research Log, capture the citation, the holding, the dispositive facts, how the case answers your current question, and your next question. That last field is what keeps the cycle moving. [NextGen Bar Exam Note] Dispositive fact identification is a named competency in the NextGen Bar Exam’s Foundational Skills Group C (see Chapter 16 ). Practicing it on every case you read builds the analytical habit the exam tests.

p: Appendix C: How to Read a Statute
s: Appendix C: How to Read a Statute
t: Reading statutory text is a different skill from reading case law. Opinions explain their reasoning; statutes do not. A statute tells you what the rule is without telling you why. It does not walk you through hypotheticals. It states the law in the most compressed, precise language the legislature could manage and leaves the interpretive work to the courts and to you. Every word carries weight. Every comma may matter. Every cross-reference pulls in another rule. The Question Method’s premise holds here with full force: a statute exists to answer the question what does the law require, and reading it well means interrogating the text with the sub-questions this appendix walks through, one defined term, exception, and cross-reference at a time. Read closely One definition, read word by word Arizona’s workers’ compensation definitions treat as a compensable injury an occupational disease that is due to causes and conditions characteristic of and peculiar to a particular trade, occupation, process or employment, and not the ordinary diseases to which the general public is exposed , and subject to section 23-901.01 or 23-901.09 or, for heart-related, perivascular or pulmonary cases, section 23-1105 .

p: Appendix C: How to Read a Statute
t: Section Number and Heading. Every section has a number (for example, 42 U.S.C. § 1983) and a descriptive heading. The heading gives you a general sense of the subject, but headings are sometimes added by codifiers rather than the legislature, and courts generally treat them as non-binding descriptions rather than operative text. Operative Text. The binding law: the substantive rule that creates rights, imposes obligations, prohibits conduct, or grants authority. Every word here matters. “ No employer ,” who counts as an employer? “ Shall discriminate ,” what counts as discrimination? “ Because of ,” what causal standard applies? Each of those is its own Question Method cycle. Definitions. Many statutes include a definitions section that controls how key terms are used throughout. A statutory definition overrides ordinary meaning, so always check whether a term you are reading is defined elsewhere in the act. Structural Provisions. Scope and applicability clauses, general rules, specific obligations, exceptions, enforcement and penalty provisions, and effective dates. Knowing where a provision sits in that structure tells you how it interacts with the rest. Give exception language particular respect: phrases like “except that,” “provided, however,” and “unless” carry as much weight as the rule itself, because a client whose conduct falls within an exception is not subject to the statute no matter how squarely the general rule seems to apply. Cross-References. Statutes refer to other sections constantly. Each cross-reference incorporates additional rules, so follow every one rather than reading a section in isolation. History and Credits. Found at the end of the statutory text or in the annotations, the history notes tell you when the section was enacted and how it has been amended over time. They also supply the Public Law number and Statutes at Large citation you will need if an ambiguity sends you into legislative history research (Chapter 10 ). Explore How a statutory chapter is usually built Scope and applicability. Does this chapter reach my client at all? Read it first. Many research questions end here. Definitions. What do the operative words mean in this chapter? A defined term controls every section that uses it, and it may differ from the same word in a neighboring chapter. General rule. What is required, prohibited, or permitted? The provision you came for. It is almost never the whole answer. Specific obligations. What exactly must be done, by whom, and when? The detail that turns the general rule into conduct. Exceptions. Is my client’s conduct carved out? Look for “notwithstanding,” “except,” and “unless.” An exception often sits several sections away from the rule it qualifies. Enforcement and penalties. Who can enforce this, and what follows from a violation? Whether a private person may sue is frequently its own research question. Effective date. Did this text govern on the date that matters? Sometimes found only in the session law.

p: Appendix C: How to Read a Statute
s: How to Engage With the Source
t: Read in context. A single subsection rarely tells the whole story. Read it alongside the definitions, the exceptions, and the cross-referenced provisions before you conclude what it requires. Anticipate how courts will read it using the canons of construction. When text is ambiguous, courts rely on established interpretive principles. Knowing the common ones helps you predict the reading a court is likely to adopt, and therefore which interpretation to build your analysis around. Plain Meaning Rule. If the text is unambiguous, courts apply it as written; legislative history and policy arguments do not override clear text. Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius. The expression of one thing implies the exclusion of others. If a statute lists specific items, courts may infer that unlisted items are excluded. Ejusdem Generis. When a general term follows a list of specific terms, the general term covers only things similar to the specific ones. “Cars, trucks, motorcycles, and other vehicles” probably does not include airplanes. Rule Against Surplusage. Every word should be given effect; courts avoid readings that make any word meaningless. In Pari Materia. Statutes on the same subject are read together and interpreted consistently. Rule of Lenity. Ambiguous criminal statutes are read in favor of the defendant. Sort it Which canon is doing the work? A statute exempts “hospitals, clinics, and nursing homes.” A court holds that a veterinary practice is not exempt. Expressio unius The legislature listed what it meant to exempt. Naming three implies the rest were left out. A statute covers “cars, trucks, motorcycles, and other vehicles.” A court holds that it does not reach a canoe. Ejusdem generis The catch-all is read to cover things of the same kind as the listed items: motorized road vehicles. A statute requires that notice be “written and delivered.” A court rejects the argument that mailing alone always suffices, because that would leave “delivered” with nothing to do. Surplusage Every word is presumed to do a job. A criminal statute can fairly be read to reach the defendant’s conduct or not to reach it. The court adopts the narrower reading. Lenity Ambiguity in a criminal statute is resolved in the defendant’s favor. A statute grants a remedy to “tenants, lodgers, or other occupants.” A court holds that a burglar is not an “occupant.” Ejusdem generis “Other occupants” takes its meaning from the lawful occupants listed before it. Spot ambiguity and turn it into your next question. Finding ambiguity is not a failure of your research; it is a core research skill. Common types include undefined terms, vague standards (“reasonable,” “substantial,” “undue,” “appropriate”), terms of art whose legal meaning differs from everyday meaning, structural ambiguity where the grammar allows more than one reading, and scope ambiguity about what falls inside or outside the statute. Each ambiguity becomes a distinct next question pointing to a distinct source. Confirm the law by going outside the text. When you hit an ambiguity, ask: Have courts in your jurisdiction interpreted this term? Does the legislative history address it (Chapter 10 )? Has the implementing agency issued guidance or regulations interpreting it (Chapters 7 and 13)? Each is a separate next question. Then make sure the statute is current; statutory text changes, so confirm you are reading the version in force for your matter. [NextGen Bar Exam Note] Ambiguity spotting is a named competency in the NextGen Bar Exam’s Foundational Skills Group C. See Chapter 16 .

p: Appendix D: How to Read a Regulation
s: Appendix D: How to Read a Regulation
t: If reading a statute calls for close attention to text, reading a regulation calls for even more. Regulations tend to be more detailed, more technical, and more intricately structured than statutes, because their job is to translate a statute’s broad mandate into specific, enforceable requirements. The same reading principles apply (read in context, check definitions, follow cross-references, look for exceptions), but regulations carry a few extra features that deserve their own attention. As with every source in this book, reading one is answering the questions the source exists to answer: what is required, of whom, on what authority, and since when. Keep your current question in the foreground and the extra apparatus becomes a checklist rather than clutter. Read closely The parts of a regulation, on a real one Part 36 — Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability by Public Accommodations and in Commercial Facilities Authority: 42 U.S.C. 12181–12189; 28 U.S.C. 509, 510. Source: 56 FR 35544, July 26, 1991, as amended at 75 FR 56236, Sept. 15, 2010. § 36.304 Removal of barriers. (a) General. A public accommodation shall remove architectural barriers in existing facilities, including communication barriers that are structural in nature, where such removal is readily achievable , i.e., easily accomplishable and able to be carried out without much difficulty or expense .

p: Appendix D: How to Read a Regulation
t: Part Heading. The general subject of the Part. Use it to navigate to related provisions. Authority Note. Cites the statute or statutes that authorize the regulations in that Part. This is your link back to the enabling legislation, and it is the starting point for any argument that a regulation exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency. Source Note. Cites the Federal Register issue where the regulation was first published or most recently amended. It is your pathway to the Federal Register preamble, where the agency explains what the regulation means. Definitions Section. Usually at the start of a Part or Subpart. Regulatory definitions control over ordinary meaning, so always check. Regulatory Text. The operative rules: what is required, prohibited, permitted, or conditioned. Cross-References. Regulations cross-reference other sections even more often than statutes do. Follow every one. Tables, Appendices, and Figures. These are part of the regulation and carry the force of law. Do not skip them, especially in environmental, workplace-safety, or financial regulation, where they often hold the specific numbers and thresholds that determine compliance.

p: Appendix D: How to Read a Regulation
s: How to Engage With the Source
t: Read in context, starting with the statute. Begin with the authority note, because the enabling statute sets the limits of what the agency can require. Then read the Federal Register preamble for the agency’s own explanation of the regulation’s meaning. Check for case law interpreting the regulation (via citators) and for agency guidance interpreting it (Chapter 11 covers this in depth). Taken together these sources give you a complete interpretive picture; any one alone is partial. Read the operative language precisely. “Shall” and “must” create mandatory obligations. “May” grants discretion. “Should” signals a recommendation. Courts enforce these distinctions, so they are worth slowing down for. Know whether you are reading a performance standard or a design standard. A performance standard specifies an outcome; a design standard specifies a method. Which one you are reading determines what your client has to do to comply: meet the outcome any way it likes, or follow the prescribed method exactly. Follow incorporations by reference. Regulations sometimes incorporate outside standards (ASTM, ANSI, ISO) by reference. The incorporated standard has the force of law even though its text never appears in the CFR, so “what does the incorporated standard require?” is a real research question, not a detail you can skip. Confirm currency before you rely on it. Regulations change frequently. Verify you are reading the current version using the eCFR, the List of CFR Sections Affected (LSA), the Federal Register, and a citator. Stopping at the CFR text without checking for recent amendments is one of the most common regulatory research errors. Explore A regulation is never read alone Authorizing statute | start here. Sets the mandate and the limit. If the regulation seems to reach further than the statute, that gap is itself a research question. Regulation | the operative text. What is required, of whom, in the agency’s words. Read with its Part’s definitions. Federal Register preamble | why. The agency’s explanation and its answers to comments. Persuasive evidence of meaning, found through the source note. Case law | how it has fared. Whether courts have upheld the rule and how they have applied it to facts. Agency guidance | how it is enforced. Manuals, FAQs, and letters. Influential, not binding (Chapter 11 ). Your analysis | the synthesis. The rule as it stands today, with each layer cited for what it is and weighted for what it is worth.

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
t: This appendix holds the model chains and answers for the single-source drills in Chapters 4 through 8. The scenarios live in their chapters; the walkthroughs live here, so you cannot read the answer by accident while you are supposed to be attempting it. Come here in two situations. If you are stuck, read just far enough to get unstuck, then go back and finish your own chain. If you are done, compare your chain to the model, one question at a time. Your questions will not match the model’s word for word, and they should not. What matters is whether each of your questions was earned by the answer before it. Where your chain diverged from the model’s, ask which version can point to the stated answer that produced its next question. Divergence can be a good sign. A question that arrived from nowhere is the thing to fix. A note on the answers. The answers here are scoped to their questions. Where the governing law is settled, they anchor to real authority; where a specific number, holding, or citation would go, you will see brackets. Confirm every anchored authority and fill every bracket against current primary law before you rely on any of this. The citations illustrate the method. They do not substitute for your own verification, and each walkthrough ends with a short reminder of what to check.

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
s: The Chapter 4 Drill: Where Do I Even Start?
t: Check your chain against this walkthrough one question at a time. Why this is a secondary-source-only exercise. This is the one source type that earns a single-source drill honestly, because mapping an unfamiliar landscape is what secondary sources are for. You begin with no legal vocabulary at all, and the whole task is to acquire it, see the structure of the area, and collect the citations a later researcher will follow. The drill ends at the boundary the method draws between secondary and primary authority: the moment your next question can only be answered by a case or a statute, you have reached the edge of this exercise. Where the researcher’s knowledge starts. No vocabulary. She knows the words “fired” and “social media” and nothing else legal. So the first move is acquisition: a plain-language search whose only job is to surface the terms of art. After that, the questions run exploratory, then foundational, then survey, all inside secondary sources. Q1. Can an employer fire someone for what they posted on social media? (Definitional / orientation, general search) Answer: A plain-language search surfaces the governing default and its name: most U.S. employment is “at-will,” meaning either side may end the relationship for almost any reason, including something the employee posted, unless an exception applies. The search also signals that exceptions and “protected activity” exist. The student now has the term “at-will” and can query a legal encyclopedia. The next question asks what that doctrine actually holds. Q2. What is the at-will employment doctrine? (Exploratory, no-clue: legal encyclopedia) Answer: An encyclopedia entry confirms at-will as the default and lists the commonly recognized exceptions at a high level: a public-policy exception, an implied-contract exception, and in some states an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. It also flags that separate bodies of law protect certain employee activity regardless of at-will status, and it cites primary authority for each. The question was broad, so a landscape answer fits, and the student records the whole landscape. Several threads now appear; the next move is to get the structure of the most promising one. Q3. What does the public-policy exception to at-will employment require? (Foundational exploratory: treatise) Answer: A treatise lays out the structure: the discharge must violate a clear public policy, often one rooted in a statute or a constitutional provision, and jurisdictions sort the qualifying situations into categories such as refusing to commit an illegal act, exercising a statutory right, or reporting wrongdoing. It cites the leading cases. The student now has the doctrinal structure but not whether this state recognizes it. That is a survey question. The treatise also confirmed the encyclopedia’s hint that a separate law may protect certain activity regardless of at-will, which becomes a sibling thread. *Relevance discovered: Only now do two facts matter. The post concerned unpaid overtime, a wage right, which maps onto the public-policy exception. And the post criticized a manager about pay, which maps onto the separate “protected activity” thread. Note these facts now, because the law just revealed they bear on the rule.* Q4. How does this state treat the public-policy exception? (Survey: ALR annotation, 50-state survey, or state encyclopedia) Answer: A survey tool shows where the state falls, whether it recognizes the exception at all and whether it reads it narrowly or broadly, and it collects the in-state cases. If the state recognizes the exception, the next question, whether this firing fits, is an application question answerable only by the primary cases. Record the citations and stop the thread here; that work belongs to Chapter 5 . Q5. Is there a separate law that protects employees who complain together about wages or working conditions? (Foundational / definitional, sibling: labor-law secondary source) Answer: A labor-law seco

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
s: The Chapter 5 Drill: Did the Store Owe a Duty?
t: Check your chain against this walkthrough one question at a time. Why this is a case-law-only exercise. The existence and scope of a common-law duty of care is built by courts, decision by decision, not set out in a statute or a regulation. So a duty question like this one is a pure case-law exercise. The attorney has supplied the vocabulary you would otherwise get from a secondary source, the claim is negligence and the contested element is duty, which lets you drill the case-law moves in isolation: find the leading decision, read it for the rule, then test the client’s facts against analogous cases. Where the researcher’s knowledge starts. Firm grip on the entry point. You have the framing and the terms duty and negligence. So you start with a focusing question rather than an exploratory one. Q1. Under our state’s law, does a business owe its customers a duty to protect them from the criminal acts of third parties on its premises? (Focusing) Answer: Locating the leading state appellate decision (through headnotes, a topic-and-key-number search, and a citator) reveals the general rule and its exception: ordinarily there is no duty to protect another from a third party’s criminal conduct, but courts recognize an exception when a special relationship exists, such as business and customer, and the harm was foreseeable. [Confirm the state’s exact formulation in the leading case.] The duty turns on two requirements the answer just surfaced: a special relationship and foreseeability. The business-customer relationship appears to satisfy the first, so foreseeability is the live question. Deepen into it. Q2. What makes a third party’s criminal act foreseeable enough to create this duty? (Focusing, deeper) Answer: Case law reveals that courts measure foreseeability through one of several recognized approaches, and that states differ: a specific-harm rule, a prior-similar-incidents test, a totality-of-the-circumstances test, and a balancing approach. The student identifies which one the state’s leading case adopts. [Confirm which test governs.] *Relevance discovered: Suppose the state follows the prior-similar-incidents test. Then whether earlier crimes occurred at or near this store, and how similar, how recent, and how numerous they were, suddenly matters, facts you had no reason to gather until the test revealed them. Had the state used the totality test instead, a broader set of facts would matter: neighborhood crime, lighting, the nature of the business. Note the facts the chosen test makes relevant.* Q3. Under that test, were there enough similar prior crimes at this location to make the assault foreseeable? (Application, fact-finding) Answer: The student finds state decisions applying the test to comparable facts and compares them to the client’s facts, identifying which facts the courts treated as dispositive: the number, proximity, recency, and similarity of any prior incidents. If the analogous cases line up one way, the duty question resolves. If they split or are distinguishable, deepen into the closest analog. Q4. How have courts treated stores with this client’s specific fact pattern, for example a single, unrelated prior theft in a low-crime area? (Application, fact-finding, deeper) Answer: The student locates the most factually analogous decisions, pins down which facts each court treated as outcome-determinative, and distinguishes the cases that cut the other way. *Precision trap: A search will surface cases on an employer’s duty to its employees, or a landlord’s duty to tenants. Those involve a different special relationship and a different line of authority. The precise question, a business owner’s duty to a customer, lets you set them aside rather than chase them.* Closure. Analytical. The case law establishes the general no-duty rule, the special-relationship exception, the foreseeability test the state follows, and how analogous cases apply it to the client’s facts. Every question is answered or identified as genu

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
s: The Chapter 6 Drill: Can the Podcaster Record the Call?
t: Check your chain against this walkthrough one question at a time. Why this is a statutes-only exercise. The client’s core question, whether recording without notice is lawful, is answered by the text of a single statutory scheme. The attorney has pointed you to it, so you can drill the statutory-reading moves in isolation: read the operative prohibition precisely, check the definitions section that controls its key term, scan for exceptions, find the penalty provision, and spot the one ambiguity that would send a later researcher outside the text. Where the researcher’s knowledge starts. Firm grip on the entry point. You are pointed to the statute, even if you do not yet know the phrase “all-party consent.” The statute’s own definitions will supply the vocabulary, so you start with a focusing question. Q1. Under California law, may a person record a phone conversation without the other party’s consent? (Focusing) Answer: Locating the provision in the annotated Penal Code (from the attorney’s pointer, or through the code’s finding aids) reveals California’s all-party-consent rule: Penal Code section 632 prohibits intentionally recording a “confidential communication” without the consent of all parties to it. [Read section 632 for the exact prohibition and its mental-state requirement.] The prohibition turns on a defined term, “confidential communication,” and on “consent.” Check the definitions before going further. Q2. What counts as a confidential communication under the statute? (Definitional, statute’s definitions section) Answer: Scanning the chapter’s section headings turns up the definitions within the same chapter, and they resolve the term: research reveals it turns on whether a party had an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation was not being overheard or recorded, which excludes conversations held where the parties could reasonably expect to be overheard. [Confirm the statutory definition’s exact wording.] Two things follow. Whether this call is confidential is now the crux, and it depends on the source’s reasonable expectation, a fact that becomes relevant here. And the phrase reasonable expectation is a standard the text does not fully resolve, which is an ambiguity to flag. *Relevance discovered: The call is a one-on-one phone interview, a private exchange, which bears directly on whether the source reasonably expected it not to be recorded. Note this fact now, because the definition is what made it matter.* Q3. Does the statute contain any exception that covers recording for journalism, or recording one’s own conversation? (Focusing, sibling: read in context for exceptions) Answer: Reading the surrounding provisions reveals the structure of exceptions, such as carve-outs allowing a party to record in order to gather evidence of certain crimes. Research reveals whether any listed exception covers routine journalistic recording; generally there is no blanket journalism exception. [Read the exception provisions and confirm none fits these facts.] If no exception applies, the all-party-consent rule controls, and the only remaining uncertainty is the confidential-communication standard. Q4. Does the statute set a penalty for a violation? (Focusing, sibling: enforcement and penalty provision) Answer: The penalty provision in the same chapter specifies the consequences of a violation, which research reveals includes the nature of the liability the client would face. [Read the penalty provision for the exact consequence.] *Ambiguity, and where it points: Whether a particular phone interview is a confidential communication, that is, whether the source had a reasonable expectation against recording, is a standard the text does not fully resolve. Under this chapter’s discipline, that ambiguity becomes the next question, and it points outside the statute: how have California courts interpreted confidential communication on facts like these? That is a focusing question for case law and possibly agency guidan

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
s: The Chapter 7 Drill: Does the Roofer Need Fall Protection?
t: Check your chain against this walkthrough one question at a time. Why this is a regulations-only exercise. The operative requirement here lives in the Code of Federal Regulations. The enabling statute sets the agency’s authority, but the height triggers, the accepted systems, and the technical specifications are in the regulation. So this is a regulation-only drill, and you practice reading a CFR section in full: the authority note that links it to its statute, the definitions section that controls its terms, the operative shall and must, the exceptions and thresholds, any incorporation of an outside standard, and the currency check the chapter stresses above all others. Where the researcher’s knowledge starts. Firm grip on the entry point. You are pointed to the OSHA construction regulations, though you may not yet know the specific part. Locating it is the first move, so you start with a focusing question. Notice, too, that the client’s ask bundles three questions, whether protection is required, at what height, and what counts as acceptable, and the method takes them one at a time, starting with the trigger. Q1. At what height do OSHA’s construction regulations require an employer to provide fall protection? (Focusing) Answer: Browsing the CFR’s structure, Title 29, then the construction standards at Part 1926, then the part’s table of contents, reveals that fall protection sits in Subpart M, with the duty provision at section 1926.501: employers must provide fall protection for employees working at heights of six feet or more above a lower level. [Read section 1926.501 for the exact trigger and the surfaces it covers.] At twenty feet the requirement is plainly triggered. The next questions are what counts as acceptable protection, and whether any exception changes the picture. Deepen, then check siblings. Q2. What forms of fall protection does the regulation accept? (Focusing, deeper) Answer: The criteria-and-practices provision, section 1926.502, specifies the accepted systems, among them guardrail systems, safety net systems, and personal fall arrest systems, each with detailed performance criteria. [Read section 1926.502 for the systems and their specifications.] Which system the client must or may use can depend on the type of roof and on feasibility, so check whether the regulation defines those terms. Q3. How does the regulation define the roof and surface categories that determine which system applies? (Definitional, regulation’s definitions section) Answer: The Subpart’s definitions section, section 1926.500(b), defines the operative terms, such as low-slope roof, steep roof, unprotected sides and edges, and lower level. Regulatory definitions control over ordinary meaning, so read them rather than assuming. [Read the definitions.] *Relevance discovered: The slope and edge configuration of this particular roof determine which systems are required or merely allowed. You now need the roof’s slope, low-slope or steep, a fact you had no reason to gather until the definitions revealed it controls the answer.* Q4. Does the regulation provide any exception or alternative for residential construction? (Focusing, sibling: exceptions and alternative provisions) Answer: Research reveals whether the regulation allows an alternative for residential work when conventional systems are infeasible, for example a written, site-specific fall-protection plan under a provision such as section 1926.502(k), and the conditions for using it. [Read the residential and alternative provisions and their conditions.] If an alternative applies, it carries its own requirements, a written plan and a showing of infeasibility. If not, the standard systems govern. Q5. What statute authorizes these regulations? (Focusing: authority note) Answer: The authority note for Part 1926 cites the enabling statute, the Occupational Safety and Health Act, which confirms the regulation’s basis and its outer limits. [Check the authority note.] A regulation confirm

p: Appendix E: Practice Drill Walkthroughs
s: The Chapter 8 Capstone: The Drone Question
t: This is the model for the capstone. Check your chain against it one question at a time, and pay particular attention to the moments where the model switches source types: those switches are the skill. Why this is the capstone. The single-source drills walled off one source at a time. This one tears the walls down. A real question like commercial drone photography is governed by an overlapping set of authorities, a federal statute, federal regulations, agency guidance, and a residual overlay of state law, and the skill this chapter teaches is moving fluidly among them while keeping a single question in view. Watch how each answer hands you a question pointed at a different source. That is the orientation step, restored. Where the researcher’s knowledge starts. No grip on the area, though you have the plain words drone and commercial. So you start in a secondary source, exploratory, to orient and acquire the vocabulary, exactly the step the single-source drills handed you for free. Q1. What law governs flying a drone for commercial purposes? (Exploratory, no-clue: secondary source) Answer: Orientation surfaces the landscape and the terms of art: commercial small-drone operation is regulated mainly by the Federal Aviation Administration under federal aviation law; the operative federal rules are known as Part 107; an operator generally needs a remote pilot certificate; and a separate overlay of state and local law addresses privacy and trespass. The source cites the governing statute and regulations. The landscape names three threads: the federal statute that grants FAA authority, the Part 107 regulations, and the state-law overlay. Start at the source of federal authority and work toward the statute, then the regulation. Q2. What federal statute gives the FAA authority over commercial drones? (Focusing: statute) Answer: Statutory research reveals that Congress gave the FAA authority over the national airspace and, through the FAA reauthorization legislation addressing unmanned aircraft systems, directed the agency to integrate small drones into that airspace. This establishes the FAA’s authority and the framework its regulations operate within. [Confirm the specific authorizing provisions.] This confirms that the FAA may regulate and that the operative requirements live in its regulations. Move to the regulation. Q3. Under the FAA’s regulations, what must a commercial drone operator actually do? (Focusing: regulation) Answer: The small-drone rules at 14 C.F.R. Part 107 set out the operative requirements: the operator must hold a remote pilot certificate, register the aircraft, and follow operational limits, for example restrictions on flying over people, beyond visual line of sight, at night, and in controlled airspace without authorization. [Read Part 107 for certification, registration, and operational limits, and check the definitions.] *Relevance discovered: Whether the client will fly over people, near airports in controlled airspace, or at night now matters, because the regulation conditions its requirements on exactly those facts. Gather them.* Q4. Does the client’s planned operation fall within Part 107’s limits, or does it need a waiver or authorization? (Application: regulation and agency guidance) Answer: Reading Part 107 together with FAA guidance reveals how the operational limits apply and the process for authorization or a waiver, for example airspace authorization to operate in controlled airspace. A currency check matters here, because the drone rules have evolved, including Remote ID requirements and rules on operations over people, so confirm the current version through the eCFR and FAA guidance. [Apply the limits to the client’s facts and confirm currency.] The federal-compliance picture resolves. The remaining thread is the state-law exposure, a lateral move to a different body of law. Q5. What state or local law exposes the client to liability for photographing private property from the air? (Exploratory an

p: Appendix F: The Chapter 3 Demonstration in Full: Research Log, Annotated Outline, and Case Chart
t: Macro question (written once, at the top): Can the principal remove articles he does not like from the school-run student newspaper without violating the First Amendment? Field Entry 1. Research Question How has First Amendment free speech protection been applied to students in school environments? Question Type Exploratory (No-Clue) Method Searched the secondary sources in my database for “free speech” and students and schools; opened the encyclopedia entry. Findings Tinker starts the student free speech case law: rights survive the schoolhouse gate, and restriction requires material and substantial disruption. Later cases set context-specific standards: Fraser permits schools to bar lewd speech inconsistent with the basic educational mission, and Hazelwood governs school-sponsored publications like a curricular newspaper, tying regulation to “legitimate pedagogical concerns.” Answers the question fully, for orientation. It also identifies which branch of the doctrine governs our facts. Source Consulted Legal encyclopedia entry, “Students, Constitutional Rights” [Encyclopedia entry citation, with currency date] Next Question What are the bounds of student free speech rights in school? Notes Tinker is foundational. Our paper is produced in a journalism class, so the school-sponsored branch ( Hazelwood ) is the thread to pull, but Hazelwood seems to build on Fraser , so Fraser gets a read after Tinker . The entry used “legitimate pedagogical concerns” without defining it; parked as a future definitional question. Field Entry 2. Research Question What are the bounds of student free speech rights in school? Question Type Focusing Method Lead from the map: read the Tinker opinion the encyclopedia entry pointed to. Findings Students do not shed their free speech rights at the schoolhouse gate. A school may restrict student expression only on a showing that it would materially and substantially interfere with the operation of the school or collide with the rights of others; an undifferentiated fear of disturbance is not enough. Answers the question fully, for the baseline. Tinker involved students’ own expression (armbands), not anything the school published or sponsored. Source Consulted Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District , 393 U.S. 503 (1969) Next Question How do courts balance a student’s free speech rights against the school’s basic educational mission? Notes Personal-expression branch; our facts sit on the school-sponsored branch. Tinker applies student rights “in light of the special characteristics of the school environment,” which is the balance the mapped Fraser question asks about. Field Entry 3. Research Question How do courts balance a student’s free speech rights against the school’s basic educational mission? Question Type Focusing Method Lead from the map: read the Fraser opinion. Findings The constitutional rights of students in public school are not automatically coextensive with the rights of adults in other settings. A school may discipline lewd, indecent, or vulgar speech (there, a sexually suggestive assembly speech) without a Tinker disruption showing, because a school may insist that speech be consistent with its basic educational mission. Answers the question fully. A short cycle, logged anyway. Source Consulted Bethel School District No. 403 v. Fraser , 478 U.S. 675 (1986) Next Question What free speech protection applies to a school-sponsored student publication? Notes The unnumbered Hazelwood entry now takes number 4. Field Entry 4. Research Question What free speech protection applies to a school-sponsored student publication? Question Type Focusing Method Lead from the map: read the Hazelwood opinion. Findings A curricular student newspaper is not a public forum unless school officials have opened it, by policy or by practice, for indiscriminate use by the general public or some segment of it. Absent that, educators may exercise editorial control over the style and content of stud

p: Appendix F: The Chapter 3 Demonstration in Full: Research Log, Annotated Outline, and Case Chart
t: Macro question: Can the principal remove articles he does not like from the school-run student newspaper without violating the First Amendment? Students retain free speech rights at school; restriction requires a showing of material and substantial disruption or collision with the rights of others. Tinker (1969). Student rights are not coextensive with adults’ rights; a school may bar lewd or vulgar speech inconsistent with its basic educational mission. Fraser (1986). Educators may regulate the style and content of school-sponsored student expression when the regulation is reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns; a curricular paper is not a public forum unless opened by policy or practice. Hazelwood (1988). A publication is considered “school-sponsored” if it is one the public might reasonably perceive to bear the school’s imprimatur: faculty-supervised, curricular, designed to teach. Hazelwood . [Our facts: produced in a journalism class, supervised by a faculty advisor, published under the school’s name. Element met; no contrary facts in the file.] Illustrative categories of a “legitimate pedagogical concern” include: learning the lesson, maturity-appropriate material, non-attribution of views to the school; a school may refuse to sponsor ungrammatical, poorly written, inadequately researched, biased, vulgar, or unsuitable speech. Hazelwood . [Our facts: removal of articles the principal did not like, containing no profanity, threats, or illegality. The stated reasons map onto no recognized category.] When is a school publication a public forum “by policy or by practice”? Nonpublic unless opened for indiscriminate use by the public or a segment of it; courts examine written policy and actual practice. Hazelwood ; Dean . [Our facts, from the client call: content decisions made by the advisor and administration; no outside contributions accepted. The paper looks like a nonpublic forum. Contested point: expect the other side to argue a Dean -style limited public forum from practice.] Outer limits: the standard does not authorize viewpoint-based censorship or restrictions unconnected to any educational purpose. Dean (E.D. Mich. 2004). [Slot: second on-point case at cite check. Dean is persuasive authority; confirm treatment.] Have courts recognized a legitimate pedagogical concern for removing articles about cultural topics? [Open. Run the targeted search from Log entry 9.]

p: Appendix G: The Worked Examples in Full
t: The scenario. Dana has been the licensed foster parent of nine-year-old M. for the past three years. M. has lived in Dana’s home that entire time, and Dana is the only mother M. has known across those years. One afternoon, as the two walk to the corner store, a driver runs a red light and strikes and kills M. in front of Dana. Dana is not physically hurt, but the experience leaves her with severe, lasting emotional trauma. She wants to know whether she can recover from the driver. The jurisdiction is California. Where the researcher’s knowledge actually is. Our researcher has heard that a person who witnesses a terrible accident can sometimes sue for the emotional harm, and has run across the phrase negligent infliction of emotional distress. That is the whole of it. She does not yet know the elements of the claim, she does not know there is a special rule about the witness’s relationship to the victim, and, this matters, she does not yet know that Dana’s status as a foster parent is the fact the whole case will turn on. She knows it as background, the way she knows M.’s age. Whether it is legally relevant is something the research has to tell her. We start, then, not by cataloguing facts, but by writing the first question we can actually write. Question 1 (Exploratory, orienting). If you witness a negligent accident that injures someone else, can you sue for your own emotional distress? Answer, scoped to the question. Yes. A secondary source on tort claims for emotional distress, an encyclopedia entry or a California practice guide, supplies the orientation: in California a person who suffers no physical injury can sometimes recover for the emotional distress of witnessing injury to another, under what the courts call a bystander theory of negligent infliction of emotional distress. (Notice the discipline: the question asked only whether such a claim is possible. The answer says yes, sometimes, and hands us the name. It does not yet list what the claim requires; that is the next question’s job, not this one’s.) The claim exists and now has a name. A claim that succeeds only “sometimes” is a claim with requirements. The next question asks what they are. Question 2 (Focusing). What must a bystander prove to recover for NIED in California? Answer, scoped to the question. The secondary source’s citations point to the leading case, and you cross from secondary to primary authority to read it. Under Thing v. La Chusa (1989) 48 Cal.3d 644, the plaintiff must show three things: (1) that she is closely related to the injury victim; (2) that she was present at the scene of the injury-producing event when it occurred and was then aware that it was injuring the victim; and (3) that she suffered serious emotional distress beyond what a disinterested witness would feel. Three requirements, each a potential question of its own. Two are not in real doubt on these facts: Dana watched the collision happen (requirement 2), and a foster mother who sees her child killed plainly suffers distress beyond a stranger’s (requirement 3). The genuinely contested requirement is the first, whether a foster parent is “closely related” to her foster child. And here is the moment a fact becomes relevant: Dana’s foster status, a piece of background a moment ago, is now the pivot of the case, because the first requirement is the one that asks about it. This is the method’s central claim in miniature: we did not list “Dana is a foster parent, not a biological parent” as a relevant fact at the outset. It became relevant the instant the research surfaced a requirement that turns on it. Question 3 (Focusing / Definitional). What relationship counts as “closely related to the injury victim”? Answer, scoped to the question. Thing itself draws the line. Absent exceptional circumstances, it limits recovery to relatives residing in the same household, or to the victim’s parents, siblings, children, and grandparents, and it describes the qualifying relationships as those

s: Borrowed Statutes and the Neighbor’s Answer (Chapter 5)
t: Sometimes your jurisdiction has no law on the precise question, but a neighboring state does, and the two states are not strangers. Your state borrowed the governing statute from that neighbor, the frameworks run in parallel, and your courts have a habit of reading the borrowed provisions the way the neighbor’s courts read them. When that is the situation, the neighbor’s resolution carries far more weight than an ordinary out-of-state opinion. It is unusually strong predictive authority, for a reason with a name: under the prior-construction (or “adopted-statute”) canon, a legislature that adopts a statute from another jurisdiction is presumed to take it with the construction the source jurisdiction’s courts had already placed on it. The researcher’s job is to recognize the silence, find the neighbor, and then weigh, carefully, how much that neighbor’s answer is really worth. The scenario. A client in Nevada has been sued for defamation over things they posted in a closed, invitation-only online forum, a private professional listserv with a few dozen members. The client wants to file an anti-SLAPP special motion to dismiss, arguing the posts were protected speech on a matter of public concern. The threshold question is whether posts in a small, closed forum like this one count as protected activity under Nevada’s anti-SLAPP statute. Where the researcher’s knowledge is. The researcher knows the client wants to use Nevada’s anti-SLAPP statute and has a rough sense that such statutes give defendants an early way out of speech-based suits. That is the starting point. The researcher does not yet know the statute’s structure, does not yet know that Nevada modeled the statute on California’s, and, importantly, has no reason yet to care about California at all. Whether California matters is something the research will reveal, and only once Nevada turns up empty. Question 1 (Focusing). What must a defendant show to prevail on a Nevada anti-SLAPP special motion to dismiss? Answer, scoped to the question. Nevada’s anti-SLAPP statute (NRS 41.635-41.670) sets up a two-step special motion. First, the defendant must show the claim is based on a protected “good faith communication in furtherance of the right to petition or the right to free speech in direct connection with an issue of public concern.” If the defendant carries that burden, the second step shifts to the plaintiff to show a probability of prevailing on the claim. The motion turns first on whether the client’s posts are protected. The relevant protected category here is speech on a matter of public concern made in a public forum. So the next question is whether posts in this particular forum qualify, and here the facts about where and to whom the client spoke start to matter. Question 2 (Focusing / Application, deeper). Does Nevada treat statements made in a small, closed, invitation-only online forum as protected speech “in direct connection with an issue of public concern” in a “public forum”? Answer, scoped to the question. Neither the statute nor any Nevada appellate decision addresses this specific kind of forum. Nevada’s courts have resolved some forum questions at the other end of the spectrum, a message broadcast to a roughly 50,000-person listserv, posts on a public neighborhood app, but not a small, closed group. On this precise application, Nevada law is silent: it is a question of first impression here. When the home jurisdiction has not spoken, the next question is whose reading of this kind of provision a Nevada court would be most likely to follow. Note what just happened: until Nevada turned up empty, there was no reason to look anywhere else. The silence is what makes the next question worth asking. Question 3 (Focusing, choosing the persuasive authority). Whose construction of this kind of provision would a Nevada court find most persuasive? Answer, scoped to the question. Two findings. First, California has a large, developed body of law on what counts as a “pu

p: Appendix G: The Worked Examples in Full
t: Research Question: Must a business make its website accessible to persons with disabilities under the ADA? Step 1, Secondary Source (Orientation). Begin with Am. Jur. 2d or a disability law treatise. The secondary source identifies 42 U.S.C. § 12182 (Title III, public accommodations) as the key statutory provision and notes that courts are divided on whether websites count as “public accommodations.” Next question: does Title III apply to websites? Step 2, Statute (Primary Framework). Read 42 U.S.C. § 12182. The text does not mention websites, because it was enacted in 1990. The annotations show many cases divided between circuits. Next question: what do the DOJ’s regulations say? Step 3, Regulation (Implementing Rules). Review 28 C.F.R. Part 36 (DOJ’s ADA Title III regulations). No specific web-accessibility regulation exists, though the DOJ has issued guidance documents and proposed regulations. That surfaces two questions, logged and taken one at a time: what does the DOJ’s guidance say? And, after it, what weight do courts give it? Step 4, Case Law (Judicial Interpretation). Find a leading circuit decision on ADA website accessibility. Use headnotes and key numbers for “Public Accommodations, Disability, Website” to locate additional cases. Check the citator for pending Supreme Court consideration. Note the circuit split. Step 5, Synthesize. Your annotated outline now holds the statutory framework, the current regulatory gap, the agency guidance and its weight, and the state of the case law including the circuit split. You can now write an accurate, complete analysis of a genuinely contested question. Notice that each step’s “next question” pointed to a different source type. That is multi-source research working as designed.

s: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: How to use this appendix. Attempt the exercise first, all the way to a finished deliverable, and only then come here. What follows are sample answers, not the only answers. Where an exercise depends on your jurisdiction, your project, or your search date, the sample models one honest instantiation and marks the variable parts in brackets, exactly as Appendix E does: brackets mean verify against current law before relying on this . Where sibling questions could run in any order, your order and the sample’s are equally correct. The test to apply is never “does my answer match the sample word for word.” It is the test each exercise’s self-check already gave you, and the sample exists to show you what a deliverable that passes it looks like on the page.

t: A passing map reaches both levels of government and at least three source types, and every row is traceable to something given: the scenario supplied the federal prohibition and the state authorization, and the chapter’s employment-dispute example supplied the template for the rest. Notice what the predictions do and do not claim: each says what the layer might contribute, because at this stage prediction is all the map entitles you to. Whether any layer actually controls is what the research will decide. Level Source type Predicted role Federal Statute The federal drug statute classifies marijuana as illegal regardless of state authorization; it may limit what protection any other layer can give. Federal or state Statute An anti-discrimination statute may exist at either level, as in the chapter’s employment-dispute example; whether one reaches a medical condition or its authorized treatment is a research question. Federal or state Regulation Where a statute at either level applies, an agency’s regulations may fill in its detail, as the chapter’s example paired agency rules with the statute they implement. State Statute The state medical marijuana statute authorized her use; whether it also protects employees from termination is a research question, since states differ. State Statute The state disability or anti-discrimination statute may treat the underlying condition, or the authorized treatment, as protected. State Case law The at-will employment doctrine is the common-law baseline; any protection has to displace it, and judge-made exceptions (such as a public-policy exception) may apply. A map that also flagged the state constitution is stronger still. A map with every row at one level or in one type fails the self-check, and so does a row invoking a doctrine neither the chapter nor the scenario gave you: at this stage, a prediction you cannot trace to the page is a guess wearing a prediction’s clothes.

t: The seven classifications, each tied to a stated rule. (a) Binding: the Arizona Supreme Court sits above the trial court in the same system, and the chapter’s own example says an Arizona trial court must follow it on state law. (b) Binding: the Court of Appeals is also a court above the trial court in the same system. (c) Persuasive: California’s decisions have no binding effect in Arizona; authority binds only when it comes from home. (d) Persuasive: a decision from a court at the same level does not bind, however sound its reasoning. (e) Persuasive: a judicial opinion binds only if it comes from a higher court in the same court system , and the federal district court sits in a different system; the chapter even notes the influence runs the other way on state-law questions. (f) Persuasive: a treatise is secondary authority, which explains the law but never binds. (g) Binding: the chapter states that all courts must comply with U.S. Supreme Court decisions interpreting the U.S. Constitution. The final sentence, from the chapter’s own list: a court is most likely to follow persuasive authority when the issue is new or unsettled at home, when the reasoning is particularly strong, or when the law is trending that way across the country. Every justification above invokes a rule the chapter stated and nothing else, which is the pass condition; no knowledge of Arizona negligence law was needed, and none was used.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
s: Exercise 1.3 — Who Gets the Last Word?
t: Rowan Companies. The Court read the statute; Congress disagreed with the reading and amended the statute; the amendment stands. Congress held the last word, because when the conflict is over what a statute means, the legislature can always answer a court by changing the text. Texas v. Johnson. The Court held the statute violated the First Amendment, and no ordinary statute could respond, because the conflict was between a statute and the Constitution. The Court held the last word; only a constitutional amendment could have answered it. The answer the two stories set up. The kind of conflict decides it, not the actors. When the conflict is over what a statute means, the legislature can always have the last word by amending the text; when the conflict is between a statute and the Constitution, the court’s word stands, because no ordinary statute can override the supreme law of its jurisdiction. The self-check’s trap is worth naming: the same two institutions, Court and Congress, appear in both stories, so any answer built on who was involved cannot explain why the outcomes differ. Only the kind of conflict can.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Three concepts hide in the dog-bite question: the animal, the injuring act, and the owner’s responsibility. A passing translation: concept one, dog OR canine OR “domestic animal” OR pet; concept two, bite OR bites OR bitten OR attack! OR maul!; concept three, owner OR keeper, paired with plain responsibility words: liable OR responsible OR fault OR damages. Joined: (dog OR canine OR pet) AND (bite OR bitten OR attack! OR maul!) AND (owner OR keeper) AND (liable OR responsible OR fault OR damages). And the root-expander trap, caught: bit! looks like a tidy way to gather bite, bites, and bitten, but it also drags in bitter, bitumen, and every other word sharing the root, so the passing answer lists the bite forms out by hand and reserves the expander for roots that survive the drag-in test, like attack! and maul!. All of these are everyday words, and that is the point: this chapter’s skill is translation from plain language, and the terms of art courts actually use will arrive with Chapter 4 ’s vocabulary work. A set built honestly from what you know today passes.

Kuhlmeier , 484 U.S. 260 (1988): case name; 484 is the volume; U.S. is the reporter (United States Reports, which itself tells you the court); 260 is the first page; 1988 is the decision year. 42 U.S.C. § 12101: 42 is the title; U.S.C. is the code (United States Code); 12101 is the section. 29 C.F.R. § 1605.1: 29 is the title; C.F.R. is the code (Code of Federal Regulations); 1605 is the part and .1 the section within it. t: Definitional: it asks what a term of art means. (b) Exploratory: it asks for the shape of an area, not a specific rule. (c) Focusing: it asks for the governing standard on a specific point. (d) Focusing, one level deeper: it narrows a broader rule (the necessity requirement) to a sub-rule. (e) Application: it asks how a rule operates on specific facts by comparison to decided cases. (f) Exploratory, survey flavor: it asks how jurisdictions divide, which points at survey sources. (g) The intruder: not a research question at all. It is a factual, investigative question; no source of law will ever answer it, only evidence will, thermostat records or witness testimony. (h) Exploratory: it asks about a statute’s purpose, and if the text proves ambiguous it may eventually justify legislative history research, but as drafted it is a landscape question. If all eight received a question type, the distinction between what you research and what you investigate needs another pass, because keeping those separate is what stops a research log from filling up with questions no database can close.

t: Answers vary with the assigned paragraph, so here is the standard modeled on a paragraph summarizing the core reasoning of Hazelwood (sentences paraphrased): Sentence: the newspaper was produced in a journalism class as part of the curriculum, under a faculty advisor. Question it answers: is this newspaper school-sponsored? (Application). Sentence: the school had never, by policy or practice, opened the paper to indiscriminate student use. Question: was the paper a public forum? (Focusing, then Application). Sentence: educators may exercise control over school-sponsored expression when their actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns. Question: what standard governs a school’s control over school-sponsored student expression? (Focusing). Sentence: the principal’s concerns involved protecting the privacy of students discussed in the articles. Question: do the stated reasons fit a legitimate pedagogical concern? (Application). The pass test: read the four questions alone, in order. They chain, each one askable because of the answer before it. If your questions read as a disconnected list, some of them answered the paragraph’s topic rather than its sentences, and the fix is to go one sentence at a time. One more thing worth noticing: the application questions in this chain are the ones the court answered in writing , applying the rule to the parties before it. In your own project those questions live in the outline’s bracketed notes, as Chapter 3 ’s demonstration shows, which is why you meet them here in a finished opinion rather than in a Research Log.

s: Exercise 4.1 — Match the Source to the Question
t: Researcher one gets a legal encyclopedia: plain-language orientation and vocabulary for a no-clue start is exactly what encyclopedias are built for. Researcher two gets a treatise: full doctrinal structure with the leading authorities organized is the treatise’s job description. Researcher three gets an ALR annotation or a fifty-state survey: a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction count on a narrow rule is survey work. Researcher four gets law review articles and working papers: the newest scholarly thinking on unsettled questions lives there, months or years before any treatise catches up. Four researchers, four different sources; if two of yours matched, the mismatched one was almost certainly researcher one or two, and the difference to internalize is orientation versus structure.

t: The annotated outline entry, scoped: under Hazelwood , a school may exercise editorial control over the style and content of student speech in school-sponsored expressive activities so long as its actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns. 484 U.S. 260 (1988). That is the question’s answer and nothing else. The collateral list, with pathways: (1) When is student expression “school-sponsored” rather than personal? — Hazelwood itself, and the personal-expression line it distinguishes, Tinker v. Des Moines , 393 U.S. 503 (1969). (2) When has a school opened a paper as a public forum, and what changes if it has? — the forum cases Hazelwood collects [record the citations from your reading]. (3) What counts as a “legitimate pedagogical concern” at the edges? — the applications discussed in the opinion, and the school-speech cases decided alongside it, including Bethel Sch. Dist. v. Fraser , 478 U.S. 675 (1986) [confirm]. Three or more collateral questions logged, none synthesized: the pathways are recorded for later cycles, which is the fourth move doing its job. An outline entry that instead summarized the whole opinion read the case; the exercise was reading for the answer.

t: Three facts survive the test, each with its sentence. The curricular production: if instead the paper had been an independent student publication rather than a journalism-class product, then the personal-expression standard rather than the school-sponsored standard would govern, because the Court’s reasoning turns on the school lending its name and resources to the expression. The forum history: if instead the school had by policy or practice opened the paper to indiscriminate student use, then the school’s editorial control would face a stricter test, because the Court’s deference rests on the paper never having become a public forum. The stated concerns: if instead the principal’s reasons had no connection to pedagogy, bare disagreement with a viewpoint, then the action would fail even the deferential standard, because the standard’s own terms require the pedagogical link. Facts like the paper’s name or the articles’ exact subjects fail the test: change them and the reasoning holds, which is what background means. Every passing sentence points at a specific passage of reasoning; a sentence that works without one was a guess, and the exercise exists to replace guessing with locating.

The two sentences: The statute decided that a national organic certification program would exist, that products sold as organic must be certified to national standards, and that USDA would run the program. The regulation supplies what the statute left open: the operative definitions, the production and handling standards, the certification machinery, and the labeling thresholds that turn the statute’s framework into rules a farmer can follow. Part 205, located through the eCFR, which supplies the definitions, standards, and labeling rules; case-law corner, [a decision interpreting either, located through an annotated code or a citator]. The edges, which are the exercise: statute to regulation, “what detail did the agency supply under this delegation, and where?”, the question that sent you from the authority note into the CFR; regulation to case law, “how have courts read and applied this standard?”, the question an annotation answers, and “has it survived challenge?”, the one a citator answers; case law back to statute, “does the regulation stay within what the statute delegated?”, the question a challenge forces, and the one courts now answer without deferring to the agency’s own view of its statute. Three full corners with empty edges fails the self-check; the corners are a catalogue, and the edges are the research.

t: The form of a passing pair, content bracketed because it comes from your own drills. The unsettled finding: “The law is genuinely unsettled on [the point]: [the leading authorities] expressly reserve it, and [the survey source] confirms the jurisdictions divide. I searched [the databases], with [the term sets, including alternatives], through [date].” Its defense earns the professional conclusion by showing the search was thorough enough that a supervisor would accept it, and by pointing at authority that says the question is open rather than at silence. The unfound confession: “I have not yet found the answer to [the point]. I searched [one database] with [one term set]; I have not yet tried [the alternative terms or source types a full sweep would include].” Its defense is honest about the gap between what was searched and what a closure-grade sweep requires. The two labels cannot trade places, because the defenses are doing different work: one demonstrates exhaustion, the other admits its absence. If yours could swap, neither defense was specific enough yet.
