What makes it a Chapter 9 translation rather than a Chapter 2 translation is the proximity work: /p binds the animal, the act, and the owner into the same paragraph, so the results discuss them together instead of merely containing them somewhere in the same document. Three strings whose only connective tissue is AND fail the self-check; the upgrade was the point.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: The deliberately bad version: landlord AND staircase AND injury AND liable. The proper version: (landlord OR lessor OR “property owner”) /p (stair! OR step OR railing) /p (injur! OR fell OR fall!) AND (guest OR visitor OR invitee), jurisdiction and source type filtered. Both counts recorded [yours will vary by platform and date]. Two passing sentences, illustrative: [The bad string returned a far larger set whose first page scattered the four words across unrelated discussions, premises pages apart from injuries. The precision string returned a fraction of the volume, and its first page discussed the landlord, the staircase, and the injury in the same breath, which is what the proximity connectors purchased.] The generic “the good one was better” fails; the sentences must name the specific difference, and the fastest place to find it, as the self-check said, is result ten in each list.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing closure record, run on any finished exercise: the final sweep documented, with the alternative terms actually listed and their results noted, even when the note is “nothing new surfaced,” because that nothing is evidence; the citator step, every authority updated, statuses recorded; the check back against the original question, confirming every sub-question is either answered or named as genuinely open, with Chapter 8 ’s unsettled-versus-unfound distinction applied to any that remain; and the explicit finding, in a sentence: “Analytical closure reached: [the questions] are answered, [any named point] is genuinely open per [the authority that says so], and further research would only refine wording.” Or, where an external limit forced the stop, the practical-closure version, naming what remains. The single pass condition is the chapter’s own line. If you cannot document why you stopped, you have not closed. You have just stopped.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Both passing shapes, modeled. The ticket earned: “The statute is ambiguous as to [the term]: the text does not define it, the definitions section [cited] omits it, the interpreting cases [cited or ‘none located after the searches listed’] have not resolved it, and no regulation [checked where] supplies content. Documented: text read; definitions checked; case search [terms, database, date]; regulatory check [where].” The record stays closed: “The term is resolved by [the definitions section § __ / the controlling decision cited]; the legislative record stays closed, and the research proceeds in [that source].” The failing shape is the one the self-check named: a completed ambiguity sentence sitting on an empty documentation list. An undocumented ambiguity claim is just an unread statute, and courts committed to plain meaning will treat it as exactly that.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: For the ADA, the identifier set the sources yield: Public Law number, Pub. L. No. 101-336; Statutes at Large, 104 Stat. 327; enactment year, 1990; bill number, S. 933; Congress, the 101st. The compiled-history check: compiled legislative histories for the ADA exist in [the compiled-history sources this chapter listed; record which one you located and what it collects]. The chapter printed these answers, and the exercise was producing them from the credit line and Congress.gov rather than from the page; the step that cannot be skipped, even with everything else right, is the compiled-history check, because on a public law this significant, someone has already assembled the record, and building your own first is the most expensive way to learn that.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing ranking, with the ADA’s committee report as the anchor: (1) the committee report passage, H.R. Rep. No. 101-485, pt. [__], at [__] (1990), highest weight, because it is the drafting committee’s collective explanation and the document courts cite most; (2) the bill-version change, [described, with the versions compared], moderate weight, because deliberate language change is evidence of intent even though it speaks without explaining itself; (3) the floor statement, [speaker and citation], variable and here lowest, unless the speaker was a sponsor or floor manager, in which case it may climb past the bill version, and with the check the self-check required: whether the statement was actually spoken on the floor or merely inserted into the Record, because an inserted statement carries reduced weight. One sentence each; and if your order differed, the sentences are where the disagreement becomes visible and fixable.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Three passing entries, compressed to their load-bearing fields: (1) 29 C.F.R. Part 1605, the framework itself; Findings open with the authority level: binding regulation, promulgated with the force of law. (2) The EEOC guidance document you located [the compliance-manual section or enforcement guidance on religious discrimination, cited as the agency publishes it]; Findings open: persuasive guidance, influential in enforcement, weighed under Skidmore in proportion to its thoroughness, not binding on anyone. (3) The adjudication decision [a decision applying the framework to facts, located through the agency’s decisions database, or the substitute agency’s decision your instructor designated, logged identically]; Findings open: binding within the agency’s own process, subject to judicial review, and the most detailed application of the framework available. The pass condition is the opening of the Findings field, with the authority level stated and unhedged on all three, because the entry with no authority level is the entry that later walks into an outline dressed as the rule.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing run, on the term the regulation genuinely leaves open: the term, [for instance, what accommodation is “reasonable,” or when hardship becomes “undue”]; the practical definition, [what the agency’s materials say the term requires in operation, with the source cited, and note that research here would also surface whether courts have recently reshaped the standard, which the agency’s materials may lag]; the product that answered, [the compliance manual, an opinion letter, or an adjudication], with the mapping sentence: a what-does-this-mean-in-operation question pointed at interpretive guidance, exactly as this chapter’s question-to-product mapping said it would. The self-check’s trap door: if the CFR text itself answered you, the term was not vague enough, and the drill only works where the regulation runs out, because that running-out is the entry point to this whole chapter.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing note, form modeled, findings bracketed: “Courts addressing [the guidance document] have [cited it under Skidmore for persuasive weight / declined to follow it on the ground that it exceeds the regulation / not addressed it, per the searches listed]. Searches: [citator run on the document where supported; terms-and-connectors search pairing the document’s name with the regulation, database, date].” The standard the self-check set: a reader should be able to place the document on the correct side of the line between legally required and the agency’s preference without reading anything else, and after Loper Bright the placement carries more consequence, because the agency’s own view of its statute no longer settles the question for a court.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: The rebuilt table, from the opinion’s own account [supply pincites from your reading]: Failure one, counsel relied on an older decision without conducting research beyond it; rule, the duty of competence, Rule 1.1, which demands the current, controlling answer; preventing step, the citator update in the closing-out protocol, which exists to catch law that has moved. Failure two, counsel did not reread the cases cited in the most recent controlling appellate decision on the issue; rule, again 1.1, competence in reading and synthesizing, not just locating; preventing step, the read-before-you-cite check, because an unread case is an unverified claim. Where your table and the chapter’s differ, apply the exercise’s own diagnostic: a failure you caught that the chapter’s table generalized over is good reading; a failure you attributed that the opinion does not support is the autopsy catching you , which is the more valuable lesson of the two.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing entry, modeled on the store-duty drill: Research Question: what controlling authority in our state cuts against the conclusion that the store owed no duty [or owed a duty, whichever your chain reached]? Question Type: Focusing, adversarial posture. Method: [database], with the searches listed as run, including the terms aimed at the opposite conclusion, not just your own conclusion restated. Findings: [the adverse authorities located, or “none located,” in which case the empty result stands]. Source Consulted: [citations for any adverse authority located]. Both outcomes pass, with one condition: the searches appear in the entry. An empty result logged with its searches is Rule 3.3 compliance in miniature; an empty log is the thing the rule refuses to accept.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Three sample lines showing the form; a full log has one line per source: Hazelwood Sch. Dist. v. Kuhlmeier , 484 U.S. 260 (1988) | verified in [database] | citator: [status and any flags, with the flagged points checked against the propositions you cite it for] | [date]. [Your state’s statute] | current text confirmed against [the official code], through-date [recorded] | pending amendments: [checked] | [date]. [The regulation] | eCFR, current through [date shown] | citator: [status] | [date]. Every line carries a status and a date, because the log’s professional function, the one Rules 5.1 and 5.3 give it, depends on a reviewer being able to see not just that you checked but when.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Entry numbers vary by case, and the case must be recent enough to live in the electronic filing era, which is why the exercise says so; a passing answer’s standard is the recognition method: Complaint, [entry number], recognized as the earliest substantive filing, plaintiff as filer, labeled as a complaint or petition. Dispositive motion and brief, [entry number], recognized by the motion’s label (to dismiss, for summary judgment), the filer, and the supporting memorandum docketed with or beside it. Resolving order, [entry number], recognized as a court-entered document, after briefing concluded, whose text line disposes of the motion. One line each on the recognition, and, where the docket text alone failed you and a document had to be opened, that failure noted, because on a metered system each open is money, and the log-reading skill is the skill of not paying for what the log already says.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: For whichever brief you located, the three harvested authorities: [as cited in the brief, full citations]. The verification entry on the one you chose: The brief’s claim, quoted or pincited as the brief made it: [the brief’s characterization]. The source’s own words, quoted or pincited from your reading of the primary authority: [what it actually says]. Verdict: [supported; supported but overstated; or unsupported], with one sentence on the gap if there is one. The pass condition is structural: both sides on the page. A verdict without the brief’s language and the source’s language is an impression, and an impression about a characterization is how the error you are checking for reproduces itself.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing ladder for whichever district you chose, numbers bracketed because they are the exercise: Rung one, the governing Federal Rule, and note that for many filing mechanics the federal rule is silent on the number you went looking for; silence recorded is a finding, because it tells you which rung actually supplies the rule. Rung two, the district’s local rule, [cited], supplying [the page or word limit], found on the court’s website. Rung three, the assigned judge’s standing order, [cited or “none”], and where one exists it typically tightens or adds: [the delta]. The self-check’s test is the delta: if two rungs say the same thing, reread, because local rules and standing orders exist to add or tighten, and the delta is what a filer gets sanctioned for missing. Where the judge has no standing order on the point, “none” recorded is a passing third rung; an empty rung known is knowledge.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing page, draftable from the printed scenario and this chapter’s parameters alone. Litigation (the neighbor has sued): Q1, what causes of action govern a complaint about drone flights over neighboring property in [State]? (exploratory shading into focusing); Q2, what are the elements of [the claim the complaint pleads]? (focusing); Q3, how do our client’s flight facts, altitude, frequency, camera use, compare to the decided cases? (application). First source: case law. Closure: controlling authority per issue, adverse authority identified, procedural requirements confirmed. Transactional (the business is being sold): Q1, what licenses or authorizations does this operation depend on? (focusing); Q2, what consents or approvals does transferring the operation require? (focusing); Q3, what compliance representations are market for a deal of this kind? (focusing, market flavor). First source: statutes, regulations, and form and practice materials. Closure: all requirements and risks identified, diligence complete. Compliance (the audit): Q1, what body of law governs operating a camera drone commercially? (exploratory shading into focusing); Q2, what state and local rules add obligations on top? (focusing, survey flavor); Q3, what do recent enforcement actions show the regulator actually prioritizes? (application, enforcement flavor). First source: the CFR and agency guidance. Closure: all obligations mapped, pending rulemaking checked. Nine questions, no two postures alike, and the page shows what the chapter argued: same facts, different parameters, because the posture sets them.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: The form of a passing pair, on an unfamiliar context [illustrative]: Cold: “Default question type: focusing, since the area feels statute-driven. Where I start: the governing federal statute. What tells me I am done: every requirement for the client’s situation identified.” Checked, after fifteen minutes in a secondary source: “Revised: the area runs on a statute plus a dense agency layer of regulations and manuals, so the starting source is the secondary source’s map of that layer, not the bare statute; the closure criterion gains a piece, because [the area’s procedural posture] adds application questions the cold guess missed. What the check changed: [named specifically].” The honesty test is the last line. A check that changed nothing means either a remarkably good guess or a remarkably thin check, and the exercise asked you to say which.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Results vary by tool and by month, which is itself the finding to internalize, so the sample models the record, with illustrative verdicts shaped like the chapter’s own demonstration: Exploratory prompt [as put], verdict: [confirmed; the orientation and the authorities it named checked out against the primary sources, listed]. Focusing prompt [as put], verdict: [confirmed with a gap; the standard was stated accurately, but the response could not reliably catalogue the cases applying it]. Application prompt [as put], verdict: [partially confirmed or fabricated; the list mixed responsive authorities with plausibly related but off-point ones, and the verification record names which]. Behind each verdict, the record: every citation traced to a primary source read, or marked unfindable, which for a citation means fabricated until proven otherwise. And the self-check’s push holds: three clean confirmations means the prompts were easier than your drill. Tighten the application prompt until the tool has to reach, because watching where it reaches, and what it grabs when it does, is the lesson this exercise exists to deliver.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Two passing sentences, illustrative: [The mega-prompt answer makes dozens of discrete legal claims woven into a single narrative, and verifying it means separating every claim back out and tracing each to a source, which is the decomposition work the small questions had already done for free. A set of small, single-question answers makes one checkable claim apiece, each verifiable against one or two primary sources in minutes.] The self-check’s boundary matters: the sentences are about verifiability, not quality. The sprawling answer may read beautifully; fluency was never the problem, and the exercise is designed to make you feel the difference between an answer that reads well and an answer you can check.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing note can be one line: “[The application prompt]: verifying the case list required running my own search anyway, so the tool added a verification burden without saving research time; wrong instrument for this question type.” That line is the signal the chapter told you to watch for, recorded where your future self will find it. And the closing discipline stands regardless of what the note says: nothing enters the outline unverified, because an answer you cannot trace to a source you have read is not an answer. It is a guess wearing a citation.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
s: Exercise 16.1 — The Clocked Cycle and the Five-Skill Audit
t: Step one, the skeleton of a passing clocked answer, modeled on the store-duty drill’s closed universe: Macro question, stated: is the store liable to the customer for the parking-lot assault? Broken into its research questions: did the store owe a duty; if so, what standard; was it breached; [the remaining elements named]. The provided authorities ranked: [your state’s highest-court decision] controls; [intermediate appellate decisions] bind subject to it; [out-of-state decisions in the set] persuade only. The ambiguity named: the duty question turns on [the point the provided authorities contest, for instance what makes third-party crime foreseeable enough to ground a duty]. Applied: [the controlling rule run on the scenario’s facts, with the analogous and distinguishable cases used as comparators]. The sufficiency call, committed: “the provided materials answer the duty question; they do not address [the named element], which is the gap, and [what would fill it] is the missing piece.” The call is present and unhedged; “probably enough” is not a call. Step two, the marks, placed on that skeleton: ambiguity spotting, at the named foreseeability point; source ranking, in the ordered list; dispositive fact identification, inside the application, where the scenario’s facts met the comparator cases’ facts; gap identification, in the named missing element; closure, in the committed sufficiency call. Every mark points at a sentence that exists in the answer, and the honest alternative also passes: “I cannot place the dispositive-facts mark” is a finding and next week’s assignment, because the audit’s function is converting a skipped skill from an invisible habit into a visible target.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
s: Exercise 16.2 — Break It Down, No Searching
t: A passing ten-minute breakdown, entirely from the provided list. Macro question: does the client’s termination for refusing Sunday work violate the state’s employment-discrimination statute? The research questions, each matched to its material: what does the statute prohibit, and does it reach religious practice? — the statute itself. What standard have the state’s courts applied under it, and what have employers been required to do? — the two intermediate appellate decisions. How do her facts compare to the decided applications? — the same two decisions, read for their facts. What have other jurisdictions done where the home authorities run out? — the neighboring state’s decision. What is the scholarly account of the area, useful for orientation and pathways but never for the rule? — the article. The ranking for the state’s trial court: the statute, binding law to be applied; the two intermediate appellate decisions, binding as decisions of a higher court in the same system; the neighboring state’s supreme court decision, persuasive; the law review article, secondary and persuasive, at the bottom. If either of the bottom two surfaced as the answer to a controlling-rule question, the hierarchy of authority needs the reread the self-check prescribed, because on the exam that misranking is the whole wrong answer.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: Five sample entries in the passing form, each a question a text left open, each with its provenance; treat the substantive claims as leads to confirm, exactly as you would your own: (1) From the Chapter 5 work: does the school-sponsored-speech standard govern student media at public colleges and universities, a question on which authorities divide [confirm the current state of the division]? Found: flagged in the secondary reading around the case. (2) From Chapter 11 : how much persuasive weight does informal agency guidance retain now that courts interpret statutes without deferring to agencies, a boundary the overruling decision left open? Found: the open edge this book’s own Chapter 11 discussion walks up to. (3) From the drone capstone: how do the traditional property and privacy doctrines the capstone surfaced apply to systematic aerial observation from navigable airspace [confirm what remains unresolved]? Found: the state-law overlay the capstone’s walkthrough marks as residual. (4) From Chapter 6 : when a strict consent statute meets an interstate call, whose law governs the recording, a question the single-state drill deliberately walled off? Found: the drill’s own boundary, noted in my log. (5) From Chapter 15 : courts and bars are still building disclosure and verification rules for AI-assisted filings; which approaches are emerging, and what should the rule be? Found: the chapter’s own observation that the rules are developing. What all five share, and what “AI and copyright” lacks, is a source that left the question open and a question shape a thesis could answer.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: A passing record, on candidate two [illustrative]: Searches run, with the distinctive terms of the claim rather than the topic: [the deference doctrine’s name paired with the overruling case and “guidance,” across HeinOnline, Westlaw or Lexis, SSRN, and Google Scholar, each logged with date]. Nearest neighbors: [the closest three pieces, by title and abstract, with one line each on what they argue]. Verdict, committed: [“needs differentiating: the closest article addresses the question for one agency context; my claim is the general framework,” or whichever verdict the abstracts force]. The hour honored, and the exercise’s consolation standing by: a preempted verdict is a celebration in disguise. The check just saved you a semester, and the inventory holds four more.

p: Appendix H: Sample Answers for the Reviewing Through Practice Exercises
t: The five passing lines, on the surviving candidate [illustrative]: I. Framework: what role did agency guidance play in statutory interpretation before the change, and under what doctrine? II. Problem: what has the overruling decision unsettled about the weight courts owe that guidance now? III. Critique: why do the emerging lower-court answers fail to give regulated parties, agencies, or courts a workable rule? IV. Proposal: what framework should govern the persuasive weight of agency guidance, and why would it serve all three audiences better? Plus the interdisciplinary line: the public administration and political science literature on agency expertise and its institutional value, which lives in JSTOR’s political science journals and Public Administration Review . Each heading is answerable, which means each section can be finished, and finished sections are the whole trick. A subject area is a shelf. This is a paper, started.

p: Appendix I: Reflection Point Sample Answers
s: Appendix I: Reflection Point Sample Answers
t: The Reflection Points scattered through the chapters are meant to be sat with before they are checked; the thinking is the exercise, and these answers are deliberately short. Each is one defensible way to put the point, not the only way. They are keyed by chapter and location. Chapter 1 — after Binding vs. Persuasive Authority. When would a persuasive decision be worth more to your client than a binding one? When your jurisdiction has not answered the question. Where binding law is silent or unsettled, the persuasive trend is the best available evidence of where your court will land, which is often the answer the client actually needs. Chapter 2 — after Practical Search Strategy. Why does the method have you draft the research question before you choose a database or a search syntax? Because the question’s type is what tells you which source, and therefore which database and which search, fits. Start from the database instead and you will quietly reshape the question into whatever that tool answers well. Chapter 3 — after The Types in Motion. A botanist, a chef, and the Tariff Act of 1883 each answer “is a tomato a fruit?” differently. What does that tell you about where a legal definition’s authority comes from? A definition is authoritative only for a purpose, and legal meaning takes its purpose from the enacting scheme, or, where the scheme is silent, from the rule courts use to fill the gap. Expertise about the thing defined is not authority about the word’s legal meaning. Chapter 3 — after Common Pitfalls. How might the research have been affected if the researcher had jumped straight to reading Hazelwood* before reading Tinker and Fraser ?* The researcher would have met the governing rule without the baseline it modifies. Hazelwood distinguishes Tinker and builds on Fraser ’s premise that student rights are not coextensive with adults’ rights, so reading it first means taking the exception before the rule. “School-sponsored” and “legitimate pedagogical concerns” would have arrived as vocabulary with nothing to push against, and the researcher might not have known which sub-questions to ask. The map set the order, not the researcher’s sense of which case mattered most. Chapter 4 — after Questions This Source Answers. If secondary sources answer exploratory questions this well, why does Chapter 3 ’s demonstration stop consulting them after its first question? Because they point rather than bind: once the landscape is mapped, authority has to come from the primary sources themselves. The demonstration uses the encyclopedia for the map and the opinions for every answer, which is the division of labor this chapter teaches. Chapter 5 — after Questions This Source Answers. Why might a case be a poor source for answering exploratory questions, especially no-clue questions? An opinion answers the dispute in front of it, in the parties’ vocabulary, and assumes the doctrinal context rather than mapping it. A researcher who does not yet have the terms or the landscape cannot even find the right case, let alone learn the area from one. Chapter 6 — after Questions This Source Answers. Why might a statute be a poor source for answering a no-clue exploratory question, even when the area turns out to be statutory? You cannot look up a provision without the vocabulary the code files it under, and a no-clue researcher does not yet have the terms of art, or even know whether the answer lives in a statute at all rather than in common law. And a located section states its rule bare, without the context or interpretation that makes the landscape legible. Chapter 7 — after Questions This Source Answers. Why might a regulation be a poor source for answering a no-clue exploratory question, even in a heavily regulated area? Regulations sit downstream: you find them through the statute that authorized them and the agency that wrote them, both of which a no-clue researcher has not yet identified. They are also the most granular layer, drafted for pa

p: Glossary
t: Every term the book defines, in one place. Flip through the terms as flashcards, or filter the full list beneath them. In the chapters, a dotted underline marks the spot where each term is first defined. Flashcards Every defined term administrative adjudication An agency’s own dispute-resolution process: an administrative law judge hears the case, with appeal to the agency head and then to federal court; published decisions may serve as precedent within the agency and are often the most detailed interpretations of a regulation available. (Chapter 11 ) ALR annotation An article in American Law Reports collecting and analyzing the case law of many jurisdictions on a narrow legal issue; a primary tool for survey questions. (Chapter 4 ) ambiguity spotting (Skill 1) Reading a legal text and identifying the terms, phrases, or provisions whose meaning requires interpretive research — undefined terms, vague standards, terms of art, structural ambiguities, scope questions. (Chapter 16 ) analytical closure The judgment that research is complete because every question has been answered or identified as genuinely open, the rule and its application are covered, and further research would only refine wording. (Chapter 3 ) annotated code A statutory code enhanced with editorial notes: case annotations, cross-references to regulations and secondary sources, and history notes. (Chapter 5 ) annotated outline The running document that records the product of research: each question’s synthesized answer, organized under the structure the final document will take. (Chapter 3 ) application question A question asking how a rule operates on specific facts, answered by locating cases with similar facts (fact-finding) or by building the rule from multiple sources when nothing is on point (constructive application). (Chapter 3 ) authority note The note accompanying a CFR part that cites the statute empowering the agency to issue it. (Chapter 7 ) binding authority Law a court must follow: the constitution, statutes, and regulations of its own jurisdiction, the decisions of higher courts in its own system, and federal law applicable within it. (Chapter 1 ) candor to the tribunal (Rule 3.3) The duty not to knowingly misstate the law to a court, and to disclose controlling authority directly adverse to the client’s position when opposing counsel has not. (Chapter 12 ) canons of construction Established interpretive principles courts use to read ambiguous statutory text, such as the plain meaning rule, expressio unius, ejusdem generis, and the rule against surplusage. (Chapter 6 ) citator A tool (KeyCite or Shepard’s) that tracks an authority’s subsequent history and treatment, showing whether it remains good law. (Chapter 5 ) closed universe The provided-materials exam format: a fixed set of sources over which you run a compressed Question Method cycle — nothing outside the set may be relied on. (Chapter 16 ) closing-out protocol The systematic end-of-project sequence: run a final sweep, update every case and statute, check the currency of secondary sources, evaluate the outline for gaps, and document the closure decision. (Chapter 9 ) code Statutes arranged by subject as currently amended, in an official or annotated compilation. (Chapter 1 ) committee report The report accompanying a bill out of committee; generally the most authoritative legislative history document. (Chapter 10 ) common law Judge-made law developed case by case through judicial decision. (Chapter 1 ) competence (Rule 1.1) The duty to bring the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation the matter requires — making research quality itself an ethical obligation; Comment 8 extends it to understanding the benefits and risks of technology. (Chapter 12 ) constructive application Answering an application question no decision squarely addresses by building the rule from the cases that exist and reasoning by analogy. (Chapter 3 ) definitional question A question asking what a word or p
